## Phase 149 (2026-07-25 — the Tier-0 round coverage ledger; a round that reviewed ~1% stops reading as a full scan)

**Why this phase.** The Codex evaluation's Q5 scale run, verified maintainer-side against the raw JSONL. Two ordinary requests — `review this codebase` and `run a security audit` — ran against a localized 1,561-file install of the leg-5 dogfood target on a persistent surface where fan-out demonstrably works: the same evaluation's Q2 run dispatched three addressed workers, each returning an evidence footer (2/2, 14/14, 15/15 files opened), merged into 15 tasks with correct provenance. Q5 dispatched nothing. **Zero `collab_tool_call` events in either transcript** (re-counted here: `q2-persistent.jsonl` 8, both Q5 logs 0). The security run narrated the step it then skipped — *"the project-specific overlay maps are localized for [the target]; I'll use those as the authoritative **dispatch map**"* — and audited solo. Explicit body coverage came to **13 and 27 files opened, ~0.8% and ~1.7%**, while the runs reported 1,477 "reviewable" and 955 "to audit" — dispatch-set sizes, not opened counts.

**Why nothing caught it.** Phase 138 scoped the Tier-2 evidence footer to fan-out runs deliberately, because a solo session emitting an `Assigned`/`Opened` worker footer would be fabricating a worker that never existed. That reasoning still holds and was not touched here. Its consequence is that a round which *should* have dispatched and didn't produces exactly the artifact a legitimately-solo round produces — and every finding came out `[verified]`, correctly, since the solo agent did open the sites it cited. **A collapsed round therefore produces a *better*-looking provenance split than an honest fan-out round**, where merge discipline forces `[reported]` defaults. That inversion is the tell.

**The reframe that set the design: the defect is not "fan-out didn't fire."** Fan-out is a means. Phase 138 measured coverage *inside* the dispatch path, so a round that never dispatches is never measured at all — and coverage can collapse three ways (dispatch skipped, harness has no sub-agent primitive, a "full" scan that was really a sample), only one of which is about dispatch. So the measure belongs at the **round** level. This is the Phase 135/141/143 thesis one layer up: an un-run check must be `failed`, not silent; a dead round must be loud; **a file nobody opened is not a reviewed file**.

**Three things in the logs changed the design, and two of them falsify the obvious fixes.**

1. **The skill body was read in full.** Both Q5 runs `sed`-ed the entire 894/938 lines in their first three commands (`1,240p`, `241,520p`, `521,900p`, then a re-read of `400,700p`). The agent read Step 3's dispatch table, the sub-agent return contract and the merge discipline, then reviewed solo anyway. **Any fix whose mechanism is "say it more emphatically at Step 3" is already disproven.** Step 3-0 below is still prose, and is not where the work happens: the mechanism that actually changed is two steps later — a *form field* in the round-header template, which is filled rather than composed, and a receipt derived from what was filled. Stated plainly because the distinction is the whole lesson: 3-0 sets the rule, 5b and 5f are what make ignoring it visible.
2. **The marker bash bookends ran faithfully on a non-Claude harness.** Both runs executed the Phase-143 pre-flight heredoc verbatim *and* the 5f clear step; the security run even appended `test ! -e …pending && echo 'round-marker: absent'` to self-verify. The one part of these skills that reliably executes as written is the bash bookend — which is what made the receipt the right place for the durable copy.
3. **The durable artifact already carried an improvised, misleading coverage claim.** `5b`'s round-header template was a bare heading, so the quality run *invented* `> **Scan:** Full, all scopes — 1,477 reviewable tracked files.` while the security run wrote no scan line at all. The committed record was both inconsistent and, in the quality case, actively false. The template now supplies the line, so the model is filling a form rather than improvising a claim.

**What shipped — `_shared/fanout-evidence.md` § Tier 0, plus three skills and two readers.**

- **Tier 0 — the round coverage ledger (universal, every round, fan-out or solo).** Five fields in one greppable line: `Coverage: <kind> · manifest <N> · opened <M> · grepped <G> · workers <K><, solo: reason>`. **Kind** is what the round *actually was* (`Full` / `Scoped (<area>)` / `Sampled (<basis>)`) — the relabel is the cheapest honesty the tier buys. **Manifest** is the round's own declared scope after exclusions, never the repository total, or every honest incremental round would read as a collapse. **Opened** is bodies read, the same strict meaning as the footer's `Opened`. **Grepped** is counted separately and never folded in — grep is legitimate looking (Tier 2 says so) but it is not a read, and merging the two is how a sparse pass inflates itself. **Workers `0` means solo, and solo is a declared decision with a stated reason**, never a silent default.
- **The hard constraint, restated at the site where it would erode.** Tier 2 now says in its own section that a run which does not fan out writes no footer, that this is deliberate and not a gap, and — literally — *"Do not 'fix' a silent solo round by making this footer fire on it."* Tier 0 borrows Tier 2's **measure** and none of its **artifact**. A drift guard pins that sentence.
- **`### 3-0. Dispatch decision (STATE IT)`** in both review skills, ahead of convention scoping. Dispatch is the default whenever the scope exceeds one context; solo is legitimate in exactly two stated cases (no sub-agent primitive, or a scope small enough to open in full) and *"'I'll just review it myself' on a scope you cannot read is case (c) — and case (c) does not exist."* Critically: **a solo run on a scope it cannot open in full produces a `Sampled` round, not a `Full` one.** `/security-audit` carries the extra clause that a solo audit still owes every OWASP category its pass, and names any category it did not reach.
- **The ledger lands in the durable artifact first** — the `review_tasks.md` round header (committed; read by `/review-close`, `/auto-fix`, `/sitrep`, the next reviewer), then the printed summary, then the receipt. A printed summary dies with the terminal. Same-day merged rounds carry **one coverage line per audit type**; neither may edit the other's.
- **`Files scanned: <N>` / `Files audited: <N>` are gone.** That field is what taught the run to launder a dispatch-set size into an apparent coverage claim, and a drift guard now forbids its bare form. The replacement states in-line that `manifest` is the one number in the ledger that is *not* a coverage claim and means nothing except beside `opened`.
- **The round receipt.** 5f's marker-clear step **reads the coverage line back out of the round header just written** and writes `sysop/runtime/round-receipts/<skill>.<nonce>.json` before unlinking. It is deliberately *not* passed in as an argument: model-authored prose interpolated into a shell argument is a command-substitution hazard (the class `/report-issues` Step 4 and `/share-wins` already fixed), and reading the committed artifact makes receipt-and-header agreement **structural** rather than an instruction the model has to remember. The parse is per-segment and whole-token, because the alternative failure is the dangerous one: a scan-anywhere regex lets a sampling basis like `Sampled (opened 3 entrypoints)` hijack `opened`, and a loose numeric class reads `manifest 1.477` as `1` — a shrunken denominator that *silences* the look-ratio check while the human-facing line still reads correctly. It is written **only on the successful clear path**: a receipt asserts "a round closed here", and the marker's existence is what proves the round-open gitignore check already passed, so a disarmed install writes neither. Every failure inside it is swallowed — evidence must never cost the cleanup it rides on — and a missing ledger records `unreported`, which is a loud value, not silence. History is bounded at the newest 50.
- **One counted number, as the anchor under `manifest`.** Every other figure in the ledger is the round's own claim, and shrinking the denominator is the one way to make a thin round look complete with no visible tell. So the receipt writer runs `git ls-files` itself and records **`tracked`** — the only fact in the receipt the round does not author. It is a raw tracked-file count, deliberately *not* scope- or exclusion-aware: `manifest < tracked` is normal and is not a defect. It is **displayed, never gated** — a `Scoped` round legitimately speaks for a fraction of the repository, and so does a `Full` round with real exclusions, so flagging on the gap would fire on the honest case. `self_check.sh` prints it beside the coverage line; `/sitrep` folds it into the details of discrepancies it already raises, because `/sitrep` reports problems and a narrow manifest is not one. The effect is the phase's own trick one level up: `opened 13 · manifest 15 · tracked 1,561` puts the shrink on the page.

- **Two readers, one for each install mode.** `/sitrep` gains `_round_coverage_discrepancies()`; `self_check.sh` prints the last round's line, which matters because **loop mode ships no `/sitrep`** and this is the only surface where a loop consumer sees a collapsed round.
- **`/test-audit` gets the ledger and explicitly no receipt.** Its base path is solo by design, so `workers 0, solo: single-agent base path` is the *normal, correct* value there — a useful demonstration that `workers 0` is not inherently a defect. It opens no round and closes none, so there is nothing for a receipt to attest; the skill says so, to stop a future author from adding a marker lifecycle to make the receipt fire and thereby reporting a round that never existed — the mirror of the fabricated-footer mistake.

**Every reader check is a self-contradiction, never a quality bar.** A `Sampled` or `Scoped` round is exempt by construction; an incremental round's manifest is its own small scope. What gets reported is a round whose numbers refute its own label (`Full` while reaching under a third of its declared scope), a `Full` round that ran solo with no reason recorded, or a round that closed with no numbers at all. **The one-third constant is not new** — it is Tier 2's existing `opened + grepped < ~⅓ of assigned` applied one level up, so the batch-level and round-level measures share one vocabulary rather than inventing a second threshold. A *numeric quality* threshold beyond this self-contradiction check is deliberately deferred: the natural ratio distribution for legitimate rounds is unknown, and the receipts are what will produce the data to set one non-arbitrarily.

**The ledger has to survive archival, which it did not at first.** `archive_review_tasks.py` collected a round as a header line plus its batches, and removed the round's whole line range from `review_tasks.md`. The coverage line sits in the gap between the two — so at the 125 KB rotation it was deleted from the live file and never written to the archive, leaving the "durable" copy nowhere (the receipt is gitignored and pruned at 50). The archiver now captures round-level blockquotes as a `preamble` and re-emits them outside the `<details>` fold, gated on the round actually leaving the live file so a partially-merged round doesn't carry its ledger in two places. Found by adversarial review, not by the suite.

**Gate.** +66 tests (1358 → 1424 collected).  `tests/test_round_coverage_ledger.py` executes the shipped 5f heredoc extracted from the SKILL.md prose (the `test_round_markers.py` pattern), so the thing under test is the thing that ships, and asserts the two copies are byte-identical. **50 mutations, all killed.**

**The adversarial round is where this phase actually got built.** Three independent fresh-context reviewers (mechanics / can-the-bug-recur / downstream-integration) found seven defects the green suite did not, four of them in the *evidence path itself* — a fix that silences the alarm it installs is worse than no fix, so they are recorded individually:

- **The coverage line was passed to 5f as a shell argument.** It is model-authored prose in double quotes: backticks and `$(…)` executed, an embedded `"` re-split the arguments, and a `;` or `&` in a solo reason would split the command so the tail matched no allow-rule — a silent deny under auto mode, stranding the marker *and* losing the receipt. Sysop had already fixed this class twice (`/report-issues` `--body-file`, `/share-wins` `-F body=@file`). Fixed by removing the argument entirely: 5f now **reads the line back out of the round header**, which also upgrades receipt-and-header agreement from an instruction to a structural property.
- **The parser truncated silently.** `manifest 1.477` and `manifest 1 477` — ordinary thousands separators — parsed as `1`, and a manifest of 1 makes the look-ratio pass trivially. Worse, the whole-line regex took the *first* match, so a sampling basis (free text the author is told to write) hijacked the field: `Sampled (opened 3 entrypoints)` reported `opened 3` over the real 600. Both directions produce a confidently **wrong** number that silences the check, which is strictly worse than `unreported`. Now parsed per `·` segment with `re.fullmatch`, and `kind` read from the first segment only, so an unfilled template no longer asserts `Full`.
- **The archiver destroyed the durable copy.** `archive_review_tasks.py` collected a round as its header plus its batches while removing the round's whole line range — and the ledger sits in the gap. At the 125 KB rotation it was deleted from `review_tasks.md` and never written to the archive, leaving the "durable" record nowhere (the receipt is gitignored and pruned at 50). Round-level blockquotes are now captured as a `preamble` and re-emitted, gated on the round actually leaving the live file.
- **`docs/loop-mode.md` promised a check that did not exist.** It told loop consumers `self_check.sh` calls out a Full round reaching under a third of its scope; the ⅓ comparison lived only in `/sitrep`, which **loop mode does not ship**. Since loop mode is the entire justification for touching `self_check.sh`, the comparison was implemented there rather than the promise withdrawn — and a drift guard now fails if doc and script disagree.
- Three lower: `/sitrep` raised `TypeError` on a well-formed receipt with a wrong-typed field and took the *whole survey* down with it (the sentinel check established "not `unreported`", never `int`); `Sampled`/`Scoped` exempted a round from the *missing-solo-reason* check as well as the ratio, making "always claim Sampled" a free escape (the reason check is a missing-field check and now sits outside that gate, and a narrowed round must name its basis); and `skill`, read from the marker body, built a receipt filename unsanitized — `../../../PWNED` escaped the gitignored runtime dir.

**Two defects were self-found before review** — `self_check.sh` picked the "newest" receipt by lexical filename sort, but receipts are `<skill>.<epoch>-<pid>.json`, so the skill name dominated and `security-audit.*` beat a *newer* `codebase-review.*`, reporting a stale round as current; and `json.dumps` defaults to `ensure_ascii=True`, which escaped the ledger's `·` so `self_check.sh` would print the escape raw. The second survived the first mutation pass because every assertion went through `json.loads` (which decodes it back) and the `self_check` fixtures wrote their own JSON — pinned now by a test that runs the real writer and greps the real bytes.

**Honest note on one guard:** atomicity cannot be observed from outside a completed write, so the tempfile + `os.replace` convention is pinned at the *source*, both halves — keeping `os.replace` while aiming `tmp` at the destination is a silent no-op that leaves no stray file for a behavioural check to catch.

**What this does not do, stated plainly.** It does not make dispatch happen — no portable mechanism can, and forcing it on a harness without a sub-agent primitive would be worse than an honest solo round. It does not detect a fabricated `opened`: there is no per-file read telemetry, which is Phase 138's own honest limit and applies unchanged. **The denominator is a weaker limit than the numerator, and saying otherwise would be the overclaim** — `manifest` is derivable, so it is anchored two ways rather than one. By instruction: both skills say the Step 1 `Files:` count *is* the manifest, that it is a scope size and not a coverage claim, and that a scope narrowing later is declared `Scoped`/`Sampled` with a basis rather than by quietly shrinking the denominator. And by measurement: the receipt's `tracked` is counted at close, so a shrunken manifest is now *visible* beside the repository it declined to speak for. What remains open, stated exactly: a round can still declare `Sampled (…)` with a small manifest and a real basis, and nothing objects — correctly, since that is the behaviour the ledger asks for. `tracked` makes that round's reach legible; it does not adjudicate it, and no mechanical check should, because the honest case and the evasive one produce the same numbers and differ only in the basis. Likewise `grepped`: the spec now excludes the Step 2b deterministic sweep from it (that sweep has its own accounting line), because a round counting it could truthfully write `grepped ≈ manifest` and retire the look-ratio permanently — an honest number defeating the check is the most dangerous kind, and only the definition holds it. What the phase does buy is that the counts must now **exist and sit beside each other**, where `opened 13 · manifest 1,477` refutes itself on sight.

**Close-out.** Inline (meta-repo convention). Docs: `WORKFLOW.md` § 4.2 gains the coverage line in the Round structure block plus a "Round metadata" paragraph stating the denominator rule; `docs/loop-mode.md` gains "ran, but barely" as a third refusal shape beside died-partway and refused-before-starting. `install.sh`'s runtime-dir comment lists `pending-rounds/` and `round-receipts/`; both are already covered by the single `sysop/runtime/` gitignore entry, so no new ignore rule and no new permission surface — the receipt rides the existing `Bash(python3 -:*)` rule the marker already uses.

## Phase 150 (2026-07-26 — the claim path stops disarming the consumer's hooks)

**Why this phase.** First and highest-blast-radius of the five GDP inbound entries (upstream #202). `claim_task.sh:351` and `batch_work.sh:290` ran `install_hooks.sh` on every worktree creation. Worktrees share one hooks directory — `$GIT_COMMON_DIR/hooks` — so from inside a new worktree that call resolved to the **main checkout's** hooks and copied the shipped skeletons over whatever the consumer had armed. For GDP it would have silently dropped 7 blocking checks (f-string SQL, raw exception in API responses and in logs, `_sanitize_log` misuse, inline `AbortError`, tasks-schema validation, skill model pins) and 15 advisory ones. Caught by human inspection at `/review-close`, not by anything in the tooling.

**Two properties kept it quiet,** both named by the reporter: `install_hooks.sh`'s `⚠️ Backed up pre-existing customized hooks` warning scrolls past inside `claim_task.sh`'s much longer output, and the failure is silent-permissive — nothing breaks, checks just stop running. This is the Phase 135/141/143/149 thesis one layer down: **a disarmed gate looks exactly like a passing one.** Phase 24b offers no cover either — it preserves consumer-*modified* `sysop/scripts/hooks/*`, and a consumer whose real hooks only ever lived in `.git/hooks/` has pristine skeleton templates, which is precisely what got armed.

**The call was exactly backwards, which is what makes removal complete rather than merely safe.** Dropping it is reporter fix 1, and the argument is stronger than "worktrees don't need it": *every* case where the call could still change something is a case where it must not. After a fresh install `install.sh` has already armed the hooks; under `--no-arm-hooks` the consumer opted out on purpose; during an `--update` reconcile window Phase 15 / ISSUE-0007 skips arming on purpose. There is no remaining state in which arming from a claim is the right move. Noted while removing it: `claim_task.sh`'s **clone** mode — the one workspace shape that genuinely gets its own `.git/hooks` — never armed at all. The auto-arm sat in the only place it could do harm and was absent from the only place it would have helped. (Filed as a Low item rather than fixed here; arming a fresh clone has the same clobber shape for a consumer whose real hooks aren't Sysop's.)

**Reporter fix 2 was rejected — though not for the reason first written down, which the adversarial pass caught as false.** The first draft argued that a hard stop on a divergent hook would break Phase 15 because "the armed copy **always** differs from the reconciled template." That is wrong. The documented reconcile is `git checkout HEAD -- sysop/scripts/hooks/…` (§ 8.2b step 6), which restores the template to the exact body the consumer previously armed — so `cmp -s` matches, no divergence arises, and this repo's own `test_no_backup_when_identical` asserts precisely that case. Divergence appears only in the *partial-accept* reconcile, where upstream changes are merged into a customized body.

The reasons that survive scrutiny: (i) **a hard stop treats the effect, not the cause.** It stops the clobber but leaves a call with no business on the claim path, now failing on every claim for any consumer with customized hooks — recurring noise inside `claim_task.sh`'s long output, which is exactly the channel the reporter identified as already being missed. Fix 1 removes the reason the call was wrong; fix 2 guards it. (ii) It would put `--force` in front of the partial-accept reconcile, adding friction to a documented path. (iii) For the one case left after fix 1 — a human running `install_hooks.sh` directly — backup-plus-warning is already the right ergonomics, because a human running it sees its output. That is the case the warning was designed for.

**Fix 3, `core.hooksPath`, turned out to be an existing internal inconsistency rather than a new design question.** `git rev-parse --git-path hooks` honors `core.hooksPath`; `$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/hooks` does not. `install.sh`'s `resolve_hook_dst` and `self_check.sh` already used the honoring spelling — `install_hooks.sh` was the lone holdout. Verified empirically both ways, including the reporter's claim that a *relative* `core.hooksPath` resolves against each worktree's own checkout (in a worktree, `--git-path hooks` returns bare `myhooks` with `--show-toplevel` pointing at the worktree). With no `core.hooksPath` set the two spellings are identical, so the swap is behavior-preserving where it doesn't matter and correct where it does.

**Which surfaced a second bug in the same family, worse than the one reported.** Because `resolve_hook_dst` *does* honor `core.hooksPath`, `arm_git_hooks` would `mkdir -p` and copy Sysop's skeletons straight into a consumer's configured hooks directory — which is typically **tracked in their tree**, that being the reason to set the config at all. #202 clobbers untracked `.git/hooks`; this clobbers files git tracks. All three sites now skip when the config is set: `install_hooks.sh` and `arm_git_hooks` refuse to write and say where git is actually reading plus the `cp` to adopt the templates by hand, and `check_armed_hooks_divergence` reports the arrangement instead of prescribing a re-arm that is now a deliberate no-op — the #205 lesson applied preemptively, that a gate a careful reader should knowingly ignore is mis-specified rather than merely noisy. **Skipped-not-failed** throughout: exit 0, no phantom install error. Sysop declines to write there rather than picking a winner, on the same trust-boundary reasoning as the Codex `config.toml` decision — sandbox and hook policy are the consumer's.

**The code bug was the expression of a documented false premise.** WORKFLOW.md said "Must be re-installed after creating a new worktree" (§ 4.3 bullet) and "after cloning the repo or creating a worktree" (§ 4.3 Installation) and "re-run after new worktree" (§ 8.4 table); WORKFLOW_GUIDE.md § 2 walked the reader through `cd ../<worktree> && bash sysop/scripts/install_hooks.sh` as a claim step. Fixing only the scripts would have left every one of those inviting a reader to re-create the damage by hand. A **fifth** site — `install_hooks.sh`'s own header comment, "Run this after cloning or creating a worktree" — survived the first pass and was caught by the adversarial review; it is the worst of the five, being the file a reader opens precisely when deciding to arm by hand. All five corrected, plus the § 8.2a permission-table note that described `claim_task.sh` shelling out, and both public-doc surfaces gained the `core.hooksPath` behavior.

**Verification.** Thirteen mutations across two rounds, all killed. Round one (pre-review, six): restore either auto-arm; drop either `core.hooksPath` skip; drop the divergence branch; revert the destination resolution. The last of those initially reported a false kill — the strengthened assertion was failing on unmutated code too, because the skip message legitimately names `.git/hooks` to say git is *not* reading there; re-scoped to the `cp` remedy line and re-run green-then-red. A fixture mishap worth recording as evidence: an `exit 1` sentinel hook blocked its own fixture's commit once `core.hooksPath` pointed at it — the config demonstrating itself. The reporter's literal three-step repro was run end-to-end: `shasum` of the consumer's armed `pre-commit` identical before and after `/claim-task`, worktree still created.

**The two-reviewer adversarial pass changed the phase substantially, and found two HIGHs the author's own mutation set could not.** Both reviewers independently landed on the same defect from different angles, which is the shape worth noting: a mutation set only tests the code paths the tests already exercise.

**HIGH 1 — the destination-resolution swap was a regression, not just a consistency fix.** `git rev-parse --git-path hooks` answers relative to the **current directory**, not the toplevel: from `src/api/` it returns `../../.git/hooks`. Anchoring that to `REPO_ROOT` resolves *outside* the repo — and in a repo nested one level inside another it lands in the **outer** repository's hooks, overwrites its armed `pre-commit`, and prints `✅ Installed` — reintroducing #202's exact defect by a new route, with a success message on top. Every test in the module ran from the repo root, where the anchoring is a no-op, so the whole `case` block could be deleted with the suite green. The two sibling resolvers avoid this by querying from the same root they anchor to; `self_check.sh:85` even documents the reason. Fixed by anchoring the probe with `-C "$REPO_ROOT"`, plus two tests that run the script from a subdirectory and from a nested repo.

**HIGH 2 — the flagship regression test was silently vacuous on the reporter's own machine.** `test_worktree_claim_does_not_rearm_the_main_repo_hooks` passes with the #202 bug **fully restored** on any machine carrying a global `core.hooksPath`: the restored auto-arm hits the new skip branch, writes nothing, and the sentinel survives. GDP — who reported #202 — runs exactly that configuration. The author had identified this hazard and fixed it one file over (`test_install_hooks_sh.py` gained `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null`) while missing it here, and in the worse direction: there the slip reddens the suite, here it goes green. Isolation added to `test_claim_task_sh.py`.

**Four more that mattered.** (i) The stated reason for rejecting fix 2 was false — see above. (ii) `core.hooksPath = ""` defeated the `-n` guard while `--git-path hooks` resolved to `./`, so an empty value would have dropped three executables into the root of the consumer's working tree and reported success; the guard is now key-set, not value-non-empty. (iii) A **global** `core.hooksPath` made Sysop skip machine-wide while advising a `cp` into a shared directory — which would apply one project's checks to every repo on the machine and let a second project silently overwrite the first; the advice is now scope-aware and offers nothing for global/system scope. (iv) `install.sh`'s remedy line mixed `rel "$TARGET"` (absolute) with `rel "$hook_dst"` (a literal `<target>` placeholder), producing a "command" that bash parses as a redirection; the path is gone from the message entirely.

**And three coverage gaps the pass exposed rather than fixed for us.** The `--dry-run`-predicts-the-skip ordering was asserted only in a comment; the `--update` path never learned about `core.hooksPath`, so it kept prescribing the Phase-15 re-arm whose remedy now deliberately no-ops; and `self_check.sh` — the designated backstop now that nothing arms automatically — told the reader to run a script that skips, while also claiming credit (`hook armed`) for hooks Sysop neither wrote nor compares. All three now have behavior and tests.

Round two (post-review, seven) covers every fix made in response: drop the `-C` anchoring; revert the key-set guard to a value test; drop scope awareness; move the arm skip after the `--dry-run` branch; move it after the `--update` branch; make `self_check.sh` hooksPath-blind again; and — the one that matters most — restore the #202 auto-arm *while* an ambient global `core.hooksPath` is set, reproducing the reporter's own machine, to confirm the new test isolation catches what it previously would have waved through.

**Final count: +46 tests (1424 → 1470), 4 skipped.**

**Drift guard.** The fix is two deleted blocks, the shape that re-accretes fastest. `tests/test_hook_autoarm_drift.py` fails if any `core/companion/scripts/*.sh` names `install_hooks.sh` in command position — discriminating invocation from mention by first word, so `self_check.sh`'s advisory "arm: bash …" message stays legal — with a non-vacuity test asserting the guard still detects the exact lines this phase deleted, plus prose guards on all three stale WORKFLOW.md phrasings and on the correction being stated.

**Close-out.** Inline (meta-repo convention). No new permission surface, no schema change, no installer flag. Zero behavior change for a consumer without `core.hooksPath` beyond the removed auto-arm.

## Phase 151 (2026-07-26 — the `/review-close` `pr`-policy bundle)

**Why one phase.** Upstream #203, #208 and #204 all live in `/review-close` Step 4 and would collide as separate branches. They also share a thesis with Phases 135/141/143/149/150: **a gate that did not run looks exactly like one that passed.** #203 commits a consolidation that dropped its own payload; #208 reports a stuck PR after a merge that landed; #204 opens a second PR for work that already had one. All three exit 0.

**#203 — the half-staged index.** `git mv` stages, `Path.write_text` does not, and Step 4c mixed both and then said only "**Commit**". The literal `git commit` recorded the body renames and dropped the `status: done` + `completed_date` flip, under a subject claiming the consolidation happened — and on a `pr` consumer that half-commit is what gets squash-merged. Reproduced in a scratch repo before touching anything: `1 file changed, 0 insertions(+), 0 deletions(-)`.

**The reporter's first proposed fix recreates the bug, which is why it was tested rather than applied.** `git add -A PROJECT_STATUS.md changelog.md UI_Iterations.md tasks/` rests on the premise that "paths that do not exist are skipped by `-A` with an explicit pathspec." They are not: `git add -A <missing>` aborts identically to `git add <missing>`, exit 128, staging nothing. `changelog.md` and `UI_Iterations.md` are consumer-authored and never created by the installer, so that command fails on the majority of close-outs — and fails *silently*, because the following `git commit` still succeeds on the rename-only index. The shipped fix instead stages the index inside the heredoc that writes it (the reporter's third option, the only one that cannot drift from what was written), gives each shared doc its own `git add`, and adds a Step-4b-style post-commit gate. The reporter's assertion #2 was also taken with a correction: its unconditional `git show --stat HEAD | grep -q 'tasks/index.yml'` false-fails whenever no pending-doc carried `roadmap_ids`, so it is now conditional on the run having closed one.

**Which surfaced the same root cause at eight sites nobody had reported.** `/codebase-review` and `/security-audit` both ship `git add <many paths> 2>/dev/null`, and `codebase-review/SKILL.md` stated outright that "`2>/dev/null` tolerates their absence in the source repo." It does not — it suppresses the *message*; the invocation still aborts and stages nothing. The worst instance is Step 7's `git add review_tasks.md review_tasks_archive.md 2>/dev/null`: before a project's first archive rotation the sibling does not exist, so the round's tasks were never committed and the step's own stated purpose ("prevents task loss when `/review-close` later stashes") silently did not happen. Wade ratified folding these in rather than filing them, on the grounds that shipping a fix for one instance of a class while its siblings and a false justification stay in place is the failure this repo keeps re-learning.

**#208 — the benign `fatal:`.** `gh pr merge --delete-branch` deletes the *local* branch too, so after the remote squash it switches to the base and tries to fast-forward it. Step 4d-1 keyed the stuck-PR branch on "`gh pr merge` refuses", so that message stops the run and skips all cleanup — branches, worktrees and locks stranded behind a close that already landed. The fix makes PR **state** the sole verdict: a `gh pr view --json state` probe runs after the merge as its own command, and 4d-1 is reworded off exit status and stderr entirely.

**#204 — the missing reuse branch.** Step 4-pre cut an integration branch unconditionally, so a single approved branch that already had an open PR got a *second* branch, a second PR, a duplicate CI cycle, and an orphan. A PR-reuse shape now lands the close on that PR's own branch. Three collisions the filing did not mention had to be closed with it: the Rule A branch guard asserts a `merge/review-close-*` pattern (the reuse shape has no pattern, so it asserts the literal Step 2a branch name — still not HEAD-derived, which is the property that matters), Step 4a would rebase the branch onto itself, and Step 6 has no integration branch to delete. `_shared/main-push-guard.md`, which the HARD RULE delegates to, gained the reuse rows so a reader following the delegation does not find a table that contradicts the skill.

**The filing's incidental note was the trap.** #204 says `gh` fast-forwards `main` itself, "so Step 6's reset + branch delete are already no-ops." The first draft rejected that outright, citing #208 — same reporter, same batch — as the counter-example, and asserted the opposite universal: local `main` "has **diverged by construction**". **Both adversarial reviewers independently killed that**, and the second supplied the resolution: #204's reporter had `origin/main == main`, i.e. was *in the reuse shape*, where the note is correct; #208 was the integration-branch shape. Neither claim generalizes. Worse, reuse **condition 3 requires** `origin/main..main` to be empty, so the phase's own new shape falsified its own justification — and a new drift guard had pinned the falsehood in place. Every statement is now scoped by shape at all five sites; the reset still runs unconditionally, load-bearing in one shape and a harmless no-op in the other.

**The two-reviewer pass found two HIGHs, one of them created by this phase's own fix.** Splitting Step 4d into two blocks made `$PR_REF` cross a step boundary — the exact hazard the skill's own persistence blockquote warns about, and the first draft omitted `$PR_REF` from that very list. An empty `$PR_REF` does not fail loudly: `gh` silently resolves the current branch, so `gh pr merge ""` merges, `--delete-branch` moves HEAD to `main`, and the verdict probe then finds no PR for `main` — a stuck-PR report and skipped cleanup after a successful merge. That is #208 reintroduced by its own fix, and *worse* than before, since the old "exits 0 **or** MERGED" disjunction would have survived it. Step 4d now re-derives `$PR_REF` and hard-fails on empty before the first `gh` call. The second HIGH: `gh pr list --head` cannot be scoped to an owner and GitHub permits several open PRs sharing a head-branch name across forks, so `.[0]` could select a third party's PR and squash-merge their code to `main` while reporting this run's work as landed. The probe now filters to same-repository non-drafts and demands exactly one match; the reuse merge pins `--match-head-commit`.

**Six more that mattered.** Reuse condition 1 keyed on the Step 2a verdict, which Steps 2d and 3b can overturn — it now reads "still approved after Step 3b". A fifth condition (not behind `origin/main`) replaces the currency guarantee that skipping Step 4a silently dropped. 4d-1's idempotency argument ("the next run cuts a **new** integration branch") is false under reuse and now has its own recovery. The heredoc wrote and staged `tasks/index.yml` unconditionally, contradicting Step 7's own "legitimately untouched" case — guarded on `closed`. `git mv` into a missing `tasks/archive/` is fatal, aborting *after* earlier renames staged and *before* the index write, which is #203's shape via a route the staging fix does not cover — the parent directory is now created first. And the `[ -e "$p" ] && git add "$p"` loop the phase first shipped **silently skips deletions**, which matters because Step 9b is the demotion step; verified side by side and replaced with `git add -A -- "$p" 2>/dev/null || true`.

**The install docs carried the same defect on the highest-traffic surface.** `git add .claude/ .agents/ sysop/ …` appears in the README, both tutorials, the update doc and the landing page — and `.agents/` is conditional (`--no-codex-links`, or a failed symlink capability probe), so those copy-paste lines abort and stage nothing. Splitting it into its own `git add` broke a deliberate Phase-142 guard requiring `.agents/` in every documented commit line; the guard was widened to accept the split form rather than the property being dropped. A blanket multi-pathspec ban would be wrong here (the other paths always exist), so the docs get a targeted `.agents/`-specific guard while the blanket ban stays scoped to `core/skills/`.

**Verification.** Eleven mutations across two rounds, all killed — and two of them only after the tests that were *supposed* to kill them were repaired. Removing the `$PR_REF` guard first passed, because the guard test searched the whole block and a commented-out guard still matched; it is now line-anchored and re-verified against both deletion and comment-out. Guarding the index write first passed, because `yaml.safe_dump` of the unchanged fixture was byte-identical to the seed — the fixture now carries comments a reserialization would destroy. The drift guard's tokenizer needed two fixes found the same way: shell operators bind tight to the preceding argument (`.gitignore;`), and splitting them turns `&&` into single `&` tokens. Beyond mutation, the git claims are pinned as executable tests rather than asserted in prose — all-or-nothing pathspecs, `-A` not rescuing a miss, and the precise (weaker) truth about a failed add after `git mv`, which the first draft overstated as "fails *worse* than doing nothing" when in fact it leaves the index exactly as `git mv` left it.

**Final count: +48 tests (1470 → 1518), 4 skipped.**

**Permissions.** Deliberately untouched. The reuse probe's `gh pr list` already ships in the template allow-list; Step 4c's new `git add PROJECT_STATUS.md` does not, and was **not** added to the pre-flight's required set — doing so would hard-stop every consumer at Step 0 on a fresh install regardless of merge policy, which is the failure shape upstream #205 reports. Reconciling the allow-list against every verb these skills name belongs to the #205 + #210 phase; this one does not widen the hole and states the non-entry explicitly.

**#208 confirmed firsthand at merge time, not merely taken from the filing.** This repo is itself a `pr`-policy consumer, so before merging PR #221 an empty throwaway commit was put on local `main` to recreate the divergence topology, and the merge run as documented. `gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch` printed the `hint:` block, `fatal: Not possible to fast-forward, aborting.` and `! warning: not possible to fast-forward to: "main"` — **and exited 0**, while `gh pr view --json state` reported `MERGED`. So exit status and stderr disagree with each other and only state is trustworthy, which is precisely what the fix now says. `gh` left HEAD on `main` without updating it; the documented `git fetch origin main && git reset --hard origin/main` is what actually re-synced it, confirming Step 6's reset is load-bearing in this shape rather than the no-op #204's incidental note called it.

**Close-out.** Inline (meta-repo convention). No schema change, no installer flag, no `settings.json` edit. A `direct`-policy consumer sees only the Step 4c staging fix.

## Phase 152 (2026-07-26 — the permission-surface reconciliation)

**Why one phase.** Upstream #205 and #210 are two reports of one surface: the shipped `.claude/settings.json` template and the skills' Step 0 "required rules" blocks drifted apart with nothing verifying them against each other. The § Medium `gh repo view` item (filed by Phase 147, deliberately left open) is the same root cause seen from the other side — a rule shipped to route *around* an unverified claim about what the harness auto-approves. All three close together, and the phase ends with the drift guard that was missing.

**The mechanical half was exactly as filed.** `/review-close` Step 0 declared 23 bullet-form rules; six were absent from the 58-rule template — `Bash(git fetch origin:*)`, `Bash(git reset --hard origin/main)`, `Bash(git branch -D:*)`, `Bash(gh pr create:*)`, `Bash(gh pr checks:*)`, and `Bash(git worktree list:*)` against a seeded bare `Bash(git worktree list)`. A `pr`-policy consumer on a non-bypass mode hard-stopped at Step 0 on a fresh install.

**The diagnostic half was not, and two `claude-code-guide` probes redirected the design.** The guard's own premise — "under `permissions.defaultMode: "auto"` with `skipAutoPermissionPrompt: true`, a missing rule surfaces as a silent halt" — is wrong in its specifics, and had been repeated across twelve shipped files (plus a test comment) for roughly thirteen phases. `skipAutoPermissionPrompt` appears nowhere in the official settings key table, the permissions docs, or the changelog. `auto`-mode denials are *surfaced* (a notification plus a retry entry under `/permissions` → *Recently denied*), so "opaque silent halt" overstates that mode. The documented no-prompt-denial mode is **`dontAsk`**, which "auto-denies every tool call that would otherwise prompt you." And Claude Code v2.1.142+ **ignores `defaultMode: "auto"` set in either project settings file** — so the mode the guard named as its hazard can never appear in the file the guard reads. The hazard itself is real and was observed (BeanRider, 2026-05-12, a `git merge --ff-only` refused with no prompt mid-merge); only the configuration name was invented. Every site now names `dontAsk`, and both the guard and WORKFLOW § 8.2a carry a dated correction rather than a silent swap.

**Three matcher facts changed what the fix could be.** Read-only forms of `git` are auto-approved **in every mode** — so a skill listing one as required hard-stops consumers for nothing. `gh` is **not** in that set at all, so every `gh` call needs a rule, including `gh auth status` and `gh repo view`. And rules match **the literal text the model sends, before shell expansion**, with `:*` a trailing wildcard at a word boundary.

**That third fact inverted the entry's own third question.** Phase 151 recorded the review skills' `git add -A -- "$p"` as unfixable-by-rule, on the premise that "a variable argument binds no static rule at all." That is the Phase-126 fact about variable *command words*, misapplied to arguments: `Bash(git add:*)` does match `git add -A -- "$p"`. Wade ratified seeding it. Two entries therefore left WORKFLOW § 8.2a's **Conscious omissions** list, each with its reason recorded — `Bash(git add:*)`, whose stated justification ("the auto-mode classifier passes these") is false under `dontAsk` and which no literal-path rule could replace; and `Bash(git branch -D:*)`, omitted "by design" while `/review-close` Step 6 hard-required it, making the documented `pr` flow unsatisfiable. The template goes 58 → 65 rules. The loop subset goes 17 → 18, adding `gh auth status` only: the adversarial pass showed `git add:*` buys loop mode nothing, because the review skills' Step 9 stages inside a `for … done` loop and `for`/`done` are not among the documented command separators, so **no** rule matches that invocation. The wildcard stays in the full template, where `/review-close` Step 4c's three plain `git add <path>` lines are exactly what it authorizes.

**Two live defects nobody had filed.** `/sitrep` — read-only, `disallowed-tools`-guarded, the session-opening skill — hard-required six git rules (`git log`, `git status`, `git branch`, `git rev-parse`, `git rev-list`, and `git worktree list:*`), **none** of which shipped in the seeded list, and closed its block with "Do not proceed." So `/sitrep` was unrunnable as documented on a fresh install in any mode. Five of the six are plainly read-only and needed no rule; the sixth turned out to need no *declaration* either, because every git call `/sitrep` makes happens inside `sitrep_survey.py` as a subprocess of the permitted `python3` call — the adversarial pass caught that, and the same spurious `Bash(git worktree list)` requirement was found in `/auto-fix` and `/auto-judge` for a command neither runs. Separately, `gh auth status` is a hard gate in five skills, ships no rule, and was justified in each by calling it a read-only op — the same false claim the § Medium item flagged for `gh repo view`. **Why nobody saw any of it:** not the bypass mode (the pre-152 guard had no mode check, so a bypass-mode agent following `/sitrep` literally would have stopped too) but the reason #205's reporter gives for their own case — the documented gate was knowingly overridden.

**The `gh repo view` item resolves as *keep*, not prune.** The open question was whether the command is auto-approved, in which case the rule and its `LOOP_ALLOW` entry were dead weight. It is not — `gh` is outside the read-only set — so the rule is load-bearing and the count does not fall back to 16. Phase 147 reached the right shipping decision through a chain it could not verify; the three skills' "read-only → don't list per § Notes" prose was the false half and is reworded. `Bash(gh auth status)` joins it for the same reason.

**The guard's verdict is now mode-aware, and deliberately narrow.** New Algorithm step 3 reads `permissions.defaultMode` and, under `bypassPermissions` only, computes the missing set, prints it as a drift report, and proceeds — Phase 150's skipped-not-failed shape. It is **not** widened to `default`/`acceptEdits`, where a missing rule costs a prompt rather than a halt: prompt behavior inside spawned sub-agents is unverified, and the conservative side of that uncertainty is the status quo. Two further refinements fell out of the probes: the guard now reads `.claude/settings.local.json` too (project-scoped, and it outranks `settings.json`), and a required rule counts as satisfied by a **broader allow-rule that already covers it** — a consumer running `Bash(git:*)` was previously reported as missing every git rule we name.

**Both directions of the mode read are wrong sometimes, and the guard says so rather than hiding it.** CLI arguments and managed settings outrank both project files, so a `--dangerously-skip-permissions` session still hard-stops (with `--skip-permission-guard` named as the sanctioned override), and a project file declaring `bypassPermissions` that a flag downgraded will skip — degrading to the pre-guard status quo *plus* a printed drift report. Stating this is the honest alternative to a check that pretends to know the effective mode.

**The drift guard is the deliverable that keeps this closed** (`tests/test_permission_surface_drift.py`, 11 tests). Direction 1: every bullet-form required rule must be satisfied by the shipped template, using the same superset semantics the guard documents. Direction 2: every seeded rule is either named by a skill or carries a written justification in `SEEDED_WITHOUT_SKILL_MENTION` — sixteen entries, which is the first complete accounting of why each unreferenced rule ships, and a companion test fails when an entry goes stale in either direction. Plus: no skill may require a read-only git verb (the `/sitrep` regression), the guard must read `defaultMode` and state that it proceeds, every hard-stopping pre-flight must point at that escape, and § 8.2a's illustrative JSON block must be a subset of the real template — which is how the stale bare `Bash(git worktree list)` survived there.

**Bullet form is the contract.** Only bullets inside a pre-flight count as required; a `Bash(...)` named in a *paragraph* is documentation — an explicit non-entry (`/review-close` names `Bash(cp:*)` precisely to say it does not ship one) or a note about what the template carries. Without that distinction a naive scan overstates the drift by a factor of two and the guard would force every mention into the allow-list.

**The two-reviewer pass rewrote a third of this phase, and its through-line is one sentence: the surface was verified at the level of rule *strings* and never at the level of the *bash* the rules authorize.** Four findings are the same defect. `PR_REF="$(gh pr create …)"` starts with an assignment, and a rule does not match past one — so the newly seeded `Bash(gh pr create:*)` does not authorize the line it was seeded for, and the phase had written that very fact into the guard's § Notes two files away. The review skills' `git add -A -- "$p"` sits inside a `for … done` loop, and `for`/`done` are not documented separators, so no rule matches it — which falsified the *sole* justification for putting `git add:*` in loop mode. A `|| true` tail is its own unmatched part. And a variable command word binds nothing. The seeded rules are still right for the bare forms and stay; what changed is that five sites which asserted coverage now state the gap, `WORKFLOW.md` § 8.2a gained an **Invocation shapes** section naming Sysop's own uncovered call sites, and reshaping them is filed rather than rushed at the tail of a phase. The authoring rule it yields: **before adding a rule, read the line of bash it is supposed to authorize.**

**Three more the pass caught.** `/report-issues` was missed by the renumber sweep entirely — still citing step 4, still hard-stopping with no mode-check carve-out — and the drift guard written to catch exactly that skipped it, because the skill hard-wraps `Do not\nproceed.` and the test searched raw text while its own sibling twenty lines above collapses whitespace *for that hazard*. `/auto-fix` and `/auto-judge` required a bare `Bash(git worktree list)` the template no longer ships, for a command neither skill runs. And a newly written sentence — "commit subjects stay pinned to the three shipped shapes" — is falsified by `/auto-fix` and `/auto-judge`'s own `fix:` / `revert(batch-N):` commits.

**Verification.** Two mutation rounds. The first: thirteen mutations covering both drift directions, the read-only ban, four ways of defeating the mode check, and a broken pre-flight heading to prove the sanity floors bite — all killed. The second round is the one that mattered: the reviewer re-ran the mode-check guards against *semantic inversions* rather than deletions and **six survived** — wrapping step 3 in an HTML comment, inverting step 4 to exact-match-only, "the allow-list is **not** inert", "**Ignore** `permissions.defaultMode`", a skill negating the escape it names, and keeping "Do not stop." as a historical note beside a halting instruction. All four of those tests were substring-presence checks over the whole file. They now parse the numbered Algorithm step in isolation, with HTML comments and blockquoted lines stripped first, and assert on that step's own text; the escape phrase is pinned as one whole clause; and every one of the six inversions now dies, along with a read-only verb smuggled past behind a flag, four pre-flight headings renamed out of the scan, a justification replaced by filler, and the mention-scan losing `_shared/`. The first round's harness was itself discarded and re-run — its revert argument was wrong, so mutations accumulated and attribution was unreadable; **cumulative failure counts are not per-mutation evidence.**

**One correction was itself wrong, caught by re-checking rather than by a reviewer.** Acting on the finding that `git add:*` does not cover the review skills' Step 9 loop, the rule was pulled out of loop mode — on the reviewer's (and the author's) shared belief that Step 9 was its only loop-mode beneficiary. It is not: both review skills also run a plain `git add review_tasks_archive.md` at **Step 7**, which no literal rule covers, so the removal would have broken the loop's own ledger commit. Restored with the correct justification. The lesson is the finding's own: the call sites decide, and reading one of them is not reading them all.

**Final count: +12 tests (1518 → 1530), 4 skipped.** Two pre-existing tests were rewritten rather than deleted. A Phase-151 drift guard pinned Step 4c's doc staging as a *deliberate non-entry* on the premise that the installer seeds only literal-path `git add` rules, which this phase makes false; it now asserts the Phase-152 decision — the wildcard is required, the literal paths stay banned — because a guard that pins a superseded statement is worse than no guard. The loop-mode disclosure test was widened to require that the subset's one write grant is named out loud.

**Known and accepted:** a consumer who `--update`s keeps the bare `Bash(git worktree list)` alongside the new `:*` form, because `install_permissions` set-unions and the namespace-migration removal set is scoped to vendor-path rules. It is redundant, not harmful, and no skill declares the bare form any more. One Phase-151 drift guard was rewritten rather than deleted: it pinned Step 4c's doc staging as a *deliberate non-entry* on the premise that the installer seeds only literal-path `git add` rules, which this phase makes false. It now asserts the Phase-152 decision — the wildcard is required, the literal paths stay banned — because a guard that pins a superseded statement is worse than no guard.

**Close-out.** Inline (meta-repo convention). No schema change, no installer flag. Consumers need `sysop-update.sh` to pick up the seven new rules; until they do, the reconciled Step 0 blocks name rules their `settings.json` lacks — which is what the guard is for, and is now reported rather than fatal under bypass.

## Phase 153 (2026-07-26 — the invocation-shape sweep)

**Phase 152 ended by filing its own unfinished business.** Its adversarial pass found that the permission surface had been verified at the level of rule *strings* and never at the level of the *bash* those rules authorize, named four shapes that defeat an otherwise-correct rule, and recorded Sysop's own uncovered call sites in `WORKFLOW.md` § 8.2a rather than rushing a reshape at the tail of a phase. This phase does the reshape. The rule it operationalizes is the one Phase 152 wrote down: **before adding a rule, read the line of bash it is supposed to authorize** — and, when the bash cannot be authorized, change the bash.

**The live defect was in `/review-close`'s `pr` path, which this repo is itself a consumer of.** Step 4-pre and Step 4d captured `gh` output into variables (`PR_NUMBER="$(gh pr list …)"`, `PR_REF="$(gh pr create …)"`), and an allow-rule does not match past an assignment. So under `dontAsk` those three calls were auto-denied *after* a Step 0 pre-flight had just vouched for `Bash(gh pr list:*)` and `Bash(gh pr create:*)` — a mid-flow halt carrying the pre-flight's blessing. Two `|| true` tails (`gh pr checks`, Step 6's `git branch -D`) were the same class: `true` is not in the documented read-only set, so the tail is its own unmatched part. And both review skills staged inside `for … done` loops at three sites each; `for` and `done` are not documented command separators, so **no** rule matches a looped invocation, which is why widening was never an option.

**Fixed at the call site, never by widening a rule.** `gh pr list` and `gh pr create` now run bare and the agent reads the value off stdout; the PR number is written out as a literal `<PR>` at every later use, and Step 6's integration branch likewise. That is not merely a permission workaround — it *removes* the hazard Phase 151 had to guard. Splitting Step 4d into two blocks had made the PR handle cross a shell-call boundary, and an empty `gh` operand does not fail: `gh pr merge ""` merges the current branch's PR, `--delete-branch` moves HEAD to `main`, and the verdict probe then reports a stuck PR **after a merge that landed**. Phase 151 guarded that with `test -n "$PR_REF"`. A literal has nothing to go empty. The bare re-derivation probe and its stop-on-empty both stay, because the *reason* has to survive the variable's removal.

**The staging loops came out by staging less, not by tolerating more.** The loops existed because `git add` is all-or-nothing across its pathspecs — one unmatched pathspec aborts the whole invocation and stages none of the others — and the `.project.*` overlays are permanently absent in the source repo. Phase 151's diagnosis was right; its shape was unauthorizable. The replacement stages only the paths the step actually wrote, one plain `git add -A -- <path>` each. The agent making the edits knows which files it touched, so the shell never needs to tolerate absence at all; the `2>/dev/null || true` could simply go. A fixture test pins the property that makes this safe: a `fatal:` on one line does **not** stop the lines after it.

**The path *list* did not change, and an early draft that changed it was wrong.** The loop ran the whole candidate set unconditionally; so does the unrolled list. That is what keeps the consumer-install `.project.*` overlay write mechanically guaranteed rather than dependent on the agent remembering it — `_shared/promotion-write-target.md` makes the overlay the durable home for a locally-promoted convention, so an agent that skips it commits a promotion that the next `sysop-update.sh` erases. A first draft of this phase narrowed the list to "only the paths you actually wrote," trading a machine guarantee for an assumption about agent behaviour; its adversarial review caught that, and the list was restored. The unrolling is about the *shape* of the invocation, not the *contents* of the list. The one cost is a `fatal:` line per absent overlay, which the loop had swallowed with `2>/dev/null`.

**The `gh`-operand item filed against six skills was mostly false, and the audit found something else.** Phase 151 filed that `/pr-dependabot`, `/report-issues`, `/contribute-convention`, `/share-wins`, `/release` and `/security-audit`'s ingest path "all shell out to `gh` with values held in variables across steps." Checked directly: `/pr-dependabot` and `/share-wins` pass zero `$VAR` operands to `gh`; `/security-audit` invokes `gh` **zero times** (its ten `gh ` grep hits are substrings of "through" and "High", and Phase 144's ingest is passive by design); and the empty-operand hazard needs a *positional* operand, which outside `/review-close` no skill passes from a variable. What the audit did find was unrelated and real: **nine unguarded `$TMPDIR` sites across four skills.** `TMPDIR` is set on macOS and usually unset on Linux, where `"$TMPDIR/sysop-issue-<id>.md"` collapses to `/sysop-issue-<id>.md`. Stated precisely — the first draft of this paragraph was not — the body file is *written* by the `Write` tool, which performs no shell expansion, so nothing attempts an unwritable write to `/`; what breaks is the *read*, when `gh --body-file` is handed a path under `/` that does not exist. The filing then fails on exactly the consumers least likely to have `TMPDIR` set. `install.sh` already used `${TMPDIR:-/tmp}`; the skills now match it. **This is not the first time it was raised:** Phase 81 saw it and deliberately declined ("N3 (`$TMPDIR` mechanics, faithful to the sibling) left as-is per the reviewer"), which is worth recording given this phase's own thesis about filings that send the next reader hunting. Filing the *audit result* honestly matters for the same reason: an entry that names six skills and is right about one would have cost the next reader a day.

**A rider: `WORKFLOW.md` said loop mode does not carry `Bash(git add:*)`, and `install.sh` seeds it.** Phase 152 pulled the rule out of loop mode, then restored it on discovering Step 7's plain `git add review_tasks_archive.md` needs it — but the prose stating the removal survived the restore in one place. Corrected, and the rule's justification widened: now that Step 9/9b are unrolled, it covers those too, which is the seat the loop had denied it.

**A three-reviewer adversarial round reshaped roughly half of this phase, and its through-line is a sentence this phase had already written about Phase 152: the surface was verified at the level of the shape removed, never at the level of the shapes that could come back.** Every guard had been mutation-tested against *the exact string it had just deleted* — the easiest possible test — and a reviewer running the space of plausible re-accretions found **33 survivors**. A backtick anywhere on a line disabled every guard at once (the "prose filter" was content-based, and house style here is backtick-dense, so a trailing comment was the likeliest trip); `|| :`, `|| true;` and `|| true  # …` all passed a guard written as `endswith("|| true")`; a multi-line `for`/`do` passed a regex requiring `; do`; the loop ban keyed on the literal `git add`, so `git commit`, `git push` and `gh pr merge` inside a loop sailed through — as did the `for sha in $(git rev-list …); do git cherry-pick` loop *living in `/review-close` at the time*, which this phase's own prose was simultaneously telling authors not to write. One rewritten test reverted a documented fix: the parent carried a line-anchoring helper whose comment said in as many words that a whole-block search had already survived a comment-out mutation, and the rewrite went back to `block.index(...)`, whereupon commenting out the Step 4d probe passed clean. And the `|| true` non-vacuity twin re-implemented its predicate inline instead of calling the production helper, so it could not fail for *any* change to the real guard. The fix is structural: fences, not backticks, delimit code; every predicate lives in one shared module; every twin calls the production predicate. All 15 named survivors are now killed.

**Three findings were defects this phase introduced, not weaknesses it failed to catch.** (1) The `/security-audit` "rider" was a **fabricated finding** — `_shared/promotion-write-target.md` states outright that a security rule's Step 9 reminder lands in the *convention* map and that `security_map.project.md` "is **not** a Step 9 reminder target," staged instead by Step 2a and Step 9b. The promotion/demotion asymmetry was the design; adding the path would sweep an unrelated Step 2a edit into a commit titled `docs: promote N conventions`. Reverted, with the reasoning now shipped at the site so it cannot be re-"fixed." Two reviewers disagreed here and the one that read the governing doc was right — a reviewer confirming that an asymmetry *exists* has not shown it is unintended. (2) `<PR>` unquoted is not a placeholder to bash but a **redirection**: `gh pr merge <PR> --squash` runs as `gh pr merge --delete-branch` reading a file named `PR`, dropping the operand and handing gh the silent current-branch fallback — the exact hazard the step's stop exists to prevent, reached by a route the stop cannot see. Quoted, an unsubstituted `"<PR>"` fails loudly (`no pull requests found for branch "<PR>"`), which is what makes the stop enforceable rather than advisory. (3) Step 6's `git branch -D merge/review-close-<run id>` was a literal **bash syntax error**, contradicted the same file's claim that `$RUN_ID` is never needed again, and justified itself with a falsehood — the name *is* re-derivable, via `git branch --list 'merge/review-close-*'`. All three are the same failure: confidence in a change that was never executed.

**Two judgment calls were reversed on review.** Dropping `|| true` from `gh pr checks` made the instruction "do not gate on the exit status" unenforceable — `gh pr checks` exits non-zero on a repo with *no* checks, so a mergeable PR now surfaced a red tool result. The resolution is `|| echo "<why>"`: `echo` **is** in the documented built-in read-only set while `true` is not, so the compound stays authorized *and* keeps the do-not-abort semantics — a better answer than either of the two the phase had considered. Similarly, `2>/dev/null` never needed removing at all; a redirection is not a command separator, so only the `|| true` had ever cost the match.

**Verification: +12 tests (1530 → 1542), guards rebuilt on a shared structural base, mutation-verified against the adversarial round's own survivor list rather than against the shapes just deleted.** Two existing files were rewritten rather than deleted, because both pinned shapes this phase deliberately replaced. `test_git_add_staging_discipline.py` asserted the six loops **exist**; it now bans a `git add` inside any `for … done` (matched loosely, so a loop returning under a different variable name or tail is still caught), bans a live command ending in `|| true`, and — the part a pure ban would miss — asserts both review skills still stage per-path, since a ban alone passes happily on a skill that stages nothing and would reintroduce Phase 151's original bug by another route. `test_review_close_pr_policy.py`'s two `$PR_REF` tests became a guard that no PR handle is ever held in a variable and that the `gh`-empty-operand *reason* survives in the persistence note. A new `test_invocation_shapes.py` carries the cross-skill invariants so a newly authored skill inherits them: no `gh` capture anywhere, `$TMPDIR` always guarded. Every guard needed a prose filter — the corrected prose quotes the retired shapes on purpose to explain them, so a naive substring scan finds every bad form in exactly the place documenting its retirement; blockquotes, bash comments and any backticked line are prose. The first draft of the `gh`-capture guard failed on precisely that, which is the cheapest possible demonstration of why the filter is load-bearing.

**Scoped out, deliberately — and the honest claim is narrower than the first draft's.** Read-only `git` probes captured into variables (`MERGE_TARGET="$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD)"` and friends) are left alone: the assignment defeats matching there too, but these are read-only commands for which Sysop ships no rule to defeat. An audit of all 20 such captures confirmed **no write command is captured into a variable anywhere in the skills**, so the carve-out is sound rather than merely convenient. The three in Step 4-pre's reuse probe were converted anyway, for uniformity inside a block already being rewritten.

**What this phase does *not* prove.** The first draft claimed "all eleven sites closed" and that the reshape covered "every staging site Sysop ships." Both were overclaims, and three classes remain uncovered, now recorded in `WORKFLOW.md` § 8.2a instead of asserted away. **(a) Loops over runtime-discovered sets cannot be unrolled** — there is no static list to write out. Five survive in `/review-close`; four are read-only, and one (Step 3b's glob-driven pending-docs strip) wraps a real `rm -f` behind `[ -e … ] &&`, a write inside two unmatched shapes at once. Every one is now enumerated in a `KNOWN_RUNTIME_SET_LOOPS` allowlist with its justification, checked for staleness in both directions — the same pattern Phase 152 used one layer up, and the reason a *new* loop now fails the suite while these do not. The `cd <worktree> && git add -A && git commit …` compounds in five lifecycle skills are likewise untouched. **(b) An assignment sharing a fenced block with a reshaped command** may still defeat the whole invocation; removing the capture from `gh pr create` did not remove `APPROVED_BRANCH=` from the block above it. The strict reading of the split rule also proves too much — if every assignment line denied its block, no consumer's lifecycle would ever have run — so the truth sits somewhere between, and Sysop does not know where. **(c) Quoting**, which decides both the three `Bash(git commit -m <prefix>:*)` rules and the two reshaped `gh pr list` commands, whose `--jq` argument contains a literal `|`. Two `claude-code-guide` probes could not settle it; the docs neither define the normalization nor show one rule example containing a quote. (b) and (c) are filed with one-run human verification recipes rather than guessed at, as is the protected-paths question Phase 152 raised. So the defensible claim is that the shapes which *provably* defeat a rule are gone — not that every invocation is proven to bind.

**Close-out.** Inline (meta-repo convention). No schema change, no installer flag, no new permission rules — the whole point is that the rules were already right and the call sites were not. Consumers pick the reshaped skills up through the plugin path automatically or on the next `sysop-update.sh`; nothing about their `settings.json` needs to change.
