**Two guards elsewhere went red or vacuous on arrival, and both were real.** `test_review_close_record_revision.py`'s Step 6 mutations `R/F1` and `R/F3` anchored on the bare `git diff --quiet HEAD --` prefix; `_sub` replaces the **first** occurrence, and `4a-post`'s new clean-tree probe sits earlier in the file, so both mutations silently retargeted to it and survived every check while the shipped Step 6 gate sat untouched. Anchored on Step 6's own arm text instead. The same class then bit this phase's own `R2` mutation, which hit Step 3's prose cross-reference to the report line rather than the Step 8 template. **Adding text to a file weakens every first-occurrence mutation in every guard over that file** — a general property worth carrying, and not one any lens had named.

**A class sweep ran; the filing enumerates 15 further sites** (the sweep reported 19, but two of those it could not establish either way and two more are the *correct* siblings it cites as counter-examples — the round caught the copied number not matching my own entry). They are filed rather than fixed (the brief's "do not work the whole queue"): the mechanism splits three ways — branch-vs-main (Phases 158/167's axis, still live in the validator and elsewhere), **index-vs-working-tree** (entirely untouched, entirely in `git-hooks/`, and the only one with a reproduced false green), and CWD-worktree-vs-main-repo-root. Its structural note is the one to keep: **the class recurs at call-site granularity, not file granularity** — in three files the sibling mechanism was already hardened and the neighbour was not (`close_batch.sh`'s lock release vs. its merge gate; `self_check.sh`'s probe 6 vs. probes 3/5; `batch_work.sh`'s `--release` vs. its claim path), and a fourth pair straddles two files (Step 2d vs. `validate_tasks.py` Invariant 13), which the round correctly refused to count as evidence for a same-file claim.

**The adversarial round — three fresh-context `general-purpose` reviewers, worktree-isolated, distinct lenses (does it execute / are its claims true / are its guards real), ~408k sub-agent tokens.** Overlap was again near zero: each lens's sharpest finding was reached by no other, matching Phase 166's ~15% measurement. Three was right here.

**The execute lens found the fix reachable-past, which is this phase's own closing lesson landing inside the phase.** Step 4a's pre-existing sentence read *"go straight to Step 4b"* — text this phase never touched. Under the PR-reuse shape Step 4a is skipped **and** nothing else re-verifies, so an agent executing literally routed past `4a-post` and squash-merged an approved branch onto a protected `main` with nothing having run against it. Inserting a step between 4a and 4b without updating 4a's forward pointer is exactly *the class recurs at call-site granularity, not file granularity* — and the guard could not see it, because pinning `4a-post`'s own "this step still runs" sentence proves nothing about a section nobody arrives at. The guard now asserts the **property** (no forward pointer anywhere jumps to Step 4b), not the site. **Its second HIGH falsified a claim already in this entry:** Step 3's item 4 (doc-only skip) precedes item 5 (stop-and-ask) and fires first on the dominant path, so a consumer with no declared commands and no detectable surface sailed through Step 3 and hit "stop and ask what to run" at `4a-post`, **after every branch had merged** — the one outcome the free stop exists to prevent. Item 5 now runs against the *run*, not the pass. It also found that `4a-post` could **re-manufacture the very defect it removes**: surface-gate every detected command out and the merged-tree pass reports green having executed zero commands. Step 3 had an explicit empty-set rule; `4a-post` had none, and now routes that case to item 5's stop.

**The claims lens falsified three sentences already written into this record, plus three shipped ones.** `/auto-build` **Step 4b does not exist** — `## Step 4` is *Confirm with Human*; the `4b.` cited is an item inside the execution-agent prompt's `### Sequence` under Step 7 (three sites, all corrected; `/claim-task` Step 7b checked out clean). The **placement rationale was false under `direct`**, the default policy: "recoverable only from a commit the run abandons" holds under `pr`, where a failed close discards the merge target, but under `direct` the commit stays on local `main` and this step's own recovery keeps it — scoped. **"the only thing that ever does"** implied something always happens, when both sibling steps say *"if both are absent, skip"*. In the record: **"19 further members" did not match this phase's own filing**, which enumerates 15 (two of the sweep's 19 it could not establish, two more are the *correct* siblings it cites as counter-examples) — I copied a sub-agent's integer instead of counting my own entry, which is the same failure Phase 169 recorded about adopting a filed claim unchecked. **"four separate files"** was three plus a cross-file pair. And the **headline arm was the uncommon one**: I led with the empty-set case, but `/review-close` *manufactures* the divergence (Step 2a's own note — Step 1b commits `review_tasks.md` to `main` before any branch is inspected), so usually the range is non-empty-but-doc-only and the pass skips. Both arms run nothing against the work; leading with the rarer one overstated, and the paragraph now states both and says which is common. Every number the lens could check held: the 2003 baseline, +48, and all four scratch-repo shapes.

**The tests lens is the one that mattered, and its number is the phase's real product: 49 of 63 mutations survived, against my reported 31/31.** Both numbers are true of different things — **26 of my 31 were reverts of the exact edit I had just made**, which measures that a guard is wired to a file and says nothing about coverage. This is rule 1 of the author-side pass, reproduced *while following it*, one phase after Phase 169 recorded the identical shape. Six distinct bypass classes, all now closed:

- **Nothing required the gate to run anything.** `check_the_gate_is_executable_at_all` was satisfied by the scope command and the clean probe — neither verifies anything. Deleting item 3, or softening it to "if convenient", left a step that resolves a list, computes a changed-file set, confirms the tree is clean, and verifies nothing. One mutation rewrote the whole step as *"OPTIONAL and skipped by default"* **while keeping all eight pins verbatim inside a blockquote**.
- **"Executable fenced line" was not implemented.** `in_fence = stripped != "```"` accepted **any** info string, so re-fencing a command block as ```` ```text ```` or ```` ```console ```` left it counting as executable — and a mutation comment I had written claimed the ```` ```text ```` half of my own A3 mutation mattered when only the `#` did. An unterminated fence also swallowed the rest of the file as executable.
- **Only the first physical line of the scope command was pinned**, so the second was corrupted five ways and every one lived: a `-- '*.md'` pathspec (4a-post doc-only-skips forever), `origin/main...origin/main` (always empty), a `:!tests` exclusion, a two-dot range hidden after a continuation, and the range hoisted into a variable.
- **Section-scoped FORBIDDEN is escapable** — reintroducing the pre-fix Step 3c coupling in Step 3 or Step 3b, one section over, survived. That is the exact regression this phase says it nearly shipped, reachable by moving one sentence.
- **Token-presence checks over the external sites and Step 8.** Rule B's instruction was **inverted** ("There is no need to RE-RUN … push without re-verifying") with both asserted tokens intact; the Step 8 template fence was deleted and replaced with prose *inviting* the reader to mention the lines "if you feel they add value"; the `--dry-run` disclaimer was moved into an HTML comment and, separately, prefixed with "It is a myth that".
- **Population: no guard read `docs/` at all.** Reverting all three public-site edits survived, and `test_doc_currency.py` carries no `4a-post` reference — a public page still describing a single pre-merge gate is the mirror-leak class, shipping to readers who cannot see the skill.

It also found the **over-strict** direction, which is the one that hides: pinning `close_batch.sh` to its bare three-argument form made a Step 4b shipping only the `--force` invocation — the invocation the skill itself mandates under `pr` — go red, and joining the scope command onto one line or writing `> /dev/null` likewise. Those are now normalised, and **five negative controls assert the guards do *not* fire on legitimate rewrites** — one of which immediately earned its keep by catching my own new `optional` regex matching `[project.optional-dependencies]` in Step 3's pytest rule.

**The deletion rung is closed, again in a different module.** `git rm tests/test_review_close_merged_tree_gate.py` left the whole suite green — every floor the module added lived inside it. The existence-and-non-vacuity assertion now sits in `tests/test_invocation_shapes.py`, the same fix and the same file Phase 169 used for its own gate; verified by deleting the module in a copy and watching the suite go red.

**Final battery: 14 checks, 53 mutations all killed, 5 negative controls all surviving, 19 pins.** **One survivor class is declined and it is a judgement no pattern encodes:** a document can always be contradicted by a *novel* added sentence. The four classes that showed up — optional-ising, non-stopping, reordering, and "historical note, no longer applies" — are closed by regex over both passes; the general form terminates at code review, not at a guard, and saying otherwise would be the "known blind spot, as designed" disposition rule 1 forbids.

**Suite: 2003 → 2086 passed + 4 skipped** (+83: 82 in the new `tests/test_review_close_merged_tree_gate.py`, plus the deletion ratchet in `tests/test_invocation_shapes.py`). **The first version of this line said 2064 and was wrong** — written from the pre-round count plus arithmetic instead of from a run. That is the class the round found three times over, so it is corrected here rather than quietly.

## Phase 171 (executed 2026-07-31 — Wave 1 item 3, part A: `/claim-task` becomes an orchestrator, and a spec that had gone stale about itself)

Upstream #220, the last open Wave 1 item and the queue's most serious defect. A real `/claim-task 536` run — a **review batch** — went `EnterPlanMode` → ~200 tool calls → `ExitPlanMode` with **no `Agent` call at any point**. The adversarial review, the finding classification, the sealed `REVIEW_REPORT:` and the halt-on-blocker gate were all bypassed together, and it surfaced only because a human asked. Phase 155 tried to make the omission *detectable* and its own round disqualified the mechanism; the replacement was specified in [`tools/CLAIM_TASK_ORCHESTRATOR_SPEC.md`](./tools/CLAIM_TASK_ORCHESTRATOR_SPEC.md) and left unbuilt through nine phases.

**Scope: this is part A of four.** Wade ratified a four-way cut — (A) the orchestrator core, (B) the readers (`/review-close` artifact reporting, `/sitrep` park predicate, close-time cleanup), (C) option C plan-only, (D) public-doc currency. The seam that made the cut worth taking is that **option C carries the whole `## Plan` body-section surface** — `tasks/schema.md`, a validator invariant, a write-back-on-`main` ordering with five refusal modes, `WORKFLOW.md` § 4.2 — and nothing in the core needs it. 7a's skip condition exists only to consume C's output, so deferring C deleted a step from the core rather than adding a stub.

### The pre-build pass found the spec three phases stale about itself, and that is most of this phase's product

The spec is a 512-line design document whose own status block had been wrong at four revisions — it says so, at `:24`: *"Do not restore the sentence 'no open decision blocks the build.' It has been written twice and been wrong twice."* It contains **zero occurrences of the string `159b`**, and Phase 159b shipped five things it lists as owed. Three lenses over it (shipped-already ledger, citation re-resolution, load-bearing premise verification by execution) plus a harness probe, then every load-bearing result re-verified here.

**Five obligations already discharged.** The third Step 2 entry state (`--entry-state`, and *not* with the spec's semantics — it prescribes "resumable by me", what shipped is `resumable` = **stop and ask**, because `claim_task.sh` records `agent: anonymous` and there is no identity to establish); the park-namespace rename; the `_rt_migration_preflight` decision the spec says to "decide at build time"; Step 8's phase-tolerant envelope read *and* its narrow delete; and the `run_in_background` deletion. **Building any of them again would have regressed working code**, and implementing the spec's `resumable` phrasing would have auto-continued into a re-claim of finished work during the `pr`-close window — the defect 159b's own round caught.

**The mechanism the spec had settled on does not work, and it fails on #220's own claim kind.** Status-block item 2 — itself the replacement for a decision an earlier round broke — keys artifact freshness on the claim lock's `started:` stamp. `batch_work.sh`'s `write_batch_lock` is **idempotent by design** and leaves an existing lock as-is (`:192-195`), so a batch re-claim inherits a **stamp-matching** stale `review.md`, and § *Failure handling*'s single most important rule ("never proceed to 7e without a fresh reviewer return") is satisfied by yesterday's review. A `--release` followed by a re-claim collides at second granularity as a second defeater. And the cited precedent (`review_index.py`'s `is_stale`/`ensure_fresh`) is not the same shape: it *regenerates* where this can only refuse, its token is a hash of the file it guards rather than borrowed from a file with an independent lifetime, and it defines a missing-**index** default (`index is None -> stale`) where the spec defines none for its borrowed token. (Its missing-*source* behaviour is to raise, deliberately — an earlier draft of this sentence said "missing-source" and the round corrected it.)

Verified by execution in a scratch repo built from the shipped scripts and validated against the real `review_index.py` parser: the re-claim exits 0 having mutated nothing (94-path inode/mtime snapshot, byte-identical), `started:` unchanged at the same inode, the worktree is the **same directory**, and a planted `review.md` survives **byte-for-byte**. The chain is real end to end.

**So freshness became structural instead of comparative.** Artifacts live at `sysop/runtime/claim/<CLAIM_ID>/<RUN_ID>/`, where `<RUN_ID>` is minted at Step 7 entry as `<UTC timestamp>-<8 hex>`. A new run cannot inherit an old run's verdict because it never looks in the old directory — both defeaters die by construction rather than by a comparison that has to be right, nothing is deleted mid-lifecycle, and a resume names the run it resumes, which is what finally makes "the artifacts on disk *are* the resume state" true rather than aspirational.

### Where the orchestrator's writes go, and why the spec's answer was stale rather than wrong

`:106` describes `/auto-build`'s park archive as *"a `mkdir -p` plus `{ printf … } > "$ARCHIVE"` block. Already Bash, so it survives the guard."* The tree says the opposite in bold: `auto-build/SKILL.md:517`, **"Write both files with the `Write` tool, not from the shell."**

**An earlier draft of this entry called that "a design collision the spec records as resolved — the one finding that would ship a broken skill." A second take adjudicated it and all three parts of that were hotter than the facts.** The spec's *design* is internally consistent (`:91` and Option C's `:215` both commit orchestrator persistence to Bash heredocs; Phase 169 bans phantom shell *variables*, not heredocs), and the spec labels a genuine collision as one where it has one — the `/document-work` bullet a line below. Reaching broken code requires not opening the file the bullet points at, whose first bold line is the `Write`-tool mandate. And `tools/` never ships, so "ship" had an unstated hop.

**It was verbatim true when written** (`bc1bbd5`); **Phase 162 deleted that block as an instance of the phantom-shell-variable defect** and Phase 169 strengthened the replacement. So: **one stale factual claim in a supporting list** — with the rider that is the part worth keeping, since `:106` now holds up, *as a working precedent for this reshape*, the exact shape this repo removed as a defect, and copying it fails **silently** as an empty archive that reads as a successful record.

The resolution is cheaper than either horn. **Sub-agents write `plan.md` and `review.md`** — they inherit no frontmatter, so `disallowed-tools` never touches them. The orchestrator writes only `classification.md` and the park archive, both through **one already-seeded `Bash(python3 -:*)` heredoc**: zero new permission surface, no dependence on the auto-classifier's treatment of bare `mkdir`/`cp`, and the park copied files that already existed rather than re-serialising context-held values. **(Superseded within this same phase: the artifact move to the main checkout collapsed the copy into a marker, whose `reason` field *is* a context-held value. The `:517` exposure argument no longer applies and the mitigation is different — the reason is substituted as a single-quoted literal, and an empty one is visible in the marker rather than hidden. Round 3 found this paragraph still arguing for the removed design.)** `/auto-build` keeps its `Write`-tool park; it carries no frontmatter guard, and re-mechanising it is out of scope.

### A live defect found on the way: the park was a one-way door

A parked claim leaves its lock intact by design, so `claim_task.sh --entry-state` answers `held` and Step 2 stops — and `claim-task/SKILL.md:632` advised the human to *"re-run `/claim-task <TASK_ID>`"*, which hits that stop. Verified across three reads. This phase creates parks at 7c, so without a way back in the artifact set would be decoration. `--resume <RUN_ID>` is now the one way past the `held` stop: the human names the run, which *is* the explicit go-ahead the `held` arm requires, and the honest limit is stated — `--resume` on a colleague's live lock takes their claim, the same trust model as `--force` elsewhere.

### The record was wrong twice before the round, and both were caught by asking for a second take

Wade's challenge — *"you often think a lot of things are wrong but change your mind after the fact"* — produced two corrections, and the pattern had already fired once unprompted (I wrote up `/auto-build`'s ruleless `mkdir` as a defect, then found `review-close/SKILL.md:34` documenting the same ruleless-`mkdir` decision as a **deliberate** non-entry — about `/review-close` Step 3b's own collect rather than `/auto-build`'s, so the class precedent holds and the site attribution in an earlier draft did not; Phase 169's rule about re-deriving a filed exclusion applies to a filed *finding* too).

**The one that would have shipped:** I wrote into `_shared/plan-review-preference.md` that an auto-closed `AskUserQuestion` is indistinguishable from a real answer, therefore the park-on-timeout rule is unimplementable. **It is implementable.** The official docs say the dialog "submits any options you'd already selected **and tells Claude you may be away from your keyboard**." The refuting sentence was inside the *first probe's own output* — it quoted the line and concluded the opposite, and I read the conclusion without reading the evidence under it. The rule now ships, keying on that signal **semantically**; the exact injected wording is not part of the documented interface, so matching a literal sentence would break silently in the direction that starts unattended implementation runs.

**Transferable, and it is narrower than "verify more":** a *negative* finding needs its own refutation attempt before it goes into shipped prose, and a probe that quotes evidence against its own conclusion has to be read against itself.

### Guards, and the three that fired on documentation

**Final battery: 9 semantic inversions, all killed; 3 negative controls, none firing; a vacuity floor.** Every mutation keeps the asserted phrases **verbatim** and inverts what the step does — the direction a revert battery cannot see, and the one that produced Phase 170's 49-of-63.

**The battery found two holes in its own guards**, both instructive. A presence check for "not delegated" survived a mutation that *added* a spawn instruction while leaving the prohibition on the page. And the batch-abandon mutation silently retargeted onto an earlier match, because `str.replace(…, 1)` takes the first occurrence and this phase added ~350 lines above Step 7 — **Phase 170's exact recorded lesson, recurring inside the battery written to catch it.** Mutations now apply at the *last* occurrence. Two further attempts at the 7c spawn check were defeated in sequence by the battery: one exempted any line mentioning "third sub-agent" (so `Spawn a third sub-agent…` walked through the exemption written for the sentence forbidding it), and one exempted any line containing a negation — which fails because a markdown paragraph is **one line**, so 7c's instruction and its prohibition share it. Only text immediately left of the verb distinguishes "do not spawn" from "spawn".

**Three separate guards fired on prose that *forbids* the thing they check** — two shipped (`tests/`), one maintainer-side (`tools/skill_audit_refs.py`), one written by this phase — — the `run_in_background` pytest ratchet, `tools/skill_audit_refs.py`, and this phase's own plan-mode check. That is `_shared/adversarial-review.md` § *Test strategy*'s named failure ("the sentence forbidding `rm -f` contains `rm -f`") occurring three times in one phase, which suggests the repo has a systematic preference for token-presence checks. Each was fixed in kind rather than by deleting the explanation: the pytest ratchet now bans the *assignment* shape and permits a bare mention only inside a prohibition (4/4 mutations killed); the skill-audit hit uses the repo's own sanctioned `<!-- skill-audit-ok: -->` waiver, which exists for exactly this; the plan-mode check matches the *instructional* shape so the file stays free to narrate the #220 incident.

**Phase 170's ratchet caught me**, which is the system working: it pins two `/claim-task` sentences verbatim so a reflow cannot soften them, and my rewrite dropped both. Restored the pinned wording rather than touching the guard.

**Superseded rather than deleted:** Phase 159b's four Step-8 tolerance guards (un-phased-first resolution order, glob fallback, `exec > review > plan` precedence, narrow delete) asserted scaffolding whose own in-tree note said it was waiting for this reshape. All three prompts now emit `PHASE:`, so the filenames are deterministic and there is nothing to resolve. The successors are **stronger**: "do not widen the delete" becomes **"do not delete at all"**, which is the defect the reshape exists to remove.

### Deliberately not done, so silence does not read as oversight

Option C (parts C), the `/review-close` and `/sitrep` readers and close-time cleanup for both claim kinds (part B), and public-doc currency (part D). Step 6 and the partial both **state** that option C is unbuilt rather than staying quiet about it — silence about a missing branch is how Steps 7–8 acquired roadmap-only vocabulary in Phase 29, which is the defect #220 reported.

**Two things stated rather than left to read as drift.** `/auto-build` uses `Step 7a/7b/7c` for *prompt templates* while `/claim-task` now uses `7a–7e` for *pipeline stages* — a cross-skill vocabulary wart, taken because the spec and the ratified cut both used `7a–7e`. And three external references to "`/claim-task` Step 7b" meant sequence-item 7b *inside* the old prompt; under the reshape `7b` is the reviewer, so they were swept to Step 7e before the steps were named. That is the ambiguity Phase 170's claims lens found one file over ("`/auto-build` Step 4b does not exist").

**Author-side pass rule 3 — run the commands the change prescribes — found the one defect the guards could not.** The three new `python3 -` heredocs were **extracted verbatim from the shipped file and executed** against a scratch repo with a real linked worktree, not retyped. Step 7-pre and the park block ran clean (the park correctly recorded absent artifacts rather than silently omitting them (then as three `.MISSING` files; now as `MISSING` lines inside the one marker), and resolved the archive to the main checkout rather than the worktree). **Step 7c crashed: `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'yaml'`.** The classification write carried a hard PyYAML dependency, so on a consumer whose bare `python3` has no PyYAML — the PEP-668 default Phase 131 documents — the pipeline would halt at 7c after the planner and reviewer had already run — **scoped by the round to the batch path only**, since on the roadmap path Step 2's `--entry-state` exits 3 and the index heredoc dies long before 7c is reached; the batch path happens to be #220's own claim kind, so the fix is still worth having. It is now **stdlib-only**, emitting the block with `json.dumps` since JSON is a subset of YAML 1.2; verified by round-tripping the written file through PyYAML, including a finding carrying embedded quotes and colons — the case hand-rolled YAML gets wrong. A guard and a ninth mutation now pin the stdlib-only property. **This is Phase 167's rule paying off a second time: a prescribed command stays text until an operator reaches it.**

**The round found the branch RED, and the leak is the more important half.** `git add -A` in the first commit tracked `sysop/runtime/locks/TECH-0007.lock` — a **real lock** a reconciliation sub-agent had created, carrying an absolute home path. Locks resolve to the **main** repo root by design (Phase 32), so any worktree's claim lands in the shared checkout. It turned `test_mirror_leak_gate.py::test_pass_1b_no_absolute_home_paths` red, and `make_public_mirror.sh`'s deny-list does not cover it, so **it would have shipped to the public mirror** — the exact class Phase 160 built that gate for. Root cause: **this repo has no `sysop/runtime/` gitignore entry at all** while `install.sh:3119` seeds precisely that for consumers, so Phase 133's "one gitignored home" was never gitignored in Sysop's own tree. Both fixed, and this phase is the first to prescribe orchestrator writes under that path, so it would have recurred.

**Two process lessons, and the first is the one to keep.** I ran the suite **before** `git add -A` and reported green — the file was untracked at that moment, so the gate could not see it. **A suite run that precedes staging does not describe the commit.** And the record's own sentence *"measured from a run, not derived"* was, at the reviewed SHA, false in the way it congratulated itself for avoiding: a real run there produced `1 failed, 2093 passed`. The number below is a post-fix run.

**Suite: 2086 → 2094 passed + 4 skipped** (+8 net: 5 new orchestrator guards, plus the Step-8 successors replacing four superseded ones; measured from a run, not derived — Phase 170's record was wrong on exactly that).

### The adversarial round — three lenses, and the phase does not close on it

Three fresh-context `general-purpose` reviewers, worktree-isolated, distinct lenses (does it execute / are its claims true / are its guards real), each anchored to `d815666` and told to verify the revision it read. **Overlap was low and each lens's sharpest finding was reached by no other**, matching the ~15% Phase 166 measured.

**The guards lens is the product: 52 mutations run, 46 survived. This phase's own new guards detected 1 of 44.** Of the six that reddened CI, three were *anchor collisions* in my own battery ("mutation is a no-op") rather than detections, and two of the three real detections came from **pre-existing** guards (Phase 169's phantom-shell-vars, Phase 159b's entry-state prose). Measured against the predicates directly, **49 of 52 are invisible to every guard this phase ships**.

My record said *"9 semantic inversions, all killed."* That set was self-selected: every one is a single-string edit at an anchor the guards were written to assert. **I report a near-perfect kill rate and an independent lens finds the opposite** — and this is not a streak I should be counting — it is the project's standing condition. Phase 161 already recorded *six consecutive* phase records where reviewers found the phase's own new guards weaker than it had just claimed, and Phase 166 measured it at **twelve of the sixteen phases from 150 to 165**. Phase 169's round ran 103 mutations and found 52 survivors against its own reported 35/35; Phase 167's found 43 of 90. Two earlier drafts of this sentence called it "the third consecutive phase" and then "the fourth such measurement in a row"; both were false, and the second was written *while correcting the first*. Writing the caveat into the record is not the same as escaping the bias — I wrote that sentence about Phase 159b in this same entry and then reproduced it.

**The survivor classes are structural, not gaps to patch.** Every check is a substring presence test over prose, so **optional-ising (5/5 survived), reordering (3/3) and "historical note — no longer applies" framing are all free**: a blockquote declaring Step 7b `OPTIONAL and omitted by default` leaves `**Always.**` on the page and nothing fires; an `**Order of operations:** 7a → 7e → 7b` puts the review after the commit it reviews — Phase 170's own defect class, reintroduced invisibly. Commands re-fenced as ` ```text ` or commented out survive. `rm -rf` walks through a guard that forbids the literal `rm -f` span. A duplicate `disallowed-tools:` key clears the list by YAML last-key-wins while the regex matches the first line. **The new `_shared/plan-review-preference.md` is 8/8 unguarded** — including inverting the resolution order and making an auto-closed question *the decision*, the file's entire reason for existing.

**Over-strictness is worse than the bypasses, and it is the direction that hides: 15 of 18 legitimate rewrites go red.** Adding *"Do not skip this step under any preference"* to Step 7b trips the check for conditionality — **the sentence forbidding the thing fires the guard for it**, the named failure mode, shipped a fourth time in this phase. `**Always**` without the period, `**This is never delegated**`, `**Do not proceed to 7e.**`, a YAML comment after `disallowed-tools:`, and a lowercase `Do **not** pass` all red. Sharpest of all: **`partial_problems` matches the literal string `away from your keyboard` — precisely what the partial it guards forbids** (*"Key on the meaning, not on a literal string… a guard matching a specific sentence would break silently the first time that wording changes"*). The guard violates the rule it exists to protect.

**Two floors are open, both verified by execution.** `git rm tests/test_claim_task_orchestrator.py` leaves the suite green — nothing outside the module references it, and `orchestrator_problems`, the battery, the negative controls and the vacuity floor all live inside it. And **`test_guards_are_not_vacuous` is itself vacuous**: both probes raise `ValueError` at `_section` and hit `continue`, so its `assert problems` never executes. Confirmed by running it.

**Population is one file while the same rules ship in three.** `WORKFLOW.md:1569` and `:1864` still prescribe *"deleted by the parent skill after consumption"* — the delete Step 8 now forbids — and § 2.2 items 4–11 restate every property `orchestrator_problems` guards, unguarded. § 8.4 has no row for `sysop/runtime/claim/`. **(The round said § 8.4; runtime directories are § 8.6, which is where the rows landed. Reproduced uncorrected here until round 3 caught it.)** That is the repo's own author-side rule 1 case: *derive the population from the source of truth, not from one file*.

**Two defects the lenses found that block on their own**, and neither is a guard problem:

1. **`--resume <RUN_ID>` is inert — this phase's headline live-defect fix.** Step 1 and Step 2 validate the run id against repo-relative `sysop/runtime/claim/<CLAIM_ID>/`, resolved in the orchestrator's CWD (the **main checkout**); Step 7-pre creates it inside the **worktree**. They never meet, so every `--resume` is rejected and the error path's "print the available run ids" itself ENOENTs. At Step 1 the check is unperformable even in principle, since argument parsing precedes the lock read that would reveal the worktree. **The fix is to put the artifact directory in the main checkout**, where the hook-written envelopes and the park archive already live and where the orchestrator runs.
2. **The skill states part-B readers in the present tense.** `:769` claims `/review-close` Step 4c "owns cleanup for both claim kinds" and `:424` that a bypassed pipeline leaves an artifact directory *"`/review-close` and `/sitrep` report on."* **There are no readers** — `grep -rn "runtime/claim"` finds only this skill and two lines of `WORKFLOW.md` prose. And it is not a flag-flip: 7c's park writes a **directory** while `review-close:1017` globs `{tid}__*.md` **files**, so it can never match. That is the reshape's central detectability claim, asserted about deferred work. A rider: **envelopes carry no run component and are now never deleted**, so on a re-claim Step 8's "first hit wins" reads the *previous* run's `exec.json` and prints "Claim complete" — per-run keying protects the artifact directory, not the artifact Step 8 actually reads.

**Status at that point: Phase 171 was NOT closed.** The mechanism findings from the pre-build pass survived scrutiny and the reshape's shape was sound, but its headline fix did not work, its central claim was stated about unbuilt work, and its guards were decorative. Recorded rather than carried in a session, because a round that found this much and left no trace is the exact failure this whole phase is about.

### The rebuild — what the round's findings actually cost

**The artifact directory moved to the main checkout, and that one move discharged four things at once.** `--resume` becomes performable at Step 1, *before* any lock has been read, because the run directory no longer depends on knowing a worktree; the artifacts outlive `git worktree remove` and `cleanup_worktrees.sh --force` on their own; the park's second copy — which existed only to rescue them from that wipe — collapses into a marker; and the orchestrator writes where it already runs, alongside the hook-written envelopes. Resolution is `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` → parent, in every block that touches the set. **Verified by execution from *both* checkouts**: run from inside a linked worktree, Step 7-pre still lands the directory in the main repo.

**One re-entry point, and it is Step 7-pre.** The three statements the round found disagreeing (Step 2 said "at Step 7", 7c said "at 7a", and 7-pre minted a new run unconditionally with no `--resume` clause) now agree: 7-pre **adopts** a named run instead of minting one, and a routing table reads the stage to re-enter off the artifacts present — no `plan.md` → 7a, no `review.md` → 7b, no `classification.md` → 7c, `verdict: BLOCKED` → 7c with the human's answer as the new input, `PROCEED` → 7d/7e. That is what makes *"the artifacts on disk are the resume state"* a mechanism rather than a slogan. A guard asserts the file names no second entry point.

**The park marker is now a file the one existing reader can actually match.** 7c wrote a directory `<CLAIM_ID>__<RUN_ID>` while `review-close:1017` globs `{tid}__*.md`; executed, it returned `[]`, so parks accumulated forever. The marker is `sysop/runtime/parked/<CLAIM_ID>__<RUN_ID>.md` — same shape as `/auto-build`'s, and **executing the real glob against a real marker now returns it**. Scoped honestly rather than claimed: `/review-close` Step 4c builds that list from **roadmap ids only**, so a `BATCH-<N>` marker is still removed by nothing. Said out loud in the skill, in `WORKFLOW.md` § 8.6 and here, because that is part B's job and silence about a missing branch is the Phase-29 defect #220 reported.

**Both present-tense claims about part-B readers are gone.** `:424` said a bypassed pipeline leaves an artifact directory *"`/review-close` and `/sitrep` report on"*; it now says the difference is durable and inspectable and that **nothing reads it yet**. `:769` said Step 4c "owns cleanup for both claim kinds"; Step 8 now states what actually happens — the lock and a roadmap park marker go, `sysop/runtime/claim/` is untouched for either kind, and close-time cleanup is unbuilt. This was the reshape's central detectability claim asserted about deferred work, and it is the kind of sentence a round has to catch because it reads as a design, not as a lie.

**The rider was the sharper half and it needed a structural answer, not a caveat.** Envelopes are keyed `<CLAIM_ID>.<phase>.json` with **no run component** and Step 8 now (correctly) never deletes them — so a re-claim's "first hit wins" read the *previous* run's `exec.json` and printed "Claim complete" for work this run never did. Per-run keying protected the artifact directory and not the artifact Step 8 actually reads. Step 7-pre now **moves** any leftover envelopes for the claim into `<ARTIFACT_DIR>/prior-envelopes/` before spawning anything: the mailbox is empty by construction at the start of every fresh run, nothing is destroyed, and the moved files gain the run attribution a shared mailbox could never give them. A resume deliberately does not move — its own `plan.json` may still be sitting there — and the one case that leaves open (another run of the same claim ran later) is stated rather than hidden.

**The five smaller round findings, each fixed at its cause.** The post-plan integrity check discussed a `$PRE_PLAN_HEAD` that existed nowhere and buried the only instruction to capture it inside a comment in the block that runs *after* the planner: the capture is now its own fenced command at the top of 7a, and the check is a **mechanical verdict** (`planner-integrity: OK | VIOLATED`) rather than a SHA for a human to eyeball hundreds of tool calls in. The two failure paths that parked "with the recorded reason" now have a reason field to record it in. Step 7-pre's comment no longer claims a PyYAML bootstrap the block does not contain. The batch path establishes `<BRANCH_NAME>` — off `batch_work.sh`'s own `│  Branch:` summary line, with the lock's `branch:` field as the fallback — which all three prompts substitute and every envelope requires. And `WORKFLOW.md`'s two *"deleted by the parent skill after consumption"* sites are corrected with the reason (that delete is #220's root cause), § 8.6 gains rows for `sysop/runtime/claim/` and the new park marker, and § 2.2 carries the moved shape.

**Author-side pass rule 3 found a live command-injection path, and it is the second phase running where a prescribed command stayed text until an operator reached it.** Every heredoc was extracted verbatim from the shipped file and run against a scratch repo with a real linked worktree — including the failure paths, which behave as documented (`--resume` on an unknown id exits 3 and lists the real runs; on a claim that has never run it prints `available runs: (none)` rather than raising, since the error path must not itself be the crash). The find: `<PARK_REASON>` is **free text returned by a sub-agent** — a `blocker` question, an executor's `BLOCKER_QUESTION:` — and it was substituted into a **double-quoted** shell argument. Verified both directions in a scratch shell: inside double quotes a `$(…)` in that text *executes*; inside single quotes it is inert and recorded verbatim. It is now single-quoted, with the one residual rule (a literal `'`) stated. Every other placeholder in the file is a shape the tree produced — an id, a SHA, a path — which is why this is the only site.

**Author-side pass rule 2 — re-read your own new prose against the code it describes — found the twin spec still narrating the retired shape, and did not find enough.** `WORKFLOW_GUIDE.md` § 2 says `/claim-task` "flips `status: open → in_progress` … and creates the lock" and then hands the reader a manual § 3 *Plan* / § 4 *Code* — true before the reshape, and now an incomplete description of a command that plans, reviews, classifies and executes. Phase 170's precedent is that the two specs move together (both had ordered verification before the merge, and all three files moved in one phase). One paragraph closes it: what `/claim-task` now does, where the artifacts land, and that §§ 3–5 are the **manual** path rather than a second set of steps to run after it. **The full human-readable re-narration is part D and is not attempted here** — the sentence that was actively wrong is fixed; the guide's overall framing is a doc-currency job.

Also verified by reading rather than assumed, since three of this phase's new sentences rest on them: `batch_work.sh:192-195` really is the idempotent-lock arm; `batch_work.sh:727` really prints `│  Branch:`; both lock writers really carry `branch:` and `workspace:`; and `/review-close` Step 4c's close list really is roadmap-only — `ids = ["<ROADMAP_ID_1>", …]` with the comment *"review_task_ids are NOT processed here"* directly above it — which is what makes the batch-marker gap a fact rather than a guess.

**Running the commands also refuted a claim the shipped file was already making.** Step 7-pre said `install.sh` appends `sysop/runtime/` to `.gitignore` "but never commits it, so on a fresh consumer the ignore rule is not yet on the branch and the directory shows in `git status`." Git honours a working-tree `.gitignore` whether or not it is committed — measured — so on a bootstrapped consumer nothing shows. The paragraph now states the true property and keeps the part that was right and load-bearing: with no entry at all, git collapses to `?? sysop/`, so keying a check on the literal `?? sysop/runtime/` is wrong.

**The guards were rebuilt against properties, and the classes came from the round's survivors rather than from imagination.** The failure was uniform: every check was a substring presence test over prose, which makes four whole classes of edit free. So — `bash_lines()` is **language-aware**, so re-fencing a prescribed command as ` ```text ` or commenting it out removes it from the executable set and the check that asserts the command is prescribed fires; `bash_blocks()` scopes a check to the fence a command belongs to, because a step-wide check was satisfied by a *neighbouring* block; `optionalising()` reads a normalised character window clipped at the sentence boundary, so `Do not skip this step` is exempt and `Under option B, skip this step` is not; `ordering_violations()` checks a *sequence*, killing `7a → 7e → 7b`; the frontmatter is parsed rather than grepped, so a duplicate `disallowed-tools:` key is caught by counting keys rather than by a regex that matches the first line YAML ignores; and no executable line in Steps 7–8 may carry a delete verb, matched as a family so `rm -rf` cannot walk through a guard written for `rm -f`. The artifact-path rule is **universal** — *every* spelled-out path must carry the run key — because a presence test for the keyed form was satisfied by one occurrence in the Step 8 summary box.

**Over-strictness was the worse half and it is fixed at the same root.** Emphasis, punctuation, case and whitespace are stripped before anything is matched, so `**Always**` without the period, `**This is never delegated**`, a YAML comment after `disallowed-tools:`, the tools reordered and a lowercase `Do **not** pass` all stay green — and `test_negative_controls_do_not_fire` carries **every rewrite the round found red, by name**, including the one that mattered most: *"Do not skip this step under any preference"*, the sentence forbidding the thing, which used to fire the guard for it. **`partial_problems`'s literal `away from your keyboard` check is deleted outright.** It asserted the harness's own wording — precisely what the partial it guards forbids — so the guard violated the rule it existed to protect. What is checked now is the *directive*: that an auto-closed question is treated as a park and never as a decision.

**Both floors are closed.** `test_guards_are_not_vacuous` **never executed its assertion** — both probes raised `ValueError` in `_section` and hit `continue`, confirmed by running it; `section()` now returns `None` and the caller records a problem, the floor asserts a *count* rather than truthiness, and it covers all three corpora. And `git rm tests/test_claim_task_orchestrator.py` no longer leaves the suite green: the existence-and-non-vacuity assertion lives in `tests/test_invocation_shapes.py`, the third rung of the ladder Phases 169 and 170 built, next to theirs.

**Population widened from one file to three.** `_shared/plan-review-preference.md` was **8/8 unguarded** — including inverting the resolution order and making an auto-closed question *the decision*, the file's entire reason for existing — and now has its own predicate and its own battery. `WORKFLOW.md` § 2.2 restated the shape's load-bearing claims with no guard of its own; it has one now — a **seven-property subset**, not the sixty checks `orchestrator_problems` runs, and the docstring says so. An earlier draft of this sentence said "every property" and "the same properties", which is the overstatement this phase criticises elsewhere. That is the repo's own author-side rule 1 applied to the guards themselves.

**37 mutations, all killed — and that number measures wiring, not coverage.** It is my own battery, written after reading which classes survived, so it is exactly the self-selection this phase has now watched three predecessors fall into. Four survivors during construction were real and each exposed a genuine hole: a negator in the *previous paragraph* exempting a plan-mode instruction (the window is now clipped at the sentence boundary), the park block standing in for the classification write, the roadmap path's `<BRANCH_NAME>` satisfying a check meant for the batch path, and a prose-only mutation that proved nothing until it was rewritten to move the executable line. Two of this module's own predicates went red against a clean tree because `norm()` stripped `__` as underscore-emphasis and deleted the separator out of `<CLAIM_ID>__<RUN_ID>`. **The round is what measures coverage.**

### The second round — the rebuild was disqualified too, and the reason was one level down

Three fresh-context `general-purpose` reviewers again, worktree-isolated, distinct lenses (does it execute / are its claims true / are its guards real), each anchored to `e3ff51f` and told to verify the revision it read.

**The guards lens is the product for the second time: 100 mutations run, 74 survived.** I had reported 37, all killed. That number was self-selected in exactly the way the first round's record predicted and the way I wrote a caveat about. **And this is not a streak I should be counting — it is the project's standing condition.** Phase 161 already recorded *six consecutive* phase records where reviewers found the phase's own new guards weaker than it had just claimed, and Phase 166 measured it at **twelve of the sixteen phases from 150 to 165**. Phase 169's round ran 103 mutations and found 52 survivors against its own reported 35/35; Phase 167's found 43 of 90. Two earlier drafts of this sentence called it "the third consecutive phase" and then "the fourth such measurement in a row"; both were false, and the second was written *while correcting the first*. Writing "the round is what measures coverage" underneath the number did not stop the number from being wrong.

**The diagnosis is one level below the first round's, and it is the design of the guards now.** Every property that matters is realised in *code* — the `python3 - <<'PY'` heredocs the skill prescribes — and I was matching *prose*. Four mutations, each inverting the phase's own headline property, survived and I re-confirmed all four by calling the predicates directly:

```
d = claim_root / run_id            ->  d = claim_root                  # every run shares one dir
main_root = Path(common).resolve().parent -> Path(os.environ['PWD'])   # back in the worktree
"OK" if now == pre else "VIOLATED" ->  "OK" if now != pre ...          # integrity verdict inverted
if resume:                         ->  if resume and False:            # --resume inert again
```

The "universal artifact-path rule" written to catch the first two matched a literal string occurring **once** in a 954-line file. So the code checks now **parse the code**: each prescribed block is pulled out of its fence and `ast.parse`d, and the checks assert properties of the syntax tree — which components a path is composed from, which branch a `mkdir` sits in, whether the comparison selecting `"OK"` is `==` or `!=`, whether an `if` test carries a literal that makes its branch dead. **That is also the fix for the over-strictness half**, which round 2 measured at **21 of 33 legitimate rewrites going red**: an f-string, a tuple unpack, `os.replace` for `.rename`, `secrets.token_urlsafe` for `token_hex` and `rev-parse --verify` all pass now, where all five went red before, and three YAML spellings of one frontmatter value stopped being a hand-rolled `split(",")`.

**The prose guards became an allowlist, because a pattern list can always be extended one phrase further than the guard.** Round 2 walked 13 of 13 optional-ising mutations through a 12-pattern list — *"superseded"*, *"retained for historical interest"*, *"legacy guidance"*, *"bypass this block when…"* — so the design inverts: Steps 7–8 may contain only the conditional clauses enumerated in `CONDITIONAL_ALLOWLIST`, derived by enumeration rather than memory, and any *new* one fires. A test asserts every allowlisted clause is still in the file, because a stale entry is a permanent hole.

**Two floors were open and both are closed.** `git rm` was already covered; **gutting was not** — the cross-module check only grepped for eight `def` signatures, and the lens verified that a module reduced to those signatures with `return []` bodies satisfied every one of them. It now *calls* the predicates from outside and requires them to detect five planted defects. And the population was three files while the rules ship in four: **`WORKFLOW_GUIDE.md` § 2 was unguarded and had been written by the same commit** — the author-side rule-1 case ("derive the population from the source of truth, not from one file") applied to the guards themselves, one paragraph after I had congratulated myself for applying it.

**Three defects that block on their own, from the execute lens, all verified here by execution.**

1. **Step 8's `BLOCKED` park sent the resume to the executor.** It recorded the blocker question as the park *reason* but never touched `classification.md`, which still read `verdict: PROCEED` — it had to, or 7e would never have spawned. The routing table therefore matched its last row and re-spawned the executor with byte-identical inputs, so **the one runtime path that produces a blocker question could never reach the row written for it**. Step 8 now rewrites the classification to `BLOCKED` before parking.
2. **A path reached 7e with the reviewer never having seen the plan it executes.** Step 7d's *revise* re-planned into the **same** run directory, so a revised `plan.md` sat beside the previous plan's `review.md` and `classification.md`; a run that died before 7b finished matched the last row and went straight to the executor. **Revise now mints a new run** — one run, one plan — which is what makes presence-based routing sound at all, and the superseded run stays on disk as the record of what was rejected. A new first row also stops a completed run from re-executing: an `exec.json` in the mailbox means the executor already ran.
3. **The batch resume established neither `<BRANCH_NAME>` nor the worktree path** — the lock-reading sentence sat in the roadmap arm, above the claim-kind split, while the batch arm said only "skip Step 4, re-enter at 7-pre". Step 4's summary box, which Step 3 names as the establishing site, is exactly what a resume skips. **That is the class the first build was disqualified for, reappearing one arm over**, and it is #220's own claim kind.

Four more: both `held` arms printed a `classification.md` that a 7a or 7b park never creates; a planner-integrity park resumed at 7b with the violation never re-gated (the routing now reads the park marker first, and that reason re-enters at 7a); **7c and the park would `mkdir` a run that Step 7-pre never minted, which Step 1's `--resume` validator then blessed** — both refuse now, verified; and Step 8's `_unparseable_*.json` fallback is unattributed by construction, so it is now stated as a hint to open and read rather than as this run's result.

**One finding refuted, decomposed clause by clause.** The lens called `git -C "<WORKTREE_PATH>" rev-parse HEAD` a new ungated command proving the "no new permission surface" claim false. It is not new — `32bffd1:530` carries it verbatim — and `_shared/permission-guard.md:117` explicitly says *not* to list read-only `git`, naming `git rev-parse`, because listing it makes a skill hard-stop on a fresh install. So the rule it asks for would be the defect. The remaining clauses (quote normalisation in the matcher) resolve the same way: the pre-existing Step 2 and 4a heredocs already ship quoted arguments under the same rule.

**The claims lens found five falsehoods, and the one that stings is inside the file I rewrote.** `claim-task/SKILL.md:246` still read *"loaded as context for **Step 6 plan mode**"* — in a file whose second paragraph says it never enters plan mode, and whose Step 6 is now the plan-review preference. It survived the reshape unedited, and **my own rule-2 pass, which I had just written up as having "found the twin spec still narrating the retired shape", walked past it.** The record now says that pass did not find enough. Four more: `/auto-build:830` told the human to *"invoke `/claim-task` to re-enter plan mode"*; `_shared/adversarial-review.md:163` still called the envelope *"the reviewer-executor's"* in the file whose own § 127 declares that variant retired; `docs/workflow.html:1379` asserted the retired self-classifying shape in the **present tense** on the public site; and `docs/install-and-update.md:211` said `/claim-task` *"does three things"*. All five fixed — **and the sweep was still incomplete**: round 3 found `_shared/adversarial-review.md:110` (two paragraphs above the `:163` I had just fixed) and `docs/workflow.html:1398` still describing the reviewer-executor leaf as current. Both now fixed too. That is the same do-not-fix-a-finding-without-sweeping-its-class rule failing twice in one phase, in the same two files. **The `docs/` fixes widen scope into part D by a few sentences and that is a deliberate call**: currency is deferred, a shipped sentence asserting the shape this phase exists to replace is not the same class. The monograph's two *figure labels* are left — they need an SVG re-layout, not a word change, and that is part D.

The lens also caught two overstatements in this very entry — `workflow_problems` described as checking "every property" and "the same properties" when it is a seven-property subset against sixty checks, which is the overstatement this phase criticises elsewhere — and a `CLAUDE.md` row 235 characters against the file's own ~200 cap. Both corrected. And `tools/CLAIM_TASK_ORCHESTRATOR_SPEC.md` still prescribed the worktree-side artifact path at four sites, so the spec was still telling the next reader to build the defect the round had just disqualified; it now carries a superseded banner and the corrected paths.

**The numbers, with the caveat stated once and meant.** The battery is now **65 mutations (2 of them structural rewriters) and 29 negative controls**, over 115 check sites across four predicates (a fifth, `reader_pairing_problems`, adds 3 more; an earlier draft said "over 116" and was derived from a `grep -c` that counted a line in a docstring). Every mutation class is copied from round 2's survivor report rather than invented, and four *more* real holes surfaced while building it — a guard satisfied by an `is_dir()` in the wrong branch, `--no-review-plan` exempting its own clause because a hyphen is a word boundary, the `<<'PY'` delimiter counted as a positional argument, and a check reading the last of three identical assignments.

**The third round's author-side pass then found the allowlist's own hole, which is worth stating because it is the general shape of an allowlist.** Exempting a conditional because an allowlisted phrase appears *near* it (a ±90-character window) let a new one be smuggled in beside it; tightening that to the same *clause* let one ride along **inside** it — `Step 7b is optional and Row 2 fires only when plan.md is absent` inherited the routing table's exemption whole. The rule now is that the matched word must fall **within the allowlisted span itself**: proximity is not identity, and neither is sharing a sentence. Four smuggling shapes tested, all detected. A related consequence, recorded because it will bite the next editor: one clause with *two* conditional tokens needs *two* entries — `WORKFLOW.md` § 2.2's solo-workflow sentence carries both `bypass` and `omit`, and the tightening turned the second into a live finding until the first was listed. **It is still my battery, and a fourth round would be the thing that measures it.** What has changed is not the number but where the checks look: at a syntax tree the mutations have to actually break, rather than at prose they can walk around.

**And Phase 170's other lesson landed on a neighbour, which is where I was not looking.** `test_batch_claim_kinds.py` asserted that Step 2's review-batch branch mentions `sysop/runtime/locks/<CLAIM_ID>.lock` **at least twice** — its way of saying "the `Pending` arm and the `In Progress` arm both check the lock". This phase's `--resume` paragraph added a *third* mention, so its own mutation test (drop the `Pending` arm's check) left the count at 2 and the guard silently stopped firing. That is verbatim *"adding text to a file weakens every count-based check over that file"*, recorded by Phase 170 and re-recorded by the first half of this phase, recurring a third time — and the fix belongs on the guard, not on the prose: it now anchors each arm and looks **inside** it, which is the claim it was always making. Verified by dropping each arm independently; both are detected, where the count check could only ever see the pair.

### The third round — 82.5% survival, and the floor was hollow

Three fresh-context reviewers again, worktree-isolated, anchored to `5915c98`, each pointed at the *new* design rather than the one its predecessors broke.

**120 mutations, 99 survived (82.5%)**, against my reported 65-plus-29-all-green. **The single most important finding is not the number — it is that the vacuity floor asserted nothing.** All 23 problems an empty corpus produces are *anchor-absence* ("Step 7b is gone", "pipeline lost ### Step 7a"). Every AST check sits behind an `if hd is None` early-out, so **the entire code layer — the checks carrying this phase's headline properties — could be deleted with the floor green**, and the lens proved it by gutting the module to ~45 lines that passed every floor while missing 7 of 8 real defects. Confirmed here by measurement: 23 of 23 empty-corpus problems are anchor-absence, 0 substantive.

**The largest survivor class was a category error in my own design.** `tokens_for` is a **set**, and the property is **structural**. Twenty-two mutations carried every required token — `$claim_id`, `$run_id`, `$common` — while sending the write elsewhere: `(claim_root / run_id).parent`, `claim_root / run_id if False else claim_root`, `_mk(claim_root, run_id)` with a lambda that discards its second argument, a dict whose `'used'` key points at the wrong path. Set membership cannot express *"the path IS this composition"*. Replaced with `path_chain`, which returns the **ordered** components of a *bare* `/`-chain and `None` for any wrapper, call, conditional or subscript; all eight of the class I re-tested are now detected, including the four that invert the phase's headline property.

Both floors are rebuilt to require **detection rather than presence**: the in-module floor now plants nine semantically-wrong-but-structurally-valid inversions and requires each to be caught, and the cross-module floor plants five. A gutted module fails both — verified by building one.

**Three live defects in the skill, and the first is self-inflicted by the previous round's own fix.** Round 2's fix for the `BLOCKED` resume added a routing row keyed on `<CLAIM_ID>.exec.json` **in the shared envelope mailbox** — which a resume deliberately does not clear. So a `BLOCKED` resume matched *that* row, went to Step 8, re-parked, and printed "resume with `--resume`" again: **a loop, and it made the `BLOCKED` row unreachable** — the row added in the same commit for the one runtime path that produces a blocker question. The same shape sent a resume of an older run to the executor. **Nothing routes off the shared mailbox any more**; Step 8 records the executor's terminal status into the run's own `outcome.md`. Second: the integrity verdict lived only in orchestrator context, so a crash between the planner's return and the check left `plan.md` with nothing recording that it was never re-gated, and the table routed it to a reviewer — laundering the exact plan the check exists to catch, by crash rather than by park. `planner-integrity.md` now records it, and carries the *original* pre-plan SHA so a re-entry does not re-baseline onto the rogue commit. Third: **7d's `abandon` left `main` in a state `validate_tasks.py` rejects** — Step 4d *committed* `in_progress`, and `claim_task.sh --release` reverses the index in the working tree only and says so on its own last line. Committed `main` read `in_progress` with no lock, Invariant 9, for everyone who pulls. Verified by execution; the abandon now commits.

**The claims lens found nine, and two are the lessons this phase was explicitly told not to re-learn.** The walk-back I wrote for the "consecutive phase" count landed in **one of three** sites — `REVIEW_CHECKLIST.md` and an earlier `PHASE_LOG.md` paragraph still shipped the refuted forms. *"Correct the artifact, not just the record"* failed while I was correcting a record. And **the corrected form was itself false**: Phase 169's round ran 103 mutations against its own reported 35/35, Phase 167's found 43 of 90, Phase 161 already recorded *six consecutive*, and Phase 166 measured **twelve of the sixteen phases from 150 to 165**. There is no streak to count — it is the project's standing condition, and all three sites now say that. The second: my `docs/`-sweep for the retired reviewer-executor shape missed `_shared/adversarial-review.md:110`, **two paragraphs above the `:163` I had just fixed**, and `docs/workflow.html:1398`, in a file I had just edited — *do not fix a finding without sweeping its class*, failing twice in one phase in the same two files. Also: a `PHASE_LOG` paragraph still argued for the park's **copy** semantics that the same entry later replaced with a marker; my spec "fix" had stripped `<worktree>` with a blind `sed` and left **no `<RUN_ID>`**, so the spec was prescribing this phase's own headline defect under a banner calling that path wrong; "116 check sites" was 115, counted from a `grep -c` that caught a docstring line; and the round-1 finding's `§ 8.4` mis-cite (runtime dirs are § 8.6) was reproduced uncorrected. All fixed.

**What I am not claiming.** The allowlist that carries the prose guards cannot be made sound — the lens walked 24 mutations through it with phrasings the regex does not contain ("discretionary", "best-effort", "where practical", "no longer part of the pipeline"), and any word list can be extended one phrase further than the guard. It is a tripwire for common phrasings, not a gate, and the docstring now says so instead of claiming Steps 7–8 "may contain only" the allowlisted clauses. The unfixed classes the round names — `delete_calls` missing `subprocess.run(["rm",…])` and truncation, `heredoc_containing` binding the first of two matching blocks, `/auto-build` stating the same properties unguarded — are recorded rather than quietly dropped.

**Suite: 2094 → 2114 passed + 4 skipped** (measured after staging; +12 are the heredoc-execution module). **An earlier draft of this line said 2108 — derived from counting checks I had added rather than read off a run. That is the third time in this one phase I have written a derived suite number, twice in sentences whose own subject was measuring rather than deriving.** The checks this round added live inside existing predicates and existing tests, so the count did not move.

### The different-model adjudication — and it corrected me in both directions

Wade's call, and it closed a gap I should have caught: `_shared/adversarial-review.md:29` **requires** at least one reviewer on a different model from the author where the harness offers one, because same-model review is *correlated* with the author rather than independent. **All nine reviewers across the three rounds inherited the session model.** Nine same-model reviewers is one tolerance profile sampled nine times. A single Fable agent was given the three rounds' findings and the tree, and asked the four questions a mutation battery cannot ask about itself.

**Its verdict: ship part A, do not run a fourth round.** And it gave the design a name I did not have. The reshape converged on one invariant — **every gate writes a file into a per-run directory in the main checkout; routing reads only those files; only Step 7-pre mints a run; nothing routes off the shared mailbox.** Read that way, *every* blocking defect the three rounds found was a place state **escaped** that invariant — a worktree-side directory, a classification left reading `PROCEED`, a same-run re-plan, a mailbox-keyed routing row, a verdict held only in context — and every fix was a **completion** of it rather than a patch around a design that had failed. It walked the full pipeline cold, both claim kinds, fresh and resumed, and found **no new blocking defect**; it independently verified the seams against the shipped scripts and re-ran the suite (2102 + 4, exact).

**It refused two of my headline framings, with reasons.** *"82.5% survival"* measures an **adversarial editor** of a prose file; the realistic threat is careless drift, and the surviving classes — hostile re-framing, novel conditional phrasings — sit mostly outside that threat model, while the guards do catch the drift classes that occur in practice. And *"the blocking count has not declined"* is arithmetically true and **diagnostically wrong**: centrality collapsed. Round 1's were design-level (the headline feature inert, readers claimed that did not exist); round 3's were one self-inflicted routing row, a crash window, and a missing commit on an exit path. Its judgement of the product is that it is **materially better than my own three-disqualifications framing suggests**, and I am recording that because a review that ratifies the author's pessimism is as uninformative as one that ratifies their confidence.

**It sharpened the method conclusion rather than accepting it.** The unguardable thing is not "author-graded batteries" — it is **the artifact type**. This is a program executed by an LLM reading prose, so optional-ising, reordering and "historical note" framing change semantics with **no anchor touched**; no static check can pin *"an LLM will still treat this as mandatory"*, and effort there is misallocated. The *code* half is guardable, and the highest-fidelity guard is **execution, not `ast.parse`**. Its evidence is the sharpest thing in the whole phase: **the four defects that actually mattered were all found by running the commands, and none of them by any of the 272 mutations.** The PyYAML halt, the park-reason injection, the placeholders that materialised instead of refusing, and the shipped `.gitignore` falsehood — all rule 3, which until now was a manual pass that ran when its author remembered.

**So the one build this round adds is that mechanisation.** `tests/test_claim_task_heredocs_execute.py` extracts all six prescribed heredocs from `SKILL.md` **verbatim** — retyping would test a copy, the failure mode rule 3 exists to prevent — and executes them against a real repo with a real linked worktree: the artifact directory landing in the main checkout *when run from inside the worktree*, a resume adopting rather than minting, the envelope move-aside sparing a prefix-sharing claim, the classification write surviving a stubbed-out PyYAML, a `$(touch)` payload in the park reason recorded inert, the park marker matching `/review-close`'s real glob, the integrity check keeping its **original** baseline across a violation, every writer refusing a run 7-pre never minted, and an uncommitted `.gitignore` being honoured. **Non-vacuity verified by planting six inversions and confirming each is caught** — including two probe attempts of my own that reported SURVIVED because `rindex` retargeted onto Step 8's copy of an anchor, which is the same occurrence-indexing trap for the fourth time in this phase.

It also found one thin spot the rounds missed: a crash between Step 8's `outcome.md` write and the `BLOCKED` classification rewrite left the run reporting as finished. The two writes are now ordered classification-first, so a crash lands in the state that routes **back into adjudication**.

**Three rounds each disqualified the state before them, and the honest conclusion is about the method, not this phase.** My own batteries have reported 9/9, 37/37 and 65/65 all-killed; independent lenses measured 46 of 52, 74 of 100 and 99 of 120 surviving on the same commits. That is not a run of bad luck — Phase 166 measured the same thing across twelve of sixteen phases. **An author-graded mutation battery measures the author's model of the code, and no amount of writing that caveat into the record has changed the number.** What did change the number is the two structural moves this round forced: parsing the code instead of matching prose about it, and building a floor that plants defects instead of counting complaints. Part A should not close on my assessment that the guards are now adequate.

**Mirror push (2026-07-31 — Phases 161–171 shipped).** Eleven phases / 27 commits since `ade2e1e`, the largest inter-cut delta yet, and the one that took the **three false monograph claims including a fabricated excerpt** off the public site. Public `b850b42` via `getsysop/sysop` PR #23 (required `pytest` green in 6m58s); tester `56098f5` force-pushed after re-confirming the repo is **private**; cold clones of both verified **byte-identical**. Gate on the exact pushed tree: Passes 1a/1b/1c/3 empty plus an extended exclusion sweep; Pass 2 **one** new site and Pass 2b **five**, both ratified accept classes; `tests/test_mirror_leak_gate.py` re-run and **agreeing** with the cut-time greps, honouring the script's own *"if one disagrees with the other, stop and reconcile"* rule; sterilized-tree suite **2030 passed / 54 skipped**. **This cut went green first time** — the Phase-160 follow-up's fix held, and running the suite *inside the sterilized tree* before pushing (not in the runbook, added here) is what confirmed it rather than public CI discovering it.

**The push found two things the leak passes are not shaped to find, and both were found by widening the read rather than by the gate.** **(1) The tree is clean; the *history* is not.** A per-commit token-scoped Pass 1a across all 17 public commits shows the two most recent clean and **15 (2026-07-15 → 2026-07-24) each carrying one leaking line** — the `PHASE_LOG.md:1121` line Phase 160 fixed at the tree level, still readable via `git log -p`. Every gate this project runs, including Phase 160's own, reads a *tree*; none reads history, so a fix that lands at the tip is silently mistaken for remediation. Accepted with no action (Wade) on the reasoning that the repo has been public since 2026-07-13 and a rewrite is both destructive and incomplete — but the general form is worth keeping: **a leak gate over the working tree cannot answer a question about a published repository.** **(2) The push and the announcement were never bound together.** Phases 147–160 shipped to testers on 2026-07-29 and were never announced; the standing thread's last entry was 2026-07-24, covering 144–146. That is the second occurrence — the 2026-07-24 note apologises for the same thing about 144–145 — so it is a missing edge in the process, not a lapse. The handoff doc tracked the push and stopped there. The 2026-07-31 tester note therefore covers **147–171**, and `tools/FIX_WAVE_BRIEF.md` § The mirror push now makes the announcement part of the push rather than a follow-on.

**Currency, stated honestly because the push does not confer it.** Shipping the files is not a currency pass: `docs/workflow.html` does not mention Phases 161–169 at all, and two SVG figure labels (`:1331`, `:2286`) still render the retired `reviewer-executor` shape — they need a re-layout, not a word change. That is #220 **part D**, deferred on purpose. `tests/test_doc_currency.py` is green and says nothing about it: Phase 118 inverted it to a no-count ratchet that asserts the monograph is never *ahead* of the tree, never that it is current. So the gate a reader would reach for to answer "are the docs up to date" does not answer that question, and the answer today is *the falsehoods are gone, the currency pass has not run*.

## Phase 172 (executed 2026-07-31 — Wave 2 item 6: the `severity: critical` check that scanned half its subject)

Upstream #235. Two pack grep checks anchored on a literal `"` while their own siblings were already quote-agnostic, and one of the two was `sql-fstring`. **Correction (Phase 224): this record called it *the registry's only `severity: critical` entry*, and that was false when written** — there were four then and six as of 2026-08-22. The figure moves as packs grow, so it is deliberately not restated here; derive it with `grep -rc 'severity: critical' core/companion/checks.yml.fragment packs/*/companion/checks.yml.fragment`. Python, JS/TS and SQL all take `'` and `"` interchangeably, so the check scanned half its subject and reported the other half clean — and the half it dropped is not an edge case for SQL. The single-quoted form is what you reach for when the statement embeds `"quoted identifiers"`, which is exactly the interpolated-identifier shape the check exists to catch. A miss and a real zero are the same output, so this shipped in every python/postgres consumer since the packs were populated.

**The sweep found three sites in the fragments, not the filed two, plus a fourth in the doc that teaches the shape.** The third is `test-app-env-before-syspath`'s `position_check.earlier`, and it is the worst of them, because a `position_check` fails *differently*: `_run_position_check` skips the **whole file** when either regex fails to match (`if e_line is None or l_line is None: continue`). A double-quote-only `earlier:` therefore does not miss a line — it disarms the check on every file written in the other style. Measured against one real corpus: of the 182 test files that set `APP_ENV` at all, **59 used only the single-quoted form and were never evaluated**. The fourth site is `WORKFLOW.md` § 6.5's format example, which shipped `pattern: 'f"(SELECT|INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE)'` as the thing to copy — the Phase-165 § 8.4-row lesson in a third place, and the reason the guard here is a class invariant over every shipped fragment rather than three pinned sites.

**Two populations swept and cleared, both by execution rather than by reading.** The semgrep rules are structurally immune: `sql_fstring.yaml` and `logger_fstring.yaml` match at the AST level, and running semgrep against a fixture holding both quote styles fires on both. Their three `metavariable-regex` uses are all over *identifiers* (`$LOGGER`, `$ERR`, `$SETTER`), never string literals. And `missing-encode-uri`'s `fetch\(`` is **not** a member — a JS template literal has no single/double-quote twin, so widening it would be a scope change rather than a fix. The predicate the guard uses encodes that distinction: backticks are never flagged.

**The widening is strictly additive, re-derived rather than adopted.** The filing reported `sql-fstring` 9 → 22 and `app-env-default-prod` 1 → 1 on the reporter's path-scoped run. Measured here whole-repo on the same corpus with a set comparison rather than a count: **21 → 33, 4 → 5, 123 → 182 — zero lost in all three**. The `app-env-default-prod` number differs from the filing because the filing was path-scoped; there is no *production* single-quoted instance in that tree today, so that half of the fix is a no-op against current code and closes the hole anyway. Of the 12 newly-caught SQL lines, three are production (`f'SELECT COUNT(*) FROM "{table}";'` — the live instance the filing cites) and nine are test fixtures the check's own `exclude: ["*test*"]` drops. **Neither of the two measured-wrong fixes was made:** no `-i` (it matches ordinary English prose) and no required same-line `FROM|WHERE|JOIN|SET` (it narrows, dropping `f"SELECT 1"` and the first line of any multi-line f-string). Both reasons are now recorded in the check's own `notes:`, where the next author will be standing.

**One narrowing I could have made and did not.** The fixture showed `f"SELECTED rows"` firing — the pattern has no trailing word boundary. Adding `\b` would kill that FP and, by inspection, drop no real hit. It is out of the filed class (an FP axis, not a quote axis), it is unmeasured, and narrowing a `severity: critical` check on my own reasoning is the exact shape the filing warns against twice. Recorded, not done.

**The secondary ask shipped with it: `# no-check: <id>`.** Grep checks had no inline-waiver equivalent to `# nosemgrep`. The only suppression was `.claude/checks_baseline.txt`, which is `file:line`-keyed and rots when a line moves — so *widening* a check, or broadening a `paths:` over a directory holding reviewed exceptions, converted a hardening into permanent CI noise and therefore did not get made. The marker is comment-syntax agnostic (`#`, `//`, `--` — it is the token that matters, since one registry scans Python, TypeScript, SQL and YAML), takes a comma list, and treats trailing text as a rationale. Two design calls are pinned by tests: **a bare `no-check:` waives nothing**, because a blanket marker would silently disable checks that do not exist yet including a future critical one; and **a waiver is never silent** — waived findings are reprinted with a `[waived]` tag and counted in the accounting header, the contract `[baseline]` already had. They do not reach the baseline file and do not trip `--fail-on-blocking`. Scope is the grep stage alone; semgrep, coverage and the typecheckers have their own pragmas.

### The author-side pass — and the harness's own first bug invalidated two runs of it
