### The round — three lenses, and the phase's central claim was wrong twice over

**Three lenses, one round, on the governor's conjunction** (the change alters what shipped
files check — three new guards — *and* the record asserts falsifiable counts). Dispatched onto
**throwaway clones** pinned at the phase commit, each gated on a symbol the phase *introduced*,
because `isolation: "worktree"` creates from the default branch and would have handed every
reviewer the pre-phase tree — a dead round that reads as a clean one. All three verified the SHA
before reading. Lenses: *does it execute and is the class closed* / *are the record's claims
true* / *are the guards real, on an independently designed battery*.

**Every finding below was re-verified by me before it was acted on.** Reviewers are the
adversary, not the authority — and one of their rows turned out to be my own battery bug rather
than a guard hole, which is exactly why the rule exists.

#### The author battery was falsified, as 44 of the previous 46 were

Lens 3 designed its own battery from the guards' assumptions without reading mine first:
**28 rows, 25 survived (89%), 9 negative controls, 4 false kills** — against my reported 13/13,
0 false kills. **Claim #47, falsified.** It also found a **fifth false kill sitting in my own
KILL column**: `A7` reworded the retirement's opener legally, the retirement still stood, and my
battery scored the rejection as a win under "vacuity". I had widened the *divergence* strip from
a byte-exact literal to a shape regex and left the *retirement* strip byte-exact — the same
defect, in the same commit, in the guard next door to the one I fixed it in.

#### HIGH-1 — the replacement was a new falsehood, refuted by the same file

The first fix replaced *"dispatch is convention-map-keyed"* with *"no section names it, so no
row can cite one"* — and that inference is false. A 3-pre row does not need to cite a section to
exist and dispatch, and the shipped table has exactly such a row: `Infra & Config` cites
**`*(none — see note)*`** and covers `Dockerfile`, `.dockerignore`, `.github/workflows/*.yml`.
Verified: no `convention_map.md` section matches `.github` or `Dockerfile`, and `.github` is a
live top-level entry in this repo — so a subtree the map never names *does* receive an agent.

**A false premise was replaced with a false inference, and the inference was written out as a
reusable rule** — worse for a reader than what it replaced, because the premise was at least
recognisably a shorthand. Both sites now state the real condition: unless a 3-pre row's **Files**
column names it.

**And the class was wider than those two sites, for the third time in this phase.** Round 2 found
the refuted inference — *a section the table does not name has no agent, however cleanly its globs
match* — still asserted unqualified at **three further sites**, two of them prose this phase wrote
in its own round-fix commit: `WORKFLOW.md`'s § 6.1 row, the new guard's own failure message, and —
worst — `codebase-review/SKILL.md:174`, **the retirement sentence the whole phase is anchored on**.
The fix had been applied to the two sites a reviewer named rather than to the class, by a phase
that names that exact failure twice in its own record. All three now say *no agent **of its own***,
with the true condition in a following sentence.

Fixing site 174 immediately tripped this phase's own laundering bound: extending the retirement
sentence pushed it past the 200-character tail the guard allows, so a **correct** edit went red.
The bound is right and the prose was wrong — the correction belongs in its own sentence, which
reads better anyway.

#### The guards failed three times, and the third fix was to stop needing one

1. **Token scanning** — 89% bypass (lens 3), and it false-fired on legal edits.
2. **A 120-character attribution rule** — defeated three ways. The row's own applies-to column
   literally reads `codebase-review, security-audit` and ends three characters before the
   description begins, so it supplied the "attribution" for free; any incidental cross-reference
   did the same; and a row asserting **both** skills are map-keyed satisfied it outright.
3. **Positive anchors** — survive inversion, but not **addition**. Lens 1 appended the false
   claim while the true statement stood further along the row; the anchor found the true half
   and passed. **That is the both-positions defect — the shape `Q-296` is an instance of —
   recurring for the third time inside the phase written to close it.**

**The fix was not a better pattern.** `WORKFLOW.md` now states `/security-audit`'s dispatch as
*"the OWASP categories a matching security-map section lists under `Check:`"* rather than the
retired shorthand, so the file uses the term **zero** times, the exemption is deleted, and the
scan covers it whole. The exemption was the hiding place: line-scoped and token-triggered, so any
line carrying the token self-exempted, and the reader took `next()` — the first match — so a
decoy could be planted ahead of the real row. Removing the term removed all of it. Re-measured
against every bypass the three lenses found: **all six killed**, including two that were still
open after my first round of fixes.

This is the brief's own rule, learned the expensive way: *prose guarded by prose is the wrong
instrument.* Three shapes were tried; the one that worked was making the prose not need a guard.

#### MEDIUM-5 — "impossible to close in kind" was untested

I declared the paraphrase residual impossible: *"No pattern detects the retired model restated
in words that avoid the token, and a guard that tried would false-fire on the honest mechanism
sentence."* Lens 1 built one in six lines. I rebuilt and measured it independently:
**zero false fires across the shipped tree**, and it kills every token-avoiding paraphrase tried
(*keyed on the convention map's globs*, *keys off the map sections*, *keyed by map-section
membership*, *keyed on the maps*). It ships. The governor's rule is that a declined survivor must
be **impossible** to close, not merely unattempted — mine was unattempted, and the word
"impossible" made a claim the phase had not tested.

The one exemption it needs is narrowed deliberately: a sentence naming `/security-audit` is
exempt only if it does **not** also name `/codebase-review`. An unnarrowed version would be the
same proximity hole the attribution rule had just failed on, twenty lines away.

#### MEDIUM-4 — the battery could not run where reviewers are required to run

`_PY = ".venv/bin/python3"`, hardcoded — the exact defect `mutation_battery.py`'s own docstring
exists to name (*"Phase 183's round is where that bit: the harness died from a linked worktree,
which never carries a venv"*). A reviewer following the prescribed procedure hit
`FileNotFoundError`, **after** the harness had printed the interpreter it had correctly resolved,
and only reached 13/13 by symlinking a venv in. **The phase's central numeric claim was
unreproducible in the environment the review convention mandates.** Now `sys.executable`.

#### The battery after the round, re-pointed and re-measured

Every rewrite above invalidated the original anchors, and the harness said so loudly — a
`STALE / AMBIGUOUS ANCHORS — battery bugs, NOT guard holes` block, rather than scoring eight
phantom survivors, which is the failure four of the nine batteries it replaced used to have.
Re-pointed against the current tree with a row for each of the round's findings.

**Final: 16 of 16 killed, 5 negative controls, 0 false kills, 3 of 16 declared reverts (18.8%).**
Groups: reversion 3/3, source-of-truth 4/4, what-it-matches-on 2/2, what-it-accepts 2/2,
where-it-looks 3/3, when-it-runs 1/1, vacuity 1/1.

**The intermediate run is the honest part of that number.** Re-pointed, it came back **15/16**,

every guard, because it carries neither the retired token nor a paraphrase of it, so the whole

divergence sentence names the row's *Files column* — inside the one sentence the strip matches,
where an addition cannot dodge it the way it dodges a file-wide anchor.

**And this number should be read the way the previous one should have been.** It is an author's
zero, measuring self-consistency. The last one was 13/13 and an independent lens found 25 of 28
surviving. The difference this time is not that the battery is trustworthy — it is that its rows
were written by three adversaries rather than by me.

### Round 2 — the mechanism was worse, and the residual I retracted was right

**Warranted by the governor's stated condition, not by appetite:** round 1 did not patch the
guards, it *replaced the mechanism* — an attribution rule retired, an exemption deleted, a
predicate added, the spec row restated — and no fresh reader had seen any of it. Two lenses,
scoped to the new material: *break the new mechanism* and *audit the round record*.

Lens A designed its own battery from the new code: **37 rows, 31 survived, 16 negative
controls, 9 false kills (56%).** Worse than round 1 in the direction that gets a guard deleted.

#### HIGH-0 — an instance of `Q-296` was live at HEAD, and the mirror test was certifying it

`core/skills/security-audit/SKILL.md:239` read *"`/codebase-review` runs the mirror of this
check against `convention_map.md` — **the map that keys its dispatch**"*. That is the retired
model, asserted about `/codebase-review`, on a shipped surface, at HEAD, with every guard green.

It survived three ways at once, and the third is the one worth keeping:

1. `security-audit/SKILL.md` is excluded from the scan **wholesale** rather than per-sentence,
   so the file is a total blind spot for false claims about the *other* skill.
2. The word order is map → keys → dispatch, which matched neither paraphrase regex.
3. **Its twin at `codebase-review/SKILL.md:225` is the TRUE statement** — `security_map.md` does
   key `/security-audit`'s dispatch — and `test_2a0_blocks_stay_mirrored_across_the_two_skills`
   normalises both to the same string by parameterising the map name away. **The mirroring
   mechanism was actively certifying the false half as consistent with the true one.** A guard
   built on the premise that the two skills are symmetric cannot see an asymmetry, and `Q-296`
   is precisely a claim about an asymmetry.

Fixed by deleting the clause on both sides — it was incidental to the sentence's point (run both
skills, audit both maps) and false on one of them.

#### HIGH-2 — the paraphrase predicate is reverted, and the retraction I made in round 1 was the error

Round 1 declared this residual impossible to close *"because a guard that tried would false-fire
on the honest mechanism sentence"*. A lens falsified that with a six-line predicate measuring
**zero false fires on the shipped tree**, and I shipped it.

Round 2 measured the same predicate against the thing that actually matters — **the class of
legal edits, not one frozen tree** — and got **19 false fires in 24 sentences (79%)**. It has no
polarity, so `Step 3 dispatch is **not** keyed on the maps` fires; so does *"do not write that
dispatch is keyed on the maps"*; so does a sentence describing this very retirement in the past
tense. And "map" is overloaded across this repo — rule map, weight map, role map, allow-rule map,
paths map — so nine of the nineteen concerned entirely different machinery. It was also
bypassable nine ways, including the exact phrasing of the HIGH-0 defect above. Simultaneously too
broad and too narrow: the signature of a wrong instrument, not of a pattern one character class
short.

**Three things to keep from that round trip, because the mistake was mine and it was not the
usual one:**

- **The original declaration was right, for the right reason, and I abandoned it because a lens
  produced a number.** The number was measured against the wrong population. *Zero false fires on
  the current tree is not zero false fires.* The governor says never to weight a finding by
  reviewer agreement; it does not say to fold to a single reviewer with an instrument, and that
  is what happened.
- **My own over-strictness control could not fire.** `N5-legal-map-prose` was written in the one
  word order the predicate was structurally blind to — a control the verifier cannot see, which
  `mutation_battery.py`'s docstring exists to name and which its `BLIND-CONTROL` status cannot
  catch for a prose target. It is replaced by a control that reproduces the actual false kill.
- **A declared residual is stronger evidence than a closed one here.** The battery now carries
  `P1-paraphrase-no-token` as a row **expected to survive**, with the 19-of-24 measurement as its
  justification. That is what "impossible to close in kind, not merely unattempted" is supposed
  to look like: a number, not an assertion.

#### The rest, all verified before acting

- **The `Files column` anchor failed in BOTH directions.** A sentence could *name* the column
  while *denying* it (*"no 3-pre row's Files column can cite one"*), and stating the true
  condition in other words was a **false kill**. Now closed both ways and checked against all
  three cases. My first negation regex still let the demonstrated bypass through, because `\w+`
  cannot cross the hyphen in `3-pre` — the same one-character class of error, twice in one phase.
- **Inversion satisfied the guard protecting the true statement:** `at Step 3 dispatch (never
  map-keyed)` passed the counterpart check. Negation is now rejected explicitly.
- **The population widening was silently droppable.** `if path.exists()` meant renaming `docs/`
  away left the guard green while it quietly stopped covering it — demonstrated by execution, and
  Phase 113 performed exactly that reorg. The roots are now asserted non-empty, and `docs/` is
  recursive (the first cut used non-recursive `glob`, missing `docs/analysis/`).
- **A 110× performance regression**, measured at 7.74s of the module's 7.77s. A cheap pre-filter
  (`"keyed" not in text`) takes it to **1.76s** over a population ten times larger than the one
  that used to cost 0.07s.

**Battery after round 2: 18 of 19 killed, 6 negative controls, 0 false kills, 3 of 19 declared
reverts (15%).** The single survivor is the declared residual above, by design.

### The cut, as executed

Cut from merged `main` **`ac59462`**, never the branch. **Public `a4394a6`** via `getsysop/sysop`
PR #36; **tester `92a891f`** force-pushed, Private re-confirmed by API after the push. Public
`main`, the tester tip and the gated build all resolve to git tree **`c8324e8`** — verified on
cold clones of both repos afterwards, 343 files each.

Gates: Passes 1a/1b/1c/3/4/4b and the rename-residue diff all empty, `GATE GREEN`; population
agreement **343 = 343, identical sets**; Pass 5/5b **103 passed** in the source repo at the cut
SHA; sterilized-tree suite **4,386 passed / 362 skipped / 0 failed** with no bytecode left behind;
cold-clone install smoke green in both modes from a third directory. Full detail in `Q-301`.

**Two gate readings were wrong before they were right, and both were one mistake.** Piping a gate
to `tail` and then reading `$?` reports *tail's* exit code: `scan_public_history.sh` actually exits
**1**, and `run_checks.sh` on a PyYAML-less host exits **2**, where the pipe reported 0 for both.
The runbook's own rule is *"Never `head` a gate"* and it is written about this exact hazard. Either
misreading would have gone into the record as a clean run.

Chasing the first one produced **`Q-300`**: the public-history gate is **permanently red**. Its
`header:` arm allow-lists two addresses, `Q-294` accepted 16 published commits carrying a third,
and those commits are immutable — so it exits 1 on every future cut whatever the cut contains.
Measured here: 29 commits, 16 header-dirty, **the same 16 as at the Phase-227 cut when the total
was 28**. Nothing new leaked, and proving that meant hand-counting against a number kept in prose,
which is precisely what extracting the script was meant to stop. It is `Q-299`'s class — a check
that always fires is a check nobody reads — sitting on the one gate between a private identity and
permanent publication.

### The cost, re-derived by execution rather than cited

The brief asks for this and it was worth asking for. `30 of 36 sections are all-placeholder`
reproduces exactly — 36 sections across the five populated packs, six carrying at least one
concrete glob — but the section count is **pack-dependent** and the entry does not say so: a
four-pack install assembles 31, a core-only install 5, and only one of the six concrete
sections (`pyrightconfig.json`) comes from a pack at all. So a core-only consumer has five
binding sections, not six.

More usefully, the cost was measured **per file** rather than per section, which is the unit
the defect is actually in. Sysop was installed into a purpose-built consumer repo — an API with
routes, an auth module, a pipeline, a frontend component, a SQL migration, tests, a
`Dockerfile`, CI — and the dispatch resolved against it. **Six of the fourteen consumer files
get an owner; eight do not; and all eight of the unowned are the application code** — the API
server, its route module, auth, the pipeline, a utility module, a frontend component, the SQL
migration and the tests. (An earlier draft of this sentence enumerated seven of the eight and
still said "all eight"; the omission was the utility module.) **The six that are owned are `.dockerignore`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `.gitignore`, `Dockerfile`,
`pyrightconfig.json` and `scripts/deploy.sh` — every one infrastructure. That is Q-212's claim,
sharpened from a section ratio into the sentence a consumer would care about.

**A related finding fell out of the same probe, and it is a shipped-code defect nobody filed.**
Step 2a-1 matches files to sections by "derived-root **prefix + extension**" — deliberately
coarse, and the skill explains why: handing `**/*.py` to `git ls-files` as a pathspec drops
direct children. That premise is true and the workaround is unnecessary. `git ls-files --
'api/**/*.py'` does drop `api/server.py`, and `'api/routes/**/*.py'` returns *nothing*, but
`git ls-files -- ':(glob)api/**/*.py'` returns both files exactly. Git has had a precise
resolver the whole time and the skill approximates around it. Filed, not fixed here — 2a-1 is
a different mechanism from this phase's, and widening scope to it is the trap this repo keeps
naming.

### The design, and the two shapes execution refused before the third

`Q-212` carries two independent disqualifications: a partition cannot be keyed on
`security_map` sections, and cannot be copied from `/codebase-review`'s hand table. The
redesign constraint it leaves is *derived from the assembled map at runtime, and it must
survive an unlocalized install.*

**The inversion that satisfies both: do not partition the map. Partition the manifest.** The
map cannot be a coverage source when 30 of its 36 sections bind nothing — but it is a perfectly
good *rule* source, and the manifest (`git ls-files`, which Step 1 already computes) is always
real and always complete. So ownership is keyed on the manifest, the category dispatch is left
**entirely untouched** for the files it already reaches, and the residual — manifest minus
mapped minus the consumer's declared coverage exclusions — is a set difference, disjoint from
the category agents' population by construction. It is *largest exactly when the map is least
localized*, which is the case that was silently empty before.

That is the third shape. **Two earlier ones were built and refused by running them**, which is
the method the brief prescribes and the reason this phase did not ship a spec describing
something that does not work:

- **Split the manifest by directory.** Guarantees single ownership; produced **55 buckets for a
  141-file repo**, most of them one file. The agent budget is the binding constraint and this
  shape ignores it.
- **Bin-pack by size.** Bounded the count to four — and destroyed reviewer coherence: bucket 2
  held the consumer's `api` alongside `.claude/skills` and `CLAUDE.md`. A load-balanced pile is
  not a subject, and the whole value of the category dispatch is that an agent has one.

The third shape takes the half of each that works: group by directory (coherence), pack the
groups into a bounded number of bins (budget), and apply it only to the residual, which is
small enough that the incoherence the second shape suffered largely does not arise.

### Seven defects, every one found by executing the thing rather than reading it

Stated in full because the fraction at the end would otherwise read as competence rather than
as a process working:

1. **The splitter silently deleted files.** A path shallower than the split depth was routed to
   a shared `(root)` key and an unsplit group then assigned over that key wholesale. Caught on
   the *first run* by the partition invariant — which is the only reason it is in this list
   rather than in the shipped tree.
2. Split-by-directory blew the agent budget (55 buckets / 141 files).
3. Bin-packing destroyed reviewer coherence.
4. **Group selection under a binding budget was alphabetical**, so it dispatched `.agents`,
   `.claude` and `CLAUDE.md` and dropped the consumer's `api` and `auth` — the exact files the
   sweep exists for.
5. **`Full` was reported over a 533-file repo whose residual had been reviewed a quarter of.**
   436 residual files packed into four agents, every file in a bucket, therefore Full. This is
   the same laundering Step 3-0 forbids for the manifest, re-minted at a new site by the fix
   for it — and it is the sharpest thing this phase found in its own work.
6. **`agents_needed_for_full` was false in both directions across two drafts.** First an
   undercount: with the group cap decoupled from the per-agent credit, one indivisible 39-file
   group could only ever be credited 25, so "4 agents reach Full" was published over a residual
   that packed to 67 of 90. Then, over-correcting, a per-group sum that claimed **360 agents
   for 486 files**, having forgotten that groups share a bin. What made the simple form true
   was tying the group cap to the per-agent credit; the arithmetic follows from the coupling,
   not from the formula.
7. **An innocuous `sorted()` undid the consumer-first ranking.** Files were packed in ranked
   order and then re-sorted alphabetically inside the bin, so truncation dropped whichever
   sorted late: a budget-bound run reported "10 of your files unreached" while keeping thirty
   of Sysop's. The ranking existed precisely to prevent that inversion and was defeated by a
   line that looked like tidying.

### The question the measurement forced: Sysop's own footprint

On a fresh four-pack install **79 of the 91 residual files are Sysop's own installed output** —
its semgrep rules and fixtures, its companion scripts, its docs and the `tasks/` scaffold.
Without an answer the sweep spends its entire budget auditing the installer and never reaches
the consumer's application.

**Two corrections the round forced on that sentence, and both matter.** An earlier version said
*"90 … 78"* and listed *"its skills … and lock"*. The numbers were measured on a fixture built
**before this phase's own script existed**, so they were one short; re-measured against a fresh
install of the shipped tree the figures are manifest 142, residual 91, vendor 79, consumer 12.
And two of the four listed items are not in the vendor residual at all: `.claude/skills/**/*.md`
is one of the **six binding sections**, so all 34 skill files are *mapped*, not residual — the
phase's own headline finding, contradicted three paragraphs later — and `.claude/sysop.lock` is
not in `managed_paths`, so the tool counts it as the **consumer's**. Which exposes the real
limit: `managed_paths` is Sysop's *managed* set, not its whole footprint, and four seeded files
(`sysop.lock`, `CLAUDE.md`, `sysop/SYSOP_ISSUES.md`, `tasks/index.yml`) sit outside it and count
as the consumer's. The claim that the population is "exact for this install" was overstated;
it is exact for what the installer *manages*.

The obvious fix — have the installer seed `## Map coverage exclusions` with Sysop's own vendor
paths — was **drafted and rejected.** Auto-excluding the shipped tool's own code from the
security audit that tool ships is a self-serving default, and this code does execute in the
consumer's repo; a supply-chain argument cuts directly against it. It would also have leaned on
`Map coverage exclusions` in a way Phase 139 settled against (that list is map-coverage-only and
does not remove a file from review), so it would have quietly reopened a closed scope.

What ships instead: Sysop's footprint is **counted and reported separately, never excluded**,
and ranked *last* so a binding budget spends on the consumer's code first. The population is
read from the install lock's own `managed_paths` — derived, not a hardcoded `.claude/`/`sysop/`
prefix list, which would have gone stale the moment the vendor layout moved, as it already did
once when Phase 128 relocated the footprint into `sysop/`. Verified at three budgets: at
`--budget 1` against a fixture where the vendor set is 40 of 43 residual files, **zero consumer
files are unreached.**

### The author-side battery: 19 of 20, and it cost four runs to get an honest number

`tools/phase231_mutations.py`, 20 mutations across five assumption classes plus three
over-strictness controls. **Final: 19 killed, 0 false kills on the controls, one declared
survivor.** Getting there took four runs and each one taught something.

**Run 1 refused its own numbers, correctly.** It declared `COLLATERAL DAMAGE` — five record
files changed mid-run — because the author was writing `PHASE_LOG.md` and the checklist while
it executed. The ledger's standing rule is *never run two batteries at once*; the adjacent rule
it does not state is **never edit the tree while one runs**, and the detector caught it. The
tree is committed before every reported run now.

**Run 2 (15/18 → 17/20 after re-scoping) produced the sharpest finding of the phase, and it
came from probing a survivor rather than from the kill count.** `C3` asked whether
`agents_needed_for_full` could revert to `ceil(residual / per_agent)`. It survived — and the
probe showed why: **that formula was still false, after two corrections.** It is a *lower
bound*, not an achievable budget, because bin-packing indivisible groups can need more bins
than the ceiling. Measured on the 486-file residual: the report named **20**, and running at
`--budget 20` reported `Sampled`. So this number has now been wrong **four times** —
undercount, overcount, lower-bound, and finally a simulation that packed without the ranking
the real call uses. It is now derived by *running the real packer*, and where no budget can
reach `Full` (a directory nested past the splitter's depth limit holding more files than one
agent's credit) it says **`UNREACHABLE`** and names the blocking groups instead of printing a
number that does not work.

**The guard could not see it because the test only checked one direction.** "Run at N, require
`Full`" falsifies an undercount and is *blind to an overcount*. The test now pins the number in
both directions — at `N` it must be `Full`, at `N-1` it must be `Sampled`.

**Runs 3 and 4 caught two of this phase's own guards being vacuous**, which is the whole
argument for doing this before spawning anyone:

- **`A4` survived a test written to kill it.** The test pointed a placeholder *section* at a
  literal `<gen>` directory — but `build()` skips placeholder sections *before* the resolver is
  reached, so the section path masks the guard completely. The guard's live path is
  `CLAUDE.md`'s exclusion globs, which reach the same resolver with no skip in front of them.
  Rewritten against that path, it kills.
- **`C3b` survived two batteries.** Every git-fixture test in the module was too small for
  ranked and unranked packing to diverge, so an assertion that looked like it pinned the
  ranking proved nothing. On the real corpus the two differ by twelve bins (32 vs 20). Closed
  with a **searched** minimal counterexample rather than a constructed one — five groups,
  twelve files, a credit of three, two groups vendor-owned; ranked needs 5 bins, unranked 4.
  Consumer-first ranking *costs* a bin there, and that is the point: the number must describe
  the packing that runs, not a cheaper one nobody performs.

**The one declared survivor is `R4`, and it is declared on a measurement rather than an
argument — a measurement whose stated size was then cut by two independent checks.** Reverting the splitter's `out.setdefault(k, []).extend(v)` to `out[k] = v` changes
nothing, because the original defect was a *pair* — a shared `(root)` sink plus this clobber —
and with the sink gone the clobber is unreachable. Settled by differential fuzz over **40,000 random trees, each tested at three caps — 120,000
trials, not 120,000 trees**, which is how the first draft of this sentence put it. An
independent lens then confirmed the claim exhaustively (59,568 cases over a deliberately
prefix-colliding 16-path universe, zero divergence) *and* noted the fuzz's four-name alphabet
at depths 1–4 never reaches the splitter's depth-5 bound at all — so the original number
described a smaller space than it sounded like. The lens also found `if out == groups: break`
fires in 0 of 59,568 cases: dead code, filed rather than removed. It is impossible to close in kind — no
test can pin a difference that cannot occur — and the code comment was corrected, because it
had claimed this line was the fix rather than defence in depth.

### Three vacuities in this phase's own guards, closed before the battery ran

Named because the battery's fraction would otherwise be measuring the fixture rather than the
guard, which is the failure the author-side pass exists to catch. The first fixture had **no
concrete section using `**`**, so reverting the `:(glob)` pathspec was undetectable; **no
directory larger than a per-agent credit**, so the group-cap coupling was undetectable; and **no
nested tree**, so the splitter's accumulate-don't-assign fix was undetectable. All three are
shipped behaviours the guards would have waved through. The fixture now carries a concrete
`svc/**/*.py` section with a direct child, and a 12-file `bulk/` tree across two subdirectories.

### What ships

- **`core/companion/scripts/security_partition.py`** — the derivation. Advisory: exits 0 on
  every degrade path (no map, no `CLAUDE.md`, empty repo, damaged lock), 2 only on a bad flag or
  an unexpected error. Ships in **both** install modes, which matters because `/security-audit`
  is one of loop mode's five skills and a named loop entry point — the reason `Q-212` was never
  invisible to a public visitor. The runway already carried that correction (Wade's call,
  2026-08-24); an earlier phrasing here implied it did not.
- **`/security-audit` Step 3-0c** — the invoker, plus a `Residual:` line beside 3-0b's
  `Reconciliation:` line in the Step 5b round header, deliberately *beside* rather than folded
  into `Coverage:`, for the reason that rule already exists: three populations, three numbers.
- **`tests/test_security_partition.py`** — 51 tests, mostly over real git fixtures (a few are
  flag, default and prose guards). Two pin the numbers by *acting* on them: the report says how
  many agents reach `Full`, and the test runs at that budget and requires `Full`. The count was
  published as "23" while the file held 26, and as "25" in the battery's docstring; it grew to
  51 closing what the round found.
- `WORKFLOW.md` § 8.4 row, **two** `settings.json` allow-rules (not four — see below), and the
  loop-bundle inventory updated.

**A fourth guard fired and this record originally said only three did.** `tests/test_intra_repo_citations.py`
went **red on the branch** and stayed red: the two allow-rule bullets added to
`security-audit/SKILL.md` shifted `next_batch_number` from `:181` to `:183`, breaking a
registered citation in two *shipped* consumer scripts (`batch_work.sh:123`,
`review_index.py:670`). The sentence "all three of those guards fired on arrival, which is what
they are for" was written while a fourth was failing. Found by a review lens, not by me — I had
run the full suite *before* adding those two lines and not again after. Fixed at all three
sites plus the registry.

**And the rule-count claim was wrong twice over.** This record said "four `settings.json`
allow-rules" in one section and "the two bare rules were dropped … only the flagged forms ship"
in the next; the diff is +2. The claim that the count comments "demanded updating in three
places" also counted them as guards that fired — only one of the three is pinned by anything,
the `LOOP_ALLOW` comment had been silently stale on `main` (it read 21 against a real 22), and
a **fourth** site was missed entirely: `tests/test_install_loop_mode.py:20`'s own docstring, in
the very file whose `LOOP_ALLOW_COUNT` this phase bumped.

### Four pre-existing guards fired on the new script, and one of them changed the design

Adding a shipped script trips a lot of machinery, and every bit of it earned its keep here:
`WORKFLOW.md` § 8.4 demanded a row, the loop-bundle inventory demanded a classification, the
prescribed-command coverage guard demanded a loop-mode allow-rule, and the installer's
rule-count comments demanded updating in three places (template total, `LOOP_ALLOW` comment,
dry-run plan string).

**The permission-surface guard did more than that — it corrected a decision.** The first cut
seeded four allow-rules, bare and `:*` for both interpreters, copying `scope_overlap.py`'s
shape. `test_every_seeded_rule_is_named_by_a_skill_or_justified` reported all four as orphans,
and working out why produced the right answer rather than the quick one: **every prescribed
invocation of this script carries `--json`, so the bare forms bind nothing.** That is precisely
what Phase 152 measured — rules seeded against invocations that bind none — so the two bare
rules were dropped rather than justified, and only the flagged forms ship. Template goes 74 →
76, loop subset 22 → 24.

**One self-inflicted defect on the way:** the `LOOP_ALLOW` insertion broke a Python set literal
embedded in an `install.sh` heredoc — `bash -n` still passed, because the syntax error was
inside a heredoc bash never parses. Caught by the loop-mode tests, not by the shell check, which
is worth remembering the next time `bash -n install.sh` is treated as validation.

### The round — three lenses, and the phase's own numbers did not survive it

**Three lenses on the governor's conjunction** (the change ships behaviour *and* a record making
numeric claims): does it execute / are the claims true / are the guards real. Fresh-context
`general-purpose` agents, worktree-isolated, instructed not to mutate the tree. Every surviving
finding was re-derived by me before being acted on; two were refuted that way.

**The execution lens found a contract violation that the phase's own record had already
condemned in writing.** `build()` computed `residual = files - mapped - excluded`, where
`excluded` is `CLAUDE.md § "Map coverage exclusions"`. That list is scoped, by
`WORKFLOW.md` § 6.1 and by `security-audit/SKILL.md` two hundred lines above the new step, to
the Step 2a coverage **audit** — *"it does not change the review/scan manifest and is not a
review-exclusion knob"*, settled by Phase 139. Step 3-0c is dispatch. So a consumer-declared
path got **no agent**, which is precisely the reading this phase's own § *vendor footprint*
section cites Phase 139 to reject — for a different design, three paragraphs earlier. The list
is now **counted and reported, never subtracted**.

**And the same lens found what that cost.** `parse_exclusions` harvested every backticked token
from every list item, so an ordinary sentence — *"we deliberately do NOT exclude `api/**` or
`auth/**`, they are security-critical"* — removed the API server, a SQL route and the auth
module from dispatch, and the report said **`Full`**. A `###` subsection did not terminate the
list; fenced blocks were read as content, so a copied `## <globs> — <Name>` template (the shape
`WORKFLOW.md` ships for consumers to copy) became a live section and emptied the residual
entirely. The parse now strips fences in **both** parsed files, ends on any `#` heading, and
takes only a list item's **leading** backticked glob.

Five more from that lens, all reproduced: **five lock shapes crashed with exit 2** against a
docstring promising every degrade exits 0 — `.get` on a non-object, the identical pair
`install.sh`'s `lock_field()` was hardened against in Phase 148, whose comment names it
verbatim — and both `open()` calls were unguarded. Two of this phase's degrade tests were
vacuous: one tested only the branch that *was* handled, and the `no-git` case never created a
map, so it exited at the no-map gate and never reached the path it is named for. **And
`_budget_for_full` was cubic** — timed at ~4 minutes on an ordinary 20k-file repo and ~27
minutes at 42k, to produce one advisory number. Binary search (monotonicity measured, not
assumed) makes 20k take 4.1 seconds.

**The claims lens found a live regression and a record that said the opposite.** The two
allow-rule bullets added to `security-audit/SKILL.md` shifted `next_batch_number` from `:181`
to `:183`, breaking a registered citation in two **shipped consumer scripts** — and the suite
was red on the branch while this record said *"all three of those guards fired on arrival,
which is what they are for."* A fourth had fired and was still failing. The cause is
mechanical and worth naming: I ran the full suite, **then** added those two lines, and did not
run it again.

It also found the numbers wrong in several directions. *"78 of 90"* was measured on a fixture
built **before this phase's own script existed** (the real figures are 91/79), and its
composition sentence named two things that are not in the vendor residual at all — the skills
are *mapped*, which is the phase's own headline finding contradicted three paragraphs later.
*"23 tests"* was 26 at the time and is 58 now; *"four `settings.json` allow-rules"* contradicted
the next section's *"only the flagged forms ship"* and the diff's +2; *"436 residual … 109
files each"* reproduces on no fixture this phase built; *"120,000 random trees"* was 40,000
trees at three caps. The `Q-212` resolution claimed finding (4) answered when only one of its
four legs is. And **`Q-304` was filed on a false premise** — both entries it names *do* carry
later `Re-routed` clauses that supersede the old ones, and *do* state their residual scope — a
falsehood this phase had already propagated into the Phase 232 brief before the round caught
it. The filing is rewritten to record the ergonomic defect that produced it.

**The guards lens is the one that matters: 69 of its 117 independent mutations survived, against
my own battery's 19 of 20.** Derived from the ledger rather than asserted: **every phase since
225 that had a battery to run has had survivors found by an independent lens — 225, 226, 227,
228, 230 and 231, six of them**, with 229 the only gap because it shipped no guard to mutate.
(An earlier draft of this sentence said "the fifth phase running", which the ledger falsifies.)
The separate standing claim — 47 *all-killed* author batteries recorded, 45 falsified, 0 intact
— is unchanged by this phase, because 19-of-20-with-a-declared-survivor is not an all-killed
claim and is not counted in it.
Its sharpest finding is not a survivor count: **the one test named for the module's defining
property had the defect as its oracle.** `test_verdict_is_full_exactly_when_capacity_covers_the_residual`
computed `expected = "Full" if budget * per_agent >= residual` — exactly the mutation that
breaks the module — so it would have *certified* the laundering this file exists to prevent.
Two more of that shape: the ranking guard pinned `_budget_for_full`'s internal call, so dropping
the ranking at the **call site** moved the same defect one line and became invisible; and the
vendor-tier guard used a fixture of homogeneous groups, on which `all` and `any` cannot diverge.
**The render layer was pinned by nothing at all** — the lens replaced `render()` with a constant
string and every test passed, with twelve realistic mutations printing numbers that disagree
with `--json` for the same run.

**Disposition: 26 of the round's findings fixed, one declared, two refuted.** The suite went
26 → 58 tests. My battery, repointed and extended with the round's own attacks, now reports
**28 of 29 killed, 0 false kills on 3 negative controls** — and the one over-strictness control
earned its place: my first defaults guard pinned the literal `(4, 25)` and the control caught
it as a **false kill**, so the guard now pins agreement between the code and the three documents
that quote those values instead. The single declared survivor is `R4`, the splitter's
accumulate-vs-assign line, which an independent lens confirmed exhaustively (59,568 cases,
zero divergence) is unreachable given the other half of the same fix — while also noting that
my fuzz's four-name alphabet never reaches the depth-5 split bound, so the number I published
described a smaller space than it sounded like.

### The suite

**4,827 passed, 156 skipped, 0 failed — in the source repo**, which is stated because
collection here is environment-dependent and a prior round compared a clone's collect count
against a source-repo pass count and reported an off-by-one that did not exist. The module this
phase added went 26 → 58 tests; the rest of the delta is the four pre-existing guards it had to
feed and the citation registry it had to repair.

The other ten Track D members. `Q-300` (the permanently-red public-history gate, filed after

(`tools/scan_public_history.sh`) is mirror-excluded maintainer tooling — but the entry is filed

## Phase 232 (executed 2026-08-26 — Track D's worktree/lock hygiene pair, and the premise that was true of one park path and not the other)

Track D's second phase, and the first to take a cluster rather than its ranking member.
Wade picked the worktree/lock pair (`Q-023` + `Q-024`) at the session's open from four
offered clusters, and ratified `Q-023`'s open design call in the same breath: a
**runtime-scoped** ignored-content probe, not a general one.

Both entries are Phase 165 filings, both live in
`core/companion/scripts/cleanup_worktrees.sh`, and they compose more tightly than
adjacency: `Q-023` changes what the removal loops do, and `Q-024` is the assertion that
those loops report what they did. The `Q-024` tests are the regression harness for the
`Q-023` change.

### The defect, reproduced before it was fixed

Every content probe in the script excludes gitignored files — the classifier's
`ls-files --others --exclude-standard`, and `--force`'s `status --porcelain`. `sysop/runtime/`
is gitignored by construction — it is the first of the **three** entries
`install.sh`'s `ensure_runtime_gitignore` appends (`install.sh:3212`; the others are
`.claude/review_index.json` and `sysop/**/__pycache__/`). An earlier draft of this sentence,
and the shipped comment it came from, said "exactly that one line", which is false and was
load-bearing for a second wrong claim: that the probe scope and the ignore scope are "one thing
rather than two lists that can drift". They are two lists, the probe's is deliberately the
narrower, and `sysop/**/__pycache__/` is ignored content inside a worktree's `sysop/` tree that
the probe does not count — correctly, because bytecode is not work. So content written *inside* a worktree under that path was invisible to the whole
script, and a parked task's branch carries no commit of its own, which makes it an ancestor
of `main`, which classifies **MERGED**.

Reproduced end to end in a scratch repo before any edit: a worktree whose only content was
`sysop/runtime/auto-build/review.md`, on a merged branch. `--clean`'s deliberately
**non-force** `git worktree remove` — the one the script's own comment describes as the thing
that "blocks the destructive op" — returned 0 and the file was gone. `--force` printed the
benign `🗑️  Removing:` rather than its uncommitted-work warning, and destroyed it just the
same. Both halves of the entry are real, and the second half is the one the entry led with.

### The premise that was true of one path and false of the other

`Q-023` is filed as a **"loudness gap, not unrecoverable loss"** on the grounds that Phase
65a's project-root mirror preserves the content, and `tools/ANNOUNCE_RUNWAY.md` re-affirms
that when declining to move it up the queue. Reading the writer rather than the filing:
**that is true of one park path and false of the other.**

`/auto-build` writes the project-root mirror in **Phase 6d**, in the `blocker` arm. The
**Phase 6a** plan-phase-violation park writes `review.md` to the worktree and then says
*"Mark this task PARKED and skip Phases 6b-6e for it"* — so it never reaches 6d, and no
mirror is written at all. For that path the in-worktree copy is the only record that the
violation happened.

And the mirror argument never covered the other runtime home at all. `/document-work` Step 3
writes a branch's documentation to `sysop/runtime/pending-docs/` **inside the worktree**, and
`/review-close` Step 3b does not copy it to main until merge time — the skill says so at
`review-close/SKILL.md:587`, and says it deliberately, because collecting early is its own
data-loss class (BeanRider ISSUE-0050). A worktree removed before that merge loses the
pending doc outright, with nothing anywhere else.

So the severity ranking was resting on a claim that holds for the *mirrored* park and no
other case. The **position** does not change — the fix is cheap and the phase took it anyway
— but the shipped `--force` warning is worded to match the tree rather than the filing: it
says a mirror *may* exist, and a test asserts the word `may` rather than the sentence, so a
later phase cannot quietly upgrade it to a promise.

**⚠ And the paragraph above overreaches about `--clean`, which this phase's round caught by
running the classifier rather than reading it.** The Phase 6a park's *trigger is a commit* —
`auto-build/SKILL.md:512` fires on `NEW_HEAD != <pre-plan head>`, i.e. the plan-only agent
committed — so its branch is never an ancestor of `main` and it was **already ACTIVE before
this phase**. Measured on both revisions, four worktree shapes:

| shape | pre-fix (`bc15a3e`) | post-fix |
|---|---|---|
| 6a park (commit + `review.md`), **unmirrored** | ACTIVE | ACTIVE |
| 6d park (no commit + `plan.md`/`review.md`), **mirrored** | **MERGED** | ACTIVE |
| pending-doc, branch unmerged | ACTIVE | ACTIVE |
| pending-doc, branch merged + not yet collected | **MERGED** | ACTIVE |

So the `--clean` half of the fix lands on exactly two shapes: the **mirrored** 6d park, and a
**merged** branch whose pending-doc Step 3b had not yet collected — the second of which this
record did not name until the round found it. The 6a park, which the prose above calls the
sharpest case, is reached only by the `--force` warning, and that is genuinely reached because
`--force` ignores classification entirely. **The honest form of the severity claim is therefore
`--force`-scoped:** under `--clean` it is one of three, not two of three. The premise about the
mirror is true; the consequence drawn from it was not established for the mechanism shipped,
and the `tools/ANNOUNCE_RUNWAY.md` amendment built on it inherited the same overreach and is
corrected there.

### What ships

**`core/companion/scripts/cleanup_worktrees.sh`** — one new helper and two consumers of it:

- `worktree_runtime_artifacts()` — `git ls-files --others --ignored --exclude-standard --
  'sysop/runtime/'`, an existence probe. The pathspec is the whole design. A missing
  directory is not an error: `ls-files` exits 0 with empty output, which is the common case.
- A `classify_worktree` arm returning **ACTIVE**, placed **before** the MERGED check, because
  MERGED is precisely the verdict it exists to prevent. `--clean` then skips.
- A `--force` warning on its **own line**, not a third arm of the uncommitted-work branch. A
  worktree can hold either loss, both, or neither, and folding them together makes one of
  them unreportable.

**The scope is `sysop/runtime/` and nothing wider, and that is the ratified call.** The
alternative the entry named — count all ignored content — protects the park record and also
makes `--clean` refuse on every worktree carrying a venv or a build directory, i.e. all of
them. That is the same cry-wolf failure Phase 165's round had to reshape the `--force`
warning to avoid, one level up in the classifier. The probe scope and the installer's ignore
scope are now the same single path rather than two lists that can drift.

**`Q-024` ships no behaviour.** It ships the tests that were missing under an accounting
summary nothing exercised — plus one test beyond its filing, named rather than slipped in
(below).

### The fixture was checked against the defect before the guards were trusted

`_repo()` in `tests/test_cleanup_worktrees_sh.py` ships **without** a `.gitignore`; no
pre-existing test in the module ever needed one. A naive fixture writing
`sysop/runtime/auto-build/review.md` into a worktree therefore produces an **untracked**
file, which the *pre-existing* probe already classifies ACTIVE — so the test would have
passed against the unfixed script and measured nothing. `_ignore()` exists for that reason,
and the headline test asserts the precondition rather than assuming it: both pre-fix probes
must return empty, or it fails and says so.

### `Q-024`'s fixture: one prescribed shape is disqualified, the other is merely worse

The entry prescribes making a removal fail by corrupting the `.git/worktrees/<name>` admin
entry **or** by pointing the worktree at an unwritable path. Both were tried first:

- **Deleting the admin entry** drops the worktree out of `git worktree list` entirely, so the
  script's loop never reaches it and the FAILED branch stays unexercised — the fixture removes
  the thing it was supposed to test. **Structurally disqualified.**
- **Unwritable path** — and here this record was wrong until its own round corrected it. The
  first draft, and the `CLAUDE.md` row built on it, said "a no-op under root, and CI often runs
  as root", concluding that *both* shapes were wrong. Measured as uid 501 it **works**:
  `error: failed to delete …: Permission denied`, exit 255. And this repo's CI is
  `runs-on: ubuntu-latest` with no `container:` (`.github/workflows/tests.yml:41`) — the
  non-root `runner` user — so the generic industry claim offered as the disqualifier is false
  for the one CI that gates this repo. **Viable, just worse.**

"Both are wrong" was the tidier sentence and the false one. The true statement is weaker: one
shape is disqualified, one is second-best.

The shape actually used is `git worktree lock`, git's own supported refusal:
`git worktree remove --force` on a locked worktree fails with *"cannot remove a locked
working tree; use 'remove -f -f' to override or unlock first"*. Deterministic,
cross-platform, and it routes through the code under test rather than around it. It also lets
the test assert the worktree **survived**, which an exit-code check alone cannot — and it needs
no permission games, so it behaves identically for a root and a non-root runner. Those are the
honest reasons to prefer it; "the alternative does not work" is not one of them.

### One test past the filing, declared

`Q-024` is scoped to `--force`. `--clean`'s `FAILED` branch and its `exit 1` had the
identical hole, in the same script, reachable by the same fixture — a *locked* MERGED
worktree. Closing one and leaving the other would mean a mutation to `--clean`'s accounting
still ships green, which is the entire complaint the entry makes about `--force`. Added as
`test_clean_failure_accounting_is_exercised_too`, and named here rather than absorbed
silently.

Re-run after closing it: **12/12 killed, 3/3 controls green, 0 false kills.** The `pre` column

**An all-killed author battery is a claim about the battery, not the code.** Re-derived with

batteries reported every mutation killed; 45 were falsified by an independent lens; 2 (Phases

Budget accordingly; the round below is where this phase's honest number comes from. **With this

### The suite

**5,008 collected in the source repo.** The phase's own delta is **+24**, all of them in
`tests/test_cleanup_worktrees_sh.py` (15 → 39), measured by diffing per-file collection counts
against `main` rather than by subtracting two totals. Eight of those 24 are the build; the other
**sixteen are the round** — which is the clearest single statement of what the three lenses were
worth.

That distinction earned itself twice. Once because the +8 the build measured became +24 after
the round, so any total recorded mid-phase was going to be wrong. And once on `main` itself:
this session's first reading of it was **4,983**;
re-measured in the same working copy an hour later, on the same commit, `main` collects
**4,984**. Nothing in the tree changed between them. At the point the build finished, the tree
collected 4,992, so subtracting would have given `4,992 − 4,983 = 9` — a delta one larger than
the eight tests actually written, leaving an extra to be attributed to something. That is how a
fabricated attribution enters a record: not by inventing anything, but by trusting arithmetic
over measurement and then explaining the remainder. The
close-out constraint already says collection is environment-dependent (the same tree has
collected 4,926 in a reviewer's clone and 4,917 in a linked worktree at earlier phases); what
it does not lead you to expect is the same instability appearing *within* one environment.
**A total is not a delta.** The ±1 was not chased further; it is recorded rather than resolved
— and recorded as what it is: a **session-internal observation with no recoverable evidence**,
two readings an hour apart with nothing logged between them. A reviewer re-derived both totals
in a fresh clone and got perfect stability across three consecutive collects (and across
untracked-file perturbation), which neither confirms nor refutes it. The durable part is the
rule; the anecdote is motivation, not proof.

## Phase 233 (executed 2026-08-26 — Track D's close-path cluster, and three defects the phase introduced into its own fix)

Track D's third phase. Wade picked the close-path cluster at the session's open from four
offered clusters — `Q-017` plus `Q-020`'s entangled `close_batch.sh` leg, with `Q-031` as
the cheap third — and attached both mirror-push prerequisites (`Q-300`, `Q-072`) to this
phase rather than to a later one.

**`Q-017` had been refused three times, and the three counted refusals were all aimed at
the wrong question.** Each declines to *retire the fallback*, for the same stated reason:
*"a refusal at that call site is overwritten by the FALSE `Not found in review_tasks.md.
Skipping.`"* — true, and about the **verdict** (should a non-canonical header close at
all?). The headline defect is the **range**.

**One earlier pass did address the range, and the round corrected this record for eliding
it.** Phase 209 disqualified the entry's *filed* range remedy — routing the shell fallback
through `review_index.py --range` — and was right to: measured on this entry's own fixture
shape, the index path reported `4 tasks closed` on a three-task batch and marked a task
existing only inside a fenced example as done. That would have swapped a silent under-reach
for silent data **corruption**. So the range had been attacked once and the attack failed on
its merits. What no pass had tried is the shape taken here: leave the grep, filter its hits
through the mask Phase 209 itself shipped. Those are separable, and separating them cost nothing: the verdict is untouched
and stays exactly as ratified 2026-08-21 (*keep closing, stop being silent*), while the
boundary search now filters its hits through `$FENCED_LINES` — the same mask `CLOSE_AWK`
has rewritten around since Phase 209. The mask is populated under
`python3 && -f $INDEX_SCRIPT`, which is **precisely the `fallback` arm's own precondition**,
so the arm where the defect was measured always has one. No caller contract changes.

### Reproduced first, on a healthy install

Not on a python3-less host — on a **healthy** one, which is what makes it live. A near-miss
header (ASCII hyphen where `_BATCH_HEADER_RE` demands an em-dash) is invisible to
`--range` and matched by the grep; a fenced ```` ```markdown / ## Deferred ```` inside the
batch body then bounds it early:

    1 of 3 tasks closed, header flipped to `Merged`, TASK-2 and TASK-3 left `[ ]`
    underneath it, exit 0, run committed.

That is the state the entry was filed for on 2026-08-03 and re-measured at Phase 220's HEAD.
After the fix: 3 of 3 closed, the fenced example untouched, `## Statistics` bounding the batch.

### Three defects this phase introduced into its own fix

Each is now a battery row, because a phase that only mutates its final state is measuring
the answer it already has.

1. **The filter routed `awk` output into `$(( ))` for the first time.** (An earlier
   draft of this line said the filter made `find_batch_range` depend on `awk` "for the
   first time". **False, and the round caught it:** `main`'s own
   `total_lines=$(awk 'END { print NR }' "$TASKS_FILE")` sits inside that same function.
   What is new is narrower and is the part that bites — the *boundary* path now depends
   on awk, and its output reaches shell arithmetic.) That is a bash **syntax error**, not a zero, and under `set -euo pipefail` it
   aborts the close mid-run with a raw shell diagnostic and no verdict. Found by
   `tests/test_close_batch_sh.py::TestShortWriteGuard`, which shims a lying `awk`.
2. **The first repair was worse than the bug.** It returned 1. The sole caller renders any
   non-zero as the FALSE `"Not found in review_tasks.md. Skipping."` with a durable
   `not-found` reason — *the exact laundering `Q-017` is filed about* — and skipping meant
   the short-write guard, whose whole job is catching a lying awk, never ran. Two guards
   weakened to protect one. The shipped shape falls back to the pre-existing fence-blind
   computation instead: the floor is what shipped before, never worse, never a new refusal.
3. **Six of this phase's own new tests omitted `_scan_available()`**, the mirror guard all
   eight pre-existing tests in that module call. In the sterilized tree they error rather
   than skip — the Phase-160 class (`tests/test_adversarial_review_gate.py` reading
   `CLAUDE.md`), introduced by the phase whose brief names it. Caught by running `Q-072`.

### The message the fix falsified, and the one it had already falsified

Making the `fallback` arm fence-aware made its own warning false — it still said *"The
fallback is fence-blind … tasks below it stay open under a `Merged` header."* Corrected per
arm: `fallback` states the range is sound and the header is not, `fallback-no-index` keeps
the fence-blind claim because there it is still true, and a guard asserts the claim appears
on exactly one of them in both directions.

**And a second site was already false before this phase touched it.** The summary line (`close_batch.sh:970` on `main`, `:1087` here)'s
summary asserted *"their headers are not canonical"* for a counter **both** arms increment —
so an operator with a byte-perfect tracker and no python3 was told their header was
malformed. That is the same wrong-cause conflation **Phase 220's own round found and fixed
in the per-batch message**, left standing in the summary 400 lines below it. `Q-020`'s
structural note (a) — *the class recurs at call-site granularity, not file granularity* —
demonstrated inside the file the phase was already editing.

A third stale site: `test_batch_range_offset_guard.py`'s docstring still said the range
*"can over-reach"*. Phase 220's round caught exactly that wording in the shipped warning and
recorded that it was *inherited from this docstring*; the message was fixed and the source
of it was not.

### `Q-020`: the gate asked about a revision the merge does not land in

`git merge-base --is-ancestor <batch branch> main`, against the literal `main`. Under
`§ Merge policy: pr` — which is **this repo's own policy** — Step 4a merges each batch
branch into an integration branch cut from `origin/main`, Step 4b runs with that checked
out, and the PR is not squashed until Step 4d. A correctly-merged branch is therefore never
an ancestor of local `main`, so Step 4b **mandated `--force` in bold on every `pr` close** —
which also silences the cherry-pick detection. An unmerged branch was indistinguishable
from a merged one on the dominant path.

Measured rather than reasoned, on a `pr`-shaped fixture:

    --is-ancestor feat/one main    -> FALSE   (refuses correct work)
    --is-ancestor feat/one HEAD    -> TRUE    (correct)
    --is-ancestor feat/never HEAD  -> FALSE   (still catches it)

The predicate is now `HEAD` first with `main` retained as a fallback — **strictly wider than
what shipped**, so no consumer gains a refusal it did not have, and under `direct` policy
HEAD *is* main and nothing changes. Both Step 4-pre shapes pass, for different reasons, and
the second was verified separately: in the **PR-reuse shape** Step 4a is skipped and `HEAD`
**is** the approved branch, so the batch branch is trivially its own ancestor. The retired
text's claim that *"a reused PR branch is by definition still unmerged"* was true against
`main` and irrelevant against the revision the commits actually land on.

### `Q-031`: nine deletions and two contract sites

The brief called this *"close to a pure delete"*. It is 9 of 11. The other two are
`run_in_background: false`, in `/auto-fix` and `/auto-judge`'s `--merge` paths, and that
value encodes a real control-flow contract — *run one agent at a time, sequentially*.
Sub-agents now run in the background by default and no parameter forces the foreground, so
a clean delete would have removed the mechanism while leaving the prose ("Sequential",
"after the agent reports") asserting it. Both sites now state the sequencing as orchestrator
discipline: spawn one, wait for its completion notification, spawn nothing else meanwhile.

`tools/skill_audit_baseline.txt` is now **empty** — those three rows were its entire
contents, so the checker's own "names its debt" block has nothing left to name.

**That emptiness broke four guards, and the fix was not to re-add debt.** Four tests in
`tests/test_skill_audit_refs.py` asserted against the real corpus — `any("auto-build" in
key)`, `BASELINED (N)`, `run_in_background` in the named block, `--no-baseline` exiting 1.
Written that way, each died the moment the defect it described was fixed. The two ways to
revive them in place were to re-add debt or to weaken the assertion, both worse than the
bug; all four now seed a synthetic corpus and test the mechanism. The `--loop-only` one
asserts its own precondition first (`demo` is outside the loop corpus), because otherwise
the fixture cannot tell a narrowed snapshot from a full one.

### `Q-300`: the gate whose exit code carried no information

`tools/scan_public_history.sh` gated on **any** header finding. `Q-294` accepted 16
published commits carrying a private address; those commits are immutable; so it exited 1
on every run forever. Derived by running it against a full clone rather than trusting the
filing's numbers:

    commits:30   header-dirty:16   content-dirty:15   exit 1

**Two arms, two separate adjudications, and the runbook documents only one of them.** The
15 content findings (2026-07-15 → 07-24, one `PHASE_LOG.md` line Phase 160 fixed at tree
level) were accepted 2026-07-31, and step 5 states that intent verbatim at
`TESTER_MIRROR_RUNBOOK.md:184`. The 16 header findings are a *different* set accepted via
`Q-294`. The runbook **does** describe that arm (`:168-171`) and carries its immutability
rationale; what it lacks is the content arm's *disposition* line — the explicit "known and
accepted, do not re-litigate it as a new finding". (This phase's brief asserted "no
equivalent intent sentence anywhere in the runbook" and this record repeated it unchecked.
The round quoted the file. Narrowed to what is actually missing.) So the fix is two allow-lists, keyed by
SHA in `tools/public_history_accepted.txt` — immutable, so the list cannot rot — and the
content arm now gates too. It was report-only, which meant a brand-new content leak printed
`content:1` in a column that already carried fifteen non-zero rows: visible in principle,
invisible in practice.

**The `SUMMARY` line was itself part of the defect.** It printed `header-findings:$fail` —
a boolean, whatever the count — so an operator wanting the number had to count rows by
hand. That hand-count is the thing `Q-300` was filed about, forced by the instrument's own
output. It now prints real counts on both arms.

Against the real published history the gate now exits **0**, with
`accepted:content=15,header=16  NEW:content=0,header=0`, and still exits 1 on a seeded
unlisted leak. **Green now means green.**

### The author-side battery: 18/18, falsified by the round at 13 behaviour-changing survivors of 75

`tools/phase233_mutations.py`, 18 rows over two files. **Run 1: 14/18, four survivors, one
false kill, one ambiguous anchor.** Run 2 after closing all of them: **18/18 + 3/3 controls,
0 false kills**, `pre: killed 10, of which 5 only by pre`.

**Run 2's fraction is not the claim, and the round proved it.** An independent guards
lens wrote 75 mutations of its own and 13 behaviour-changing ones walked these guards. The
number this phase reports is **13/75**, not 18/18. What follows is why the author battery
could not have found them.

**The `pre` column is the one worth reading.** Phase 232's **first** battery reported `pre: killed 0 of 12` — its lens diagnosed that as a
set written against the new lines only, never asking whether they are safe *in the code they
sit inside*, and then walked 29 of 45 behaviour-changing mutations through the guards. (Its ledger row records the *final* run at `pre: killed 1, of which 0 only by
pre`; the `0 of 12` is the first set, and the two are different runs rather than
disagreeing records.) This one kills 10 in `pre`, 5 of them only there, which is the shape that says the rows reach
pre-existing behaviour as well as new. It is still an author battery and cannot escape the
fixtures the author designed.

**All four run-1 survivors were real, and `A3` is the one worth recording.** The filter maps
a grep hit's stream offset to an absolute line as `start + $1`; shifting it to
`start + $1 - 1` changed behaviour and every guard stayed green. The reason is that
`_fenced_mask` masks the fence **delimiters** as well as their content, so in the ordinary
fixture the fenced `## Deferred` *and* the ```` ```markdown ```` opener above it are both
masked — consulting the wrong one of two masked lines is invisible. The frame only matters
where a **real** boundary sits immediately after a fence close, which no fixture had. The
closing test asserts that precondition directly (`mask[b2-2]` true, `mask[b2-1]` false), so
it cannot quietly stop measuring the thing it was written for.

`B3` is `Q-020`'s own structural note (a) — *the class recurs at call-site granularity, not
file granularity* — reproduced **inside this phase's own fix**: every test drove the local
branch arm, so reverting the remote arm to `main` stayed green. That is the same shape the
phase had just found live in the summary line of the file it was already editing.
`B2` showed the retained `main` fallback — the arm that makes the widening *strictly wider*
— was a claim rather than a guard. `C2` showed nothing in that module had ever produced a
content finding at all.

**One false kill, fixed rather than excused.** `N3` reworded the accepted-marker's spacing
and reddened the suite: the tests pinned `ACCEPTED(header)` literally. The marker's spacing
is not the contract; *"the row is marked accepted on the header arm"* is. Loosened to a
spacing-tolerant match — an over-strict guard is how a maintainer learns to weaken a correct
one.

**And one battery bug, which is not a guard hole and is recorded as neither.** `N2` anchored
on `_merged_into_target`, which occurs three times (definition plus both arms), so the runner
refused it as `ANCHOR-AMBIGUOUS` and the row never ran. Renaming one of the three would have
been an undefined function — a real behaviour change, not a control. Replaced with a legal
reformat of the HEAD arm.

**Declared, not hidden: one control the battery does not reach.** `grep -qxF` → `grep -qF`
in `_accepted()` survives. `-x` is defense-in-depth — every accept-list entry is a full
40-character SHA, so a prefix match is unreachable in the current input space, and a test for
it would assert a shape the format forbids. Recorded as unexercised rather than given a
contrived guard or quietly dropped.

### The round: three lenses, and the battery was falsified

**Governor count: three** — the phase ships behaviour *and* a numeric record, which is the
conjunction the governor names. Independent fresh-context `general-purpose` agents in their
own worktrees, distinct lenses, none seeing another's findings.

**The guards lens wrote 75 mutations of its own. 27 survived; 13 of those change behaviour
(17% of mutations, 48% of survivors), against 10 controls with 0 false kills.** The author
battery's 18/18 is **falsified**. Re-derived with `tools/ledger_stats.py` **after this
phase's own ledger row landed** — which is the only point the number is true —
the standing claim is **49 all-killed author batteries, 47 falsified by a lens, 2 unknown
(166, 211), 0 intact.** Phase 233 is the 49th and the 47th. *Unknown is not vindicated*, and
the two are not evidence for the battery; they are phases whose round ran no independent
battery at all. Before its row landed the figure was 48/46/2/0, so any draft citing that is
reading a pre-close-out tree. Its verifiers covered
ten modules to the author battery's five.

**Two HIGH, both in this phase's own fix, and both found independently by two lenses.**

1. **`Q-017` was not fixed.** When every `##` after the batch start is fenced — i.e. the
   batch is the file's last section — the awk filter correctly prints nothing, and the
   degradation guard read that as *"awk broke"* and recomputed the fence-BLIND answer. The
   filed defect, reinstated by its own fix, **while the run printed the claim that the range
   was fence-aware**. Measured: 1 of 3 closed, exit 0, committed. Not exotic — this file's
   own comment records that some consumers author no `## Statistics` block, so for them it is
   the last batch on **every** close. The comment claiming the floor was *"never worse"* was
   false in that direction: it was a ceiling overriding a correct answer. Fixed with a `0`
   sentinel — three outcomes, not two.
2. **`Q-020` certified unmerged work as merged.** `--is-ancestor X HEAD` is trivially true
   whenever HEAD sits at the branch tip. Reproduced: checked out on `feat/five`, merged
   nowhere, `main` not containing it — `✓ Branch 'feat/five' verified merged.` and the header
   flipped. **The shipped gate refused that.** The change was sold as *"cannot introduce a new
   refusal"*, which is true and was the wrong thing to check: it introduced a new
   **acceptance**, in the one case the gate exists for, and `batch_work.sh` puts an operator
   exactly there by creating the batch worktree checked out on the batch branch. Fixed with
   strict containment. The PR-reuse shape cannot be certified by ancestry at all — HEAD *is*
   the branch — so it keeps `--force`, and this record's earlier claim that both shapes were
   covered is corrected rather than trimmed.

**A third defect surfaced from writing the test for the second fix.** The degradation floor
covered an awk that exits 0 with unusable output and **not** one that exits non-zero: the
filter is a pipeline in a command substitution on a plain assignment, so under `pipefail` and

## Phase 234 (executed 2026-08-26 — Track D's wrong-tree residue, and the wrong acceptance the fix for a wrong read opened)

**Members:** `Q-020` (mechanism 3, closing the entry outright), `Q-307` leg (b), `Q-022`.
Wade's call at the session's open, chosen over the `tasks/` schema cluster and the
orchestrator group. The framing is one class, not three items: **a tool resolved the wrong
tree.** Two scripts asked `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`, which answers *which worktree is
the caller standing in*, while every use of the value meant *which checkout is the primary*.
The validator is the same class one level up — it read a record off the filesystem while
that record lives on a branch.

`Q-307`(b) was also wrong about its own severity, in the safe direction. It says the real
primary "classifies ACTIVE" and that the failure needs `--force`. Measured: it classifies
