## Phase 238 (executed 2026-08-27 — option C, and the doc sweep that was guarding a falsehood)

**Scope, on Wade's call at the open.** Four questions were put to him before any code was
written, each with options and a recommendation: **(1)** whether Part D rides this phase or the
push; **(2)** two lenses or three; **(3)** where `Q-317` goes; **(4)** what to do with an
untracked branch-refs file. His answer was **go** on all four recommendations. So: **Part C plus
Part D's tiers 1–2** — the corrections — with tier 3's new prose (monograph, colophon,
`install-and-update.md`, `WORKFLOW.md` §§ 8.4/2.8) riding the mirror push, **three lenses**,
**`Q-317` → E1**, and the branch-refs file committed as a recovery record.

**The Part D split is the one call worth re-deriving rather than inheriting.** The brief sized
part D at "~0 standalone". It is **23 sites across 10 files**, and the brief was wrong about its
own named surfaces: `WORKFLOW.md` §§ 2.2 / 2.4 / 2.8 are named as the drift, and all three were
already current bar a single sentence in § 2.2. The seam that mattered was not defect class but
**whether the site was false or merely absent** — eleven corrections, twelve omissions — and
Part C changes the very surfaces the omissions describe. Writing the `## Plan review` template
and the tutorial's Step-6 paragraph before Step 6 settled would have been writing them twice.

### What Phase 237 left behind, and what was enforcing it

**Phase 237 shipped part B's readers and left the shipped tree asserting they do not exist.** Two
sites in `claim-task/SKILL.md` — one of them the sentence *"Do not describe those readers as
existing"* — plus `WORKFLOW.md` § 2.2, which **contradicted itself ~230 lines below**, where the
same file documents `/review-close` Step 2e — and again at § 8.4, ~1,850 lines below,
where it documents `/sitrep` reading the park markers. **An earlier draft gave one figure
for both citations.** They differ by an order of magnitude, and quoting the near one for
both overstated how locally visible the contradiction was.

**Five guards were enforcing the falsehood, and one of them had been deliberately re-anchored to
it a phase earlier.** Phase 236 built leg 3, correctly narrowed its guard from "part B is
unbuilt" to "the READERS do not exist", and wrote a comment explaining that pinning the wider
claim *"would force the file to keep a falsehood"*. Phase 237 then built the readers and swept
none of it. The suite was green over the whole thing, twelve tests passing.

That is the shape this repo keeps recording from the other side: a guard that pins a **claim**
rather than a **property** becomes, the moment the claim changes, a machine for keeping the tree
wrong. Every one of the eight retired assertions here was **re-pointed, not deleted** — and the
retirement carries the rule the brief names: a correction has to quote the retired phrase in
order to retire it, so `assert phrase not in file` fails on the fix and passes only if the record
of the fix is deleted. The sweep below therefore exempts the retiring sentence by name.

### Part C — option C, plan-only (`Q-235` leg #435)

**Shipped with zero validator change**, and the argument is stronger than the one that retired
`## Test decision`'s Invariant 13 in Phase 234: that invariant fired on every *claimed* task; a
`## Plan` presence check would fire on nearly every task in the *queue*, because option C is one
of three interaction modes and most tasks never take it.

- **`tasks/schema.md`** gains a `## Plan` body section — optional, written only by option C,
  holding the plan verbatim plus the sealed `REVIEW_REPORT:` that passed it. Ordered **after**
  `## Test decision` on purpose: the embedded plan carries its own `## Test decision` line inside
  the wrapper fence, so the body holds two textual occurrences and one real heading, and the
  ordering is what keeps a fence-blind first-match reader correct. Stated as a residual: a
  fence-blind **last**-match reader would still be wrong.
- **Step 1 rejects `--plan-only` for a `BATCH-*` claim.** It cannot live at Step 6, and that is
  the whole point: resolution tier 1 outranks the offer and says "never prompt when tier 1
  resolves", so the one path that skips the offer would have been the one path that got it wrong.
  Placing it at Step 1 also means the batch is **not yet claimed** when the rejection fires.
- **Step 7a's skip is a presence test and it skips the planner, never the reviewer.** A body
  marker is a string any agent with `Bash` can write, so the fix is to remove what forging it
  would buy rather than to defend it. Re-reviewing a day-old plan is correct on its merits: it
  was reviewed against a `main` that has moved.
- **Step 7f** — write, commit under Rule A, release, commit the flip. The ordering is the design:
  `claim_task.sh --release` refuses five ways, and an ordering that released first lost the plan
  on every failure path.

**Three divergences from the spec, each because running the thing contradicted reading it.**

1. **The spec's four "silent-failure" fixes are three.** Its third — *name the main checkout in
   7a's Input and hard-fail on a missing body* — is **already built**, at
   `claim-task/SKILL.md`'s planner prompt, in both halves. Phase 171 shipped it; the spec
   predates it.
2. **The plan is read from the run directory, never passed through the shell.** The spec implies
   substitution. `plan.md` is a multi-kilobyte sub-agent document, and putting it through a shell
   argument is how a quoting bug becomes a code-execution bug — the `<PARK_REASON>` lesson, one
   artifact larger. Only the one-line `<TEST_DECISION>` is substituted, single-quoted, with the
   same warning the park block carries.
3. **A `plan-only.md` record, which the spec does not have.** Without it, a `--resume` after a
   *refused release* reaches 7-pre's routing table, matches `verdict: PROCEED`, and walks to the
   executor — implementing a task whose human asked only for a plan. The spec's abort rule leaves
   exactly that window open and does not see it.

**And one design decision the spec leaves open: how to embed a plan inside a body section.**
Demoting the plan's own `##` headings would need a fence-aware rewriter over sub-agent prose.
Fencing it needs arithmetic — a wrapper longer than the longest backtick run inside. The boring
mechanism was chosen, and it makes the round-trip exact: Step 7a copies the section back out by
delimiter rather than by heading scan.

### Part D tiers 1–2 — eleven sites, and a knob nobody could configure

Six flat falsehoods (the three part-B sites above, the tutorial's *"Claude Code runs them
there"*, `WORKFLOW_GUIDE.md`'s claim that the validator warns on a missing test decision — Phase
234 residue, not orchestrator residue — and the monograph's `/sitrep` glossary missing three
shipped states), plus five stale identifiers: `/claim-task` **Step 6** cited twice as where
the test decision is authored (`review-close/SKILL.md`, `tasks/schema.md`), the retired
name **reviewer-executor** at two sites (`document-work/SKILL.md`, and
`validate_tasks.py`'s own retirement comment), and `WORKFLOW_GUIDE.md`'s pre-171 framing
of `/claim-task` as a command that stops at the claim — corrected four lines below itself
in the same file, but the sentence a reader meets first.

> **An earlier draft of this paragraph enumerated four of the five and still said five.**
> The round's claims lens caught the arithmetic and concluded the true count was ten. It
> is eleven: the defect was the enumeration, not the total, and the fifth site is the one
> now named. Recorded rather than silently fixed, because a reviewer being right about a
> defect and wrong about its remedy is the case the adjudication rule exists for.

**`## Plan review` was documented nowhere.** A shipped consumer knob, read by Step 6 since Phase
171, absent from `docs/configuration.md` and from `WORKFLOW.md` § 6.1 — the two places the
shipped docs promise it would be. A consumer could not configure it without reading skill source.
Worse, `configuration.md` opened with a hand-maintained count — *"Four are pure configuration"* —
that a reader uses to judge whether the table is complete. The new guard **derives** that count
from the table rather than asserting it.

### The author-side pass — 20/28, then 29/29

**Run 1 killed 20 of 28 with 0 false kills.** Every one of the eight survivors was a real hole,
and they fall into two groups that say the same thing about how the guards were written.

- **Four were prose nothing executes** — Step 7f's four steps reorderable (the release could be
  moved *ahead* of the plan commit, which is the exact ordering the step exists to forbid), the
  abort-rules table deletable, its never-retry row invertible, and Rule A droppable from the plan
  commit. The **code** layer was strong — 11 of 14 Step 7f rows died on the first run, because an
  execution layer runs that block against a real repo — and the layer sequencing it did not exist.
- **Two were population gaps**, and they are the sharper finding: I fixed two Tier-1 falsehoods
  and then guarded them **only in the files I had edited**. `docs/getting-started.md` and
  `WORKFLOW_GUIDE.md` were in no guard's population at all, so both falsehoods were reinstatable
  with every other guard green. That is rule 1's *derive the population from the source of truth,
  not from an index of it* — applied here to my own diff, which is the worst index available.

  The closure is a **`git ls-files`-derived retired-claim sweep** over the whole shipped tree,
  excluding `tools/`, `tests/` and the four maintainer records that narrate this history on
  purpose. Its non-vacuity test drives the real function over a planted population and checks
  three directions: every phrase must fire when planted, the phrase carrying an exemption must
  not fire inside its own retiring sentence, and that same phrase far from any retiring
  sentence must fire again.

  > **That sentence was false when this entry first carried it, and the round proved it.**
  > The first version of the test computed `norm(phrase) in norm(text_it_had_just_written)`
  > — a substring check against a string it had interpolated itself — and never called
  > `retired_claim_problems()` at all. `return []` at the top of the sweep left the entire
  > suite green. It checked *neither* direction, let alone both. The test now drives the real
  > function, a second test pins that the sweep is not deletable, and the sweep's population,
  > case-sensitivity and exemption window were closed alongside it. **Disclosed rather than
  > quietly repaired**, on the same rule the two corrections above follow — and it is the
  > sharpest instance in this phase, because it is a false claim about the phase's own newest
  > guard, written one paragraph after quoting the rule that a guard pinning a claim rather
  > than a property keeps the tree wrong.
- The remaining two: **`C09`**, which kept `fence_mark` and reduced the closer to `elif mark:` —
  presence of the helper is not fence *awareness*, and my AST check proved the wrong thing; and
  **`E05`**, which dropped `ask` from § 6.1's value enumeration and passed because the row spells
  each value again in its `always` → option A mapping. The incidental-hit failure, again.

**Final: 29/29 killed, 4 negative controls green, 0 false kills, 0 stale anchors.** Reported as
what it is — an author's number, which measures self-consistency. Three of 29 are declared
reverts (10%), which is the minority rule 1 asks for.

**One row was mis-anchored twice, and the instrument caught it both times.** `D01`'s anchor was
typed from my memory of the line's wrapping rather than read off the file, so the mutation never
applied. The harness reported `ANCHOR-STALE` rather than scoring it, which is precisely the
instrumentation Phase 237 added after a mis-anchored mutation was briefly recorded as a survivor.
The `mis-anchored mutation` class, first recorded in Phase 177, now on its **35th** phase — and
its lesson is the fixture rule the governor already states, arriving from a third direction.

### Three defects in my own work, all found by running rather than reading

The write-back **appended instead of replacing in place**, so the first run pushed both sections
below `## Surfaced by` and broke the order `tasks/schema.md` documents. It **accreted a blank
line per run**, so it was not idempotent. And its fence handling was wrong for **its own widened
fence**: `startswith("```")` treats a 3-backtick block inside a 4-backtick wrapper as a closer.
None is visible by reading; all three came from running the block twice against a real repo and
diffing.

**And one self-inflicted on the guards.** The new write-back is the third prescribed block
opening `import sys, json, subprocess`, so two `rindex`-anchored mutations silently retargeted
onto it and stopped testing the classification write they are named for. That is the **fourth**
recorded appearance in this corpus of *"adding text to a file weakens every occurrence-indexed
mutation over it"* — and the first where the text was added by the same phase that had to notice.
Both are now anchored on the classification block's own unique line.

### Filed, not fixed

- **`Q-317`** (parked `BATCH-` claim still invisible to `/sitrep`) routes to **E1** on Wade's
  call. The orchestrator group therefore closes with a **named-open gap**, said out loud in
  `claim-task/SKILL.md` Step 8 and in `WORKFLOW.md` § 2.2 rather than left for a reader to
  discover: `/sitrep`'s predicate is reached on the roadmap path only.
- **`_prose_guard_helpers.section()` is fence-blind**, and `WORKFLOW.md` § 6.1's body is mostly
  fenced templates whose content lines are literal `## Merge policy`, `## Plan review`. A guard
  using it over that section silently reads the first ~40 lines and passes vacuously on the rest.
  Found by writing the new module, which slices by its own heading pair instead and carries a
  non-vacuity test naming two templates that bracket the span. **Worth a sweep of other
  `section()` callers; not done here.**

### The adversarial round — two rounds, and the second one is the finding

**Round 1: three lenses** (does it execute / are its claims true / are the guards real), the third
on a different model than the author, each in its own worktree. **Round 2: two lenses** over the
rewrite, spawned on the governor's stated second-round condition — *the fixes themselves produced
substantial new material no fresh reader has seen*, which a guard layer rewritten rather than
patched plainly is.

| | Round 1 | Round 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Independent mutations | 86 | 62 |
| **Survived** | **70 (81%)** | **47 (76%)** |
| Negative controls | 24 | 24 |
| **False kills** | **13 (54%)** | **13 (54%)** |
| Author's own battery, same subject | 29/29, 0 false kills | 35/35, 0 false kills |

**The fiftieth consecutive falsification** of an author battery in this project's log, and the
second round is what makes it worth recording rather than filing as more of the same:
**a full rewrite of the guard layer moved survival five points and moved over-strictness by
zero.** That is evidence about the *axis*, not about the effort — which is why `Q-318` files the
class instead of scheduling a third pass at it. Wade's call at the close, put to him with both
rounds' numbers in hand, as the governor requires for anything past the second round.

**What the split says.** The **execution** layer — `tests/test_claim_task_heredocs_execute.py`,
which extracts the prescribed heredocs and *runs* them against a real git repo with a real linked
worktree — killed everything it covered, in both rounds. The prose and AST layers around it did
not. Round 2's own words: *"the new checks are still occurrence counts, substring presence, and
single-regex spellings."*

#### Two HIGH shipped defects, both found by running rather than reading

**The sealed report used a fixed three-backtick fence while the plan got a computed one** — ten
lines apart, same class, and only one was protected. A reviewer quoting a fenced snippet in a
finding's `evidence:` field is ordinary output, not an adversarial payload; it breaks the wrapper,
and the *next* option-C run's section strip then desyncs and **deletes every section after it** —
silently, exit 0, in a tracked file. The fence is now computed over both documents, and an
unterminated fence anywhere in the body is a **refusal** (exit 6) rather than a rewrite.

**"the branch is about to be deleted by `--release`" was false.** `claim_task.sh` defaults
`DELETE_BRANCH=false`. The stale branch is then reused by the next claim from a pre-option-C fork
point, and the close hits a real content conflict in the task body — demonstrated by execution, on
the path Step 7f's own final message recommends. Now `--delete-branch`, gated on
`git rev-list --count main..<BRANCH_NAME>` being `0`, because the script force-deletes.

#### A shipped falsehood this phase introduced by omission

`WORKFLOW.md` § 8.3's `plan-review-preference.md` manifest row still read *"Two options … the
reviewer runs on **both**"* and omitted `--plan-only` — **in the same file this phase corrected at
§ 2.2**. A doc sweep that fixes one restatement of a contract and misses another in the same file
is the population failure again, one level up from the guards.

#### The record falsehood, which is the sharpest thing in this phase

This entry claimed the retired-claim sweep's *"non-vacuity test checks both directions."* It
checked **neither**: it computed `norm(phrase) in norm(text_it_had_just_written)` — a substring
check against a string it had interpolated itself — and never called the sweep at all, which could
`return []` with the entire suite green. Written by the session that had, one paragraph earlier,
quoted the rule that a guard pinning a claim rather than a property keeps the tree wrong. Both the
test and the sentence are corrected above, with disclosure.

**And the fix commit fixed it in code while leaving it standing in the record** — round 2's claims
lens caught that, noting that two *other* corrections in the same diff carried explicit
"an earlier draft…" blockquotes. The practice was applied inconsistently inside one commit.

#### Three guards were keeping the tree wrong, not one

The phase opened by naming Phase 237's failure and then reproduced it three times: the part-B
reader guards, `test_claim_artifact_reaping.py`'s pin on the spec table's stale
*"Leg 3 BUILT — Phase 236"*, and the sweep's own vacuity claim. **Naming a class does not confer
immunity to it**, and that is the transferable half of this phase.

#### Four mis-anchored mutations, all mine, all one cause

Every one was written from memory of a line's wrapping or without checking which occurrence a
`replace(..., 1)` would hit — the last of them silently mutated Step 7d's abandon arm instead of
Step 7f's step 4, and briefly read as a surviving guard hole. The harness reported `ANCHOR-STALE`
rather than scoring the ones it could see, which is Phase 237's instrumentation working. The
`mis-anchored mutation` class, first recorded Phase 177, now on its **35th** phase — and the
standing lesson generalises: derive the anchor from the file, never from your model of it.

#### Dispositions

**Fixed:** both HIGH shipped defects, the CRLF and symlink defects, the § 8.3 falsehood, the
record falsehood, the spec table's currency line and a pre-existing duplicated clause, plus every
guard that was **rejecting correct code** (`os.replace` refused by a check whose own message asks
for an "os-level replace"; a Rule A regex rejecting `[ … ]` and a multi-line brace body; a
half-applied rename tolerance; a config header-cell equality that made every row unparseable) and
every guard gap that protected **data loss or the anti-forgery argument** — Step 7f's ordering by
command position, Rule A by position rather than count, the abort rules against an appended
contradiction, Step 7a's plan-presence skip, Step 1's batch rejection, `schema.md`'s `### Plan`
contract, the fence-length AST check, the sweep's population/case/exemption window, the
destructive-command regex (which had **no `git branch -D` arm**, in the phase that introduced a
force delete), and a decorative `co_consts` assertion that could never fail.

**Filed as `Q-318` (§ Medium, → E1):** the residual ~40, all one class. Filed under Medium and not
High deliberately — the shipped code is correct and the guards are weak, so it is not a *live
defect in shipped code* and must not reset the announce clock by mis-filing.

**Declared residual:** contradiction-blindness in prose checks generally. Phase 179 measured
polarity-by-string-matching at 0 of 21 and abandoned it; this phase is the second independent
measurement pointing the same way. The specific instances guarding data loss and the forgery
argument were closed with negation-aware checks; the general case is `Q-318`'s subject.

**Author battery, final: 35/35 killed, 4 negative controls green, 0 false kills, 0 stale
anchors** — reported as what it is, an author's number, which measures self-consistency. The
round's own six attack classes are kept permanently in `tools/phase238_mutations.py` as rows
`R01`–`R06`, marked `origin="round-1"`.

### `Q-319` — the close path halts on the ordinary cycle, and the filing's fix was refuted

`/review-close` Step 4b opened unconditionally with `bash sysop/scripts/close_batch.sh <N1> <N2>

`git log -1 --pretty=%s | grep -q '^docs: close Batch '`. A `/claim-task` single-task cycle carries
no review batch, so that commit never exists and never will — and the step said `Halt before Step
4c`. The halt lands *after* step 5's merges, and it stops the compliant operator specifically: the
one who infers a no-op gets through, the one who follows the written step does not.

**The filing named a fix source, and running it refuted the source.** `Q-319` said Step 4c step 1b
*"already parses the set — `review_task_ids = pending.get('review_task_ids') or []` at `:1939` — it

`close_batch.sh TASK-0001` is rejected at **argument parsing** — `❌ Unknown argument: TASK-0001`,
exit 1 — so it never reaches a batch lookup. `/document-work`'s namespace section says so outright; two further sites — Step 4c's routing
note and `close_batch.sh`'s *"Step 4c has no batch-id list to iterate"* — say the adjacent thing
(that Step 4c does not consult the field), which is not the same proposition. The first draft
called all three the same claim.

**Then my own replacement prose was wrong in the same way, and execution caught that too.** The
first draft said the script *"takes integers"*. It does not: `BATCH-1` is accepted (the prefix is
stripped), so the shorthand is wrong in the direction that matters — it implies the `BATCH-` form
fails. Both facts are now stated in the step and pinned by a test that runs the script.

Shipped: Step 4b determines its batch set from the `BATCH-<N>.lock` files, resolved through the
lock rather than the branch name (Step 2e's rule, same reason — `--branch` and the index's

**Three on the governor's behaviour-plus-numeric-record condition**, fresh-context

checkout. Lenses: *does it execute* / *are its claims true* / *are the guards real*. Overlap was
essentially nil — each found what the others structurally could not, which is the ~15% figure
Phase 166 measured, holding again.

had already refuted two claims. Rule 4 not triggered. **And 24/24 meant what the ledger says it
means:** an independent lens then wrote 46 rows and 26 survived.

## Phase 240 (executed 2026-08-28 — the post-spawn assertion gains a config arm, and the arm gets an invoker)

**Member:** `Q-049` — closed. Wade's call at the session's open, taken over `Q-325` (spec-only),
`Q-322` (`PHASE_LOG.md` dedupe) and E1 (the instrument bundle). Preceded by a standalone inbound
triage commit (`633c2ee`) that is not part of this phase; the two are separate on purpose, because
triage ships no behaviour and this does.

### The premise was measured before it was built on

`Q-049` is a consumer report, and this repo cannot exhibit the bug — `git config --get
core.hooksPath` is unset here, which is exactly why the maintainer's own rounds never surfaced it
and GDP's did. So the first act of the phase was to reproduce it rather than accept it: set a
relative `core.hooksPath` (`.githooks-probe`), spawn one agent with `isolation: "worktree"`, read
the value back. It had become an absolute path rooted at the repo — `<repo-root>/.githooks-probe`, in the shared
`--local` config, with no worktree teardown restoring it. The probe was then reverted and the full
local config diffed against a pre-probe snapshot: **identical**. One spawn, ~7 seconds, and the
report's central claim is a measurement rather than a citation.

**Why that mattered beyond diligence.** The reporter had already established that a plain `git
worktree add`/`remove` does *not* reproduce it, so the trigger is the harness's isolation setup.
Had that been taken on faith, the natural fix would have been aimed at git's worktree machinery,
which is the wrong layer and would have shipped inert.

### The fix site is the shared file, and the report scoped it one step too narrowly

The report proposes extending `/review-close` Step 2b's HARD RULE. That covers a minority of the
spawn sites. `_shared/adversarial-review.md`'s worktree-isolation section prescribes `isolation:
"worktree"` for **any** ad-hoc review round — and this project's own convention requires such a
round every phase — so the rewrite rides along with every round run here and in any consumer, plus
the `/codebase-review` and `/security-audit` fan-outs that section explicitly covers. The third
caveat therefore lands in the shared file, with Step 2b inheriting it.

It carries an **executed** recipe, not a warning: snapshot `git config --local --list` before the
spawn, diff after, restore from the baseline. That is deliberate. `Q-318` measured prose guards at
76–81% survivable across two lenses, Phase 179 measured polarity-by-regex at 0 of 21, and Phase
239's round walked two successive tightenings of the same guard — so a rule that can be *run* is
worth more than a rule that can be *matched*, and this is the smallest available instance of the
`Q-325` execution-layer direction rather than another regex.

### The trap that would have made a targeted detector report clean

`git config --list` lower-cases the key: the rewritten value renders as `core.hookspath=…`, not
`core.hooksPath=…`. A detector grepping for the camelCase spelling — which is how the key appears
in every document that discusses it, including `WORKFLOW.md` and `Q-049` itself — finds nothing
and certifies a rewritten repo as clean. That is why both the shared file and Step 2b diff against
a captured baseline instead of probing for one key, and why the remedy prose names the lower-cased
form. `test_a_targeted_grep_for_the_camelcase_key_would_report_clean` pins it, and is written to
fail loudly if git ever changes that rendering, since the warning would then be stale.

### The arm had no invoker, which is Phase 166's finding applied to this phase

Adding a config check to Step 2b's assertion buys nothing for an ad-hoc round, because that
assertion runs only during a close. Phase 166 recorded the same shape — a rule with no invoker
would not have run — and this phase found the evidence sitting in its own repo: **four leaked agent
worktrees and four `worktree-agent-*` branches from Phases 238 and 239 were live on this checkout**,
and `self_check.sh` matched that shape nowhere. **Corrected by the round:** an earlier draft of this sentence said *neither* `self_check.sh` nor `cleanup_worktrees.sh` matched it, and the execution lens refuted that half by running the script — `cleanup_worktrees.sh` lists an agent worktree and classifies it `✅ MERGED (safe to clean)`, because its parser filters by nothing. So the residue was visible to a shipped tool; what was missing is a *report* anyone reads outside a close. So `self_check.sh`
gains section 4b: it reports isolation residue and the `core.hooksPath` shape.

Three properties of that arm are deliberate and guarded:

- **Detection only.** It never removes anything. Phase 165 deleted a `--force` rollback that
  prescribed a wholesale worktree wipe, and a residue report is exactly where that would come back.
  The report instead says what to check first — and states the trap that makes the obvious check
  wrong: **after a squash-merge an ancestry test reports non-zero for correctly merged work too**,
  which is what three of this repo's four leaked branches look like right now.
- **Advisory, not fatal.** Residue does not move the exit code. A `self_check.sh` that goes red on
  a leaked worktree is unusable mid-round, which is when you would most want to run it.
- **It reports the property, never a defect.** `self_check.sh` cannot know what the owner
  originally configured, so an absolute `core.hooksPath` is reported with its consequence and the
  restore command — not asserted to be a rewrite.

### Some of the guards run the shipped commands instead of retyping them

`tests/test_step2b_baseline_delta.py`'s existing helpers **retype** the commands they test. That is
the defect Phase 239 paid for — a hand-typed twin let a shipped gate be weakened to `grep -q '^docs:
'` with the whole suite green — so the new rows in *that module* do not repeat it: `_fence_after()` extracts the
fenced commands from the shipped skill, blockquote prefixes stripped, and executes those. If the
skill's command changes, the test changes with it; if the fence is emptied, the extractor raises
rather than passing over nothing.

`test_the_prose_and_the_fence_agree_on_the_command_count` exists for a narrower reason: "assert all
four" is a count in prose, and a count is falsifiable by the fence beside it. **An earlier draft
justified it by saying Phase 200's version of this gate shipped inert "because prose and
mechanism drifted apart"; the round checked, and that is not what Phase 200 records.** Its
defect was *ordering* — the baseline capture sat 82 lines after the spawn it had to precede,
found by walking the file in reading order. The count test is worth having on its own terms;
it just does not have that precedent behind it.

### The round: three lenses, and it changed the phase rather than ratifying it

Three fresh-context `general-purpose` lenses — execution, guards, claims — each in a throwaway
clone checked out at the phase tag and gated on a symbol the change *introduced*, because
`isolation: "worktree"` hands a reviewer the default branch and this work was on a feature branch.
The governor's conjunction applies: behaviour plus a numeric record, so three rather than two.

**Four HIGH findings, two of them shipped defects this phase introduced.**

1. **The "executed recipe" was not executable markdown.** The bash fence opener was appended to
   the end of a 1,491-character prose line, so it never opened a fence — and the lone closer that
   followed opened an *unterminated* one. Measured: `fenced_text` 30,253 characters against 196
   after the repair, `live_command_lines` **75 against 2**, `fenced_blocks` **0**. Seven guard
   modules read that machinery; two iterate fenced blocks and were therefore **inert over this
   file**, and five were scanning 73 prose lines as live shell. The file is
   `_shared/adversarial-review.md` — the procedure `CLAUDE.md` requires every phase to follow.
   The execution lens ran the collapsed recipe and it returned **exit 0, silent, even with the
   rewrite it exists to detect already planted**, because the diff had ended up inside a comment.
   My own guard asserted `"```bash" in body` and passed over all of it.
2. **The phase turned a publication gate red.** `test_pass_1b_no_absolute_home_paths` is
   MUST-be-empty with no allowlist and was green at the parent commit; an absolute home path in
   this entry and in the shared file broke it. A cut could not have run.
3. **`Q-049` was recorded closed and was not.** No Phase-240 commit had touched
   `REVIEW_CHECKLIST.md` or `REVIEW_ARCHIVE.md` at all.
4. **`Q-322`'s correction reproduced the error it was correcting** — `[0-9]+[A-Za-z]?` does not
   consume `.1` either, so the "corrected" 67 still carried phantoms. The tree supports **66**.

**The guards lens falsified the author number, and the specific way is the useful part.**
My battery reported 18/18 with 0 of 3 controls reddening. An independent 37-row set killed
**17, 46%**, with 20 survivors — every one of which was then re-run against the full 5,143-test
suite and caught by nothing. Its 13 controls reddened at **30.8%**. It reproduced my three columns
exactly (A 7/7, B 7/7, C 4/4), so the number was arithmetically right and worthless as evidence.

**My stated confidence ordering was inverted.** I predicted the prose column would be weakest and
rated `self_check.sh` "detection is fine, scope is the weakness". The lens killed 40% on the shared
file, 75% on the skill, and **20% on `self_check.sh`** — the surface with the *most* execution had
the *weakest* discrimination, because its ten tests were ten happy paths over one homogeneous
fixture. That is a sharper authoring rule than "author batteries are weak": **execution coverage
is not discrimination if every fixture is the same shape.**

**The recipe had zero execution coverage, and four independent breakages of it survived the whole
suite:** the two halves naming different files (my regex accepted both — the C02 class I had
claimed to close, one level up), `&&` inverted so it prints *unchanged* exactly when it changed,
the two lines swapped, and `| sort` on one side only, which false-FAILs *every* clean round because
`git config --local --list` emits in file order. All four now die to tests that extract the recipe
and run it. Fixing them exposed a design point rather than a test gap: **the snapshot path must be
derivable, not held in a shell variable**, because the round genuinely runs between the two halves —
two shells in practice. It now derives from `git rev-parse --git-common-dir`, carries the `rm -f`
the skill calls load-bearing for the tree baseline, and no longer writes a fixed `/tmp` name that
collides between repos and concurrent rounds.

**A guard that could not fail.** `test_the_caveat_slicer_fails_closed`'s second assertion was
`.index` over a string literal, with no dependency on the repo; the lens demonstrated the vacuity by
running my test body verbatim against a deliberately fail-*open* slicer, and it passed.

**Three defects in code I wrote, all Medium, all found by execution rather than reading.**
`self_check.sh` read the **merged** config while making a `--local` claim, so a deliberate
`--global` absolute path was blamed on a spawn and the printed remedy would have written a
`--local` key shadowing it. `~/gh` was reported *relative* though git expands it, pinning every
worktree — the exact property the arm exists to warn about, given a green tick. And the residue
detector scoped to `agent-` while Step 2b's own assertion greps the directory: `EnterWorktree`'s
`name` parameter makes `agent-` the default shape and not the only one, so **two shipped surfaces
disagreed about what a leak is.** I sided with the skill and rewrote the test that had pinned my
first answer, stating the cost — a human who parks a worktree there is now reported too, which is
why the report is advisory and removes nothing.

**The new capture broke a self-cancel invariant the same file asserts.** Writing the config
baseline *after* `git status` left it absent from the tree snapshot and present in the tree it is
compared against, so the third assertion command false-fired on the step's own artefact — with the
remedy telling the operator to revert it. `SKILL.md`'s claim that this "cannot happen in either
location" was true for the tree baseline and false for the one I added. Config is captured first
now, proven by running the shipped commands in a repo with no gitignore.

**Two false statements in my own commit records, corrected in place.** That a guard pinned the
`BEFORE any spawn` *ordering* — it was token-presence and survived the lines being swapped — and
that `cleanup_worktrees.sh` could not see agent worktrees, refuted by running it: it lists one and
classifies it `✅ MERGED (safe to clean)`.

**And the battery under-reported twice, both times looking like coverage.** Run 2 reported four
survivors in the shared file while the guards closing them were already written and passing — the
verifier simply never ran the module holding them, and had I believed it the record would say
*"prose guards do not close polarity"*, a conclusion that agrees with three prior measurements and
was false. Then after the round's fixes, four rows went **ANCHOR-STALE** and did not run while the
report still read 18/18. Final, all anchors resolving: **22/22 killed, 4 controls, 0 false kills** —
and that number is wiring, not coverage, which is the whole point of the paragraph above.

### Suite

**5,148 passed, 160 skipped, 0 failed — measured at the record commit `547ea3b`**, i.e. after
`PHASE_LOG.md`, the `CLAUDE.md` row, the ledger row and the brief rewrite landed, not at the code
commit. `tests/test_archive_accounting.py` is deselected as environment-dependent.

The two reds that stood through the phase were the `Q-272` structural window — the next-session
brief and the ledger row — and both closed at close-out, as designed. **Two further reds were
NOT structural and were introduced by this phase**: the fence-balance gate and the
`Pass 1b` publication gate. Both were green at the parent `633c2ee`, neither was named in the
phase's own record until a lens found them, and **no author battery could have seen either**,
because a battery's green-start check is its own verifier modules rather than the gate the branch
must pass. That is now a close-out warning in the Phase 241 brief.

**Delta: +34**, derived per-file against `main` rather than by subtracting totals —
`test_adversarial_review_gate.py` **+12**, `test_self_check_sh.py` **+13**,
`test_step2b_baseline_delta.py` **+9**. `test_archive_accounting.py` shows +5 in the same diff and
is **excluded**: it parametrizes over sibling consumer checkouts, so the figure tracks which
directory the collection ran in, not this branch. `test_mirror_skip_discipline.py` is unchanged,
which is the expected result — it gains a case only when a test *module* is added, and this phase
added rows to three existing modules and no new one.

### Deliberately not done

- **No row spawns a real isolated agent.** The rewrite was reproduced by hand once; nothing re-runs
  it, because that needs the harness rather than a fixture. So the **premise** is measured and the
  **regression** is not — if the harness stops rewriting the value, or starts rewriting a different
  one, nothing here notices. Stated rather than left for the round.
- **Nothing restores the value automatically.** Both the shared file and Step 2b name the restore;
  neither performs it. An automatic restore would be a write to shared config from inside a review
  step, which is the class of action this phase is complaining about.
- **The four leaked worktrees on this checkout were not removed.** They are reported, not reaped.
  Three carry pre-squash commits, which is what correctly-merged work looks like after a squash, and
  deciding which are safe to delete is not this phase's business.
- **`extensions.worktreeConfig` was not written into the remedy.** It is suggested inside the
  upstream issue that was closed as not-planned, and `Q-049` explicitly records it as unverified.
  Adopting an unmeasured workaround to fix a measured bug is how the next entry gets filed.

## Phase 241 — the `/review-close` cluster (`Q-326` + `Q-327` + `Q-328` + `Q-329`)

Four § High filings, all against one skill, all filed 2026-08-28 by the Phase-240 inbound-issue
triage pass, none of them routed to a track. Four wrong durable states: a merge that should not
happen, a task marked done that isn't, a convention gate that does not run, and a silent false
close. `Q-330` (the `sysop-update.sh --dry-run` false refusal) was deliberately left out — it is
`install.sh`, a different file and a different failure surface, and its own entry routes it to
whichever phase next opens the installer.

**All four filings verified against the shipped tree before anything was built**, because this
repo's record has a ratified prescription refused by execution four phases running. All four held.
The line numbers in every one of them had drifted — Phase 240 edited Step 2b above them — which is
what the entries themselves warned would happen, so every anchor here is a string.

### `Q-329` — the batch-set reader that could not run

Step 4b derived its batch set through `bash sysop/scripts/review_index.py --list`. Measured by
execution rather than by `bash -n`, because the run is the evidence: **exit 2, zero bytes on
stdout**. Bash lexes the module's docstring as one quoted word; nothing is written, nothing is
destroyed, and the command names no batch. Step 4b's empty-arm predicate is written in terms of
what the command *named*, not what it *returned*, so a **failed measurement is byte-for-byte
indistinguishable from a measured-empty set** — and on a cycle carrying a `Pending` batch the step
reports `4b: no review batches this cycle` over it, leaving the batch open, its boxes unticked and
its lock in place, while the close reports success.

It was the only `bash <x>.py` in the entire shipped tree, and the seeded rule is `python3`, so the
prescribed spelling also bound nothing.

The fix is the one word, plus the half the filing left open: the empty arm now reads the **exit
code**. Verified by execution on a fixture built from `WORKFLOW.md` § 4.2's own format — `--list`
exits **0** on a genuinely empty tracker and **1** when the tracker is absent — so the exit code is
a real discriminator and non-zero is a could-not-measure that stops.

**The orphan-rule list and the broken command word were one defect seen from two ends.**
`test_permission_surface_drift.py` carried `Bash(python3 sysop/scripts/review_index.py:*)` on its
`SEEDED_WITHOUT_SKILL_MENTION` list with a Phase-220 justification saying no skill step invokes it.
That was true when written and had since become false — Step 4b invokes it, just unrunnably. The
list entry was the half that looked healthy. Retired, and the guard reddened correctly the moment
the skill started naming the rule, which is the guard doing its job.

### `Q-326` — the merge that runs on an unmeasured check surface

Step 4d's command 4 annotation *names* the zero-checks state and routes it onward. Command 5's
`gh pr view --json state,mergeStateStatus` is labelled *"confirm mergeability"* and **no arm reads
its output**; the `gh pr merge --squash` on the very next line is unconditional. Step 4d-1's
enumeration of causes runs *after* the merge, so it classifies a merge that already happened.
Green and red and no could-not-measure — the one shape this repo's whole gate discipline exists to
forbid. Three exhaustive greps over `core/` confirmed the negatives: `no checks reported` 0,
`total_count` 0, `check-runs` 0.

New command 4b counts check runs on the PR head before the merge. **Verified live against GitHub
rather than assumed** (source-verification): `{owner}`/`{repo}` placeholders are real `gh api`
features, and the endpoint returned `1` on PR #518's head — the commit that ran `pytest` — and `0`
on `main`'s squash tip, which is also why the probe reads `headRefOid` and not `HEAD`. A `0` is
could-not-measure and halts.

**There is deliberately no polling loop, and the file says why**, so the next reader does not
"fix" it into one: `sleep` is in no seeded rule and not in the harness's documented read-only set,
a loop around a runtime condition binds nothing, and re-invoking command 4's `--watch` returns
*immediately* with zero checks registered — which is the defect. The wait is the operator's, and
it is one re-run of one bare command.

The reporter's own correction is the part that makes this ordinary rather than exotic: they first
blamed an Actions outage and a spend limit, and both were wrong. The cause was **registration
latency** — `total_count: 0` held for ~30 minutes across `opened` and a first `synchronize`, then
registered on a second and all passed. This fires on ordinary days.

### `Q-327` — a task marked done whose human step never happened

Step 4c's `tasks/index.yml` round-trip never read `user_action` — Sysop's own schema field, which
`validate_tasks.py` requires as a bool on every `open`/`in_progress` task. Zero occurrences in Step
4c's whole span. Step 3c is not a backstop: it deliberately excludes `## User ops` from its phrase
set, and its waive outcome does not halt, so a waived smoke and a passed smoke are indistinguishable
to the round-trip. `tasks/schema.md` § *User ops* had already conceded the gap in prose. The
consumer measured three tasks in two days reaching `done` with the production effect unshipped.

**The filed remedy was built, and it was wrong — this phase's own author-side pass caught it.**
Rule 2 (re-read your own new prose against the code it describes) tested a sentence I had just
written, that a held task "stays claimable". It does not: it stays `in_progress`, which is off the
frontier. Pulling that thread found the real defect. Step 4c's step 6 deletes the pending-docs *this step
consolidated*; a routed doc is consolidated; and **the pending-doc is the only carrier of
`roadmap_ids` into this round-trip**. So the narrow remedy — route the docs, hold only the three
completion mutations — deletes the carrier. The task sits `in_progress` with its lock held and its
body under `open/`, and nothing can ever close it: `clear_user_action.py` flips the flag and prints,
in its own output, that an `in_progress` task stays off the frontier. **A silent permanent stall,
arriving from a fix for a silent false close.**

So the hold moved up. New Step **1c** holds the **whole pending-doc** back at 1b's filter point,
before any routing, reusing the held-back path 1b already has — no new machinery, no duplicated
`CHANGELOG` entry, and the doc survives to close the task on a later run through the ordinary path.
The heredoc arm stays as **defence in depth** and is labelled as such, because `ids` is a
hand-substituted literal that can be pasted from a previous run.

Two costs, both written into the file rather than discovered later. A held task's documentation
**lags its merge**, visibly, in `Held-back docs:` on every run until the human step is done — the
honest ordering, since those files say a task is *Complete*. And granularity is the **whole doc**:
a doc naming a held and an unheld task holds both, because splitting it means routing half a doc
and re-routing the rest later, which is the duplication the ordering exists to avoid.

Rule 4's hostile corpus produced the last decision. Across seven values, the predicate is
truthiness-based: a malformed string value **holds**. That is wrong-looking and it is the safe
direction — holding a task that should have closed costs one `clear_user_action.py`; closing one
that should have held is the defect. The obvious tightening to an identity test would make a string
`"true"` **close** a task whose human step is outstanding, inverting the bias on exactly the
malformed input the strictness was for. Recorded in the file and pinned by a parametrized test, so
nobody tightens it later.

### `Q-328` — the convention gate that read one section of three

Step 2b's doc-only skip fired when the diff touched no code files **and** `## Prevention
Conventions` held no governing rule. The escape was sealed inside the same section. Two things
were wrong with that, and the corroboration is Sysop-internal, which is what makes it general
rather than a consumer quirk. `WORKFLOW.md` § 6.1's required-sections table lists **`## Testing
Patterns` as its own top-level section**, beside `## Prevention Conventions` and not inside it —
while `review-close/SKILL.md` offered "Testing Patterns" as an example *subsection of* it. The
skill contradicted the template it ships, and the predicate rode the contradiction. And the
predicate was **map-blind**: the convention map is the one artifact that routes globs to
conventions, which is precisely the question being asked, and it was consulted nowhere.

Widened to three sources, with the escape widened to match, and the false subsection example
corrected. Step 2d's cross-reference to this predicate was updated in the same pass — it described
the old one-section shape.

**One thing was deliberately filed rather than built.** If `## Testing Patterns` is genuinely a
sibling section, then step 1's *paste* — which sends the reviewer `## Prevention Conventions` only
— also under-reads, and reviewers never see testing conventions. That is a larger behavioural
change than the filing names, it moves what every 2b reviewer receives, and self-initiated scope
additions are the highest-risk part of any change. Filed as `Q-342`; not built here.

### The author-side pass, and what it cost

**The battery ran five times.** Not in pursuit of a zero — the shared file is explicit that an
author's zero measures self-consistency and exhaustion is the reviewers' measurement — but because
three of the runs found defects in the guards rather than in the tree, and one found a defect in
the battery itself.

Run 1: **20/26 killed, 6 survivors, 2 ANCHOR-STALE, 0 false kills.** The stale pair is the finding
the brief warned about — two rows written with line breaks the file does not contain, which **did
not run at all** while the report read as a fraction. A battery that under-reports looks exactly
like a battery that passes.

**Three of the six survivors were the same class, `Q-340`, three separate times: a guard asserting
a token that survives next door.**

- `.venv/bin/python3 sysop/scripts/review_index.py` **contains** `python3 sysop/scripts/…`, so the
  command-word check passed over a spelling that binds no allow-rule.
- An incidental `exit \`0\`` three sentences later satisfied the exit-code regex while the sentence
  that makes the exit code a discriminator had been deleted.
- `HELD_USER_ACTION` appears twice in the Step 8 fence, so gutting the `Remaining:` bullet left the
  token alive in the accounting row.

A fourth appeared on run 2 and a fifth on run 4: the three-source check sliced far enough to sweep
in the note that follows, which names `## Testing Patterns` for a different purpose; and `stranded`
occurs in the paragraph above the sentence a mutation deleted. **Five instances of one class in one
phase.** The lesson is narrower than "scope your assertions": every one was a check written against
a *token* where a *sentence* or a *position* was the real subject.

`P01` was not a guard hole at all — it deleted a lead-in sentence and left the numbered list doing
the work, a **no-op wearing a reversion's label**, which reads as a guard hole when the weak thing
is the mutation. Re-pointed to excise the whole widening.

The author-side arc finished at **50/50 killed, 0 survivors, 0 false kills, 4 negative controls
clean**, across eight runs — and **the round then showed what that number is worth.**

### The round, and the number the author's battery could not produce

Three lenses, isolated worktrees, one round. **Every one of them found its sharpest finding alone**,
and two of the three findings that mattered most were in work this phase had already declared done.

**The guards lens wrote its own battery: 40 mutations, 9 killed, 31 survived — 78% — against the
author's 50/50, plus 3 false kills of 18 controls.** That is the fifty-third consecutive
falsification of an all-killed author battery in this ledger's window, and the widest gap yet. It is
also the single most useful thing this phase produced, so the specifics are worth the space:

- **The guard docstring'd *"the class, not the instance"* killed 0 of 7** — including an unindented
  positive control planted in a plain ` ```bash ` fence. Three independent causes. Its fence
  extractor matched only *empty or shell* info strings, so every ` ```yaml `/` ```json ` fence
  desynchronised the pairing and it read **the prose between fences as code**: 46 regions and
  118,448 characters against a correct pairing's 47 and 94,095 — 25% more text, and **the command
  this phase itself added was outside its window.** Its `^` anchor was defeated by one leading
  space (47% of the lines it did read were unreachable). And its population skipped `install.sh`,
  `scripts/`, the extensionless git-hooks and every `.py` — *"one such guard excluded the
  installer"* is a sentence in the shared file, and the guard written after reading it did the same
  thing. Rewritten: correct pairing, whitespace-tolerant anchor, 153-file population, plus a
  vacuity control that plants positive probes at four real command sites.
- **The executed column's fixture was incomplete.** `for tid in closed:` widened to `closed + held`
  drops a held task's lock, its **parked marker** — plan and verdict, never committed, therefore
  unrecoverable — and its claim artifacts. The fixture created none of those directories, so the
  column this phase rated strongest was blind to the one mutation that causes data loss. Fixed, with
  a negative control proving an ordinary close still cleans up.
- **Three false kills, all on this phase's own verbatim pins**: `__do not skip__` rejected for
  `**do not skip**`, `by hand` for `by HAND`, `STOP — do not run` for `STOP. Do not run`. Pinning
  prose to close a polarity instance makes the guard reject ordinary copy edits, which is how a
  pinned guard gets weakened later by someone who is not wrong to be annoyed. All three relaxed.

The claims lens and the execute lens each independently reproduced the author's battery exactly and
neither wrote its own — which is precisely the argument for keeping the guards lens in the default
two.

**The polarity class got its fourth measurement, and this phase is the strongest evidence yet.**
The author pinned two directives verbatim (`P04`, `P05`); the guards lens then inverted **eight
more** while keeping every token the guards require — `**STOP** … do not take the empty arm` →
`continue`; `resolves **against** merging` → `**in favour of**`; Step 1c's `If **any**` → `If
**all**`; `user_action: **true**` → `**false**`. Four measurements, four phases, four subjects, all
agreeing: `Q-318` 76–81%, Phase 179 **0 of 21**, `Q-325` 26 of 46, this one **31 of 40**. Filed as
`Q-343`, with the two things Phase 241 adds — the **cost** of pinning (3 false kills of 18 controls)
and the eight-instance token-next-door class beside it.

**Six directives are pinned anyway, on a stated rule: only those that flip a gate into producing a
wrong durable state.** The rest are deliberately left, because pinning the class is exactly what the
three prior measurements refuted. **Pinning closes the instance, not the class.**

**The contrast inside this phase is the cleanest data point available for `Q-325`'s candidate.** The
`E*` rows RUN the shipped heredoc against fixtures differing in one field and read durable state off
disk: **8 of 8 killed**, and the guards lens's own attempt on that column was killed too. The prose
column was walked at 78%. Same phase, same author, same afternoon — the difference is whether the
oracle is a string or a file on disk.

### Numbers, and where they were measured

- Suite: measured at the phase's final commit, **after** the record — stated that way because an
  earlier draft of this line cited a pre-record commit, and the record itself then turned the suite
  red in two places (the missing ledger row and a `NEXT_SESSION_PROMPT.md` still briefing 241). Both
  are close-out steps, not defects, and both are done.
- Test delta: **+45**, derived by diffing per-file collection counts against `main`, not from the

- Author battery: **50/50** after eight runs, 7 of 50 declared reverts (14%), 4 controls, 0 false

- Round: **3 lenses × 1 round**, the governor's behaviour-plus-numeric-record condition. Findings:

### What this phase did NOT do

- **`Q-330`.** The installer's `--dry-run` false refusal. Different file, and its own entry routes

## Phase 242 — the gate that judged the checker's age (`Q-330`)

`Q-330`, filed 2026-08-28 by the Phase-240 inbound triage pass from a consumer report.
`sysop-update.sh --dry-run` told the consumer their model-role override *"would NOT be
applied; skills would stay at Sysop's shipped defaults"* on an install whose mapping was
fine. The documented reaction to that message is to abort the update; the reporter
proceeded only because an agent read ~5,000 lines of installer.

**Routing.** This phase was chosen from an open slot — Track D is closed, the mirror push
is done, and `A2-announce` remains deferred by Wade's 2026-08-22 call, which was
re-confirmed at this phase's open rather than assumed. The § High bundle the next-session
brief proposed was **cut to one member on Wade's call**: `Q-308` and `Q-317` were both
already routed to E1 and both say in their own text that they need a different instrument,
not a narrowing, so bundling them would have put two undesigned design questions and three
unrelated subsystems in one phase.

### The filing was right, and the reproduction came first

A pre-Phase-223 consumer built from a source worktree at `34c5ead~1` (the commit before
`--managed-only` existed), installed, committed clean, then updated from `HEAD`. The
preview said `would REFUSE` with an argparse usage dump; the real apply on the same tree,
minutes later, said `APPLIED: 0 pin(s) across 0 file(s) resolved`. All four line numbers
the filing cited were exact.

The mechanism is that `--dry-run` copies nothing, so the target's vendor dir still holds
the checker from the consumer's **last** install. Handing it `--managed-only` — a flag
Phase 223 added — makes argparse exit 2, and the arm captured no exit code
(`! _dry_chk="$(…)"`), so every non-zero became a refusal. The bias is the worst available:
it fabricates *"your deliberate pins will silently revert"* on exactly the installs
furthest behind, which are the ones most worth updating.

### Two independent causes, so two independent fixes

1. **The two arms judge with the copy that matters to each** — the preview with the SOURCE
   checker (the vendored one can predate the flags `install.sh` passes it, which is `Q-330`),
   the apply with the VENDORED one (it is the copy that runs beside the executor). The
   version-skew class closes *for the checker* rather than for the `--managed-only`
   instance; any future flag change would otherwise mint this bug again.

   **This is the second formulation. The first said both arms take the source copy and that
   preview and apply therefore agree "by construction", and both halves were wrong** — see
   § *What the round found*. Two lenses independently reproduced preview/apply disagreements
   that have nothing to do with the checker, because the gate has four inputs and this fix
   aligns one of them. The honest claim is narrow: **the checker no longer skews.**

2. **A checker that could not parse its own invocation is never read as a verdict**, in
   either arm — a capability probe classifies that as its own outcome (rc 3) instead of
   letting argparse's exit 2 masquerade as the checker's own exit 2.

**The filing called the second one latent. It is reachable, and running it is what showed
that — though "not latent" overstates it, and the round said so.**
A consumer-modified `check_skill_models.py` is *preserved* by the Phase 24b divergence
guard, so `install_companion_scripts` leaves the stale copy in place and the apply arm
printed `REFUSED (unreadable config)` — the arm written specifically to stop conflating
causes, conflating them. I met this by accident: my first aging method edited the target's
checker, which tripped preservation, and the apply then refused where the filing said it
would not. The accident was the finding.

**A third defect, unfiled, in the same function.** With no PyYAML interpreter the apply arm
warns that the override will not be applied, while the preview fell through to the benign
*"no-op under default mapping"*. Same preview-disagrees-with-apply class as `Q-330`,
pointing the other way, four lines below it. Fixed here rather than filed.

**The direction this must not be fixed in.** Phase 223 added the dry-run gate to close the
mirror-image *false negative*. Both directions stay closed, and both ends are held by tests.

### A shipped guard was pinning the defect

`tests/test_phase223_derivations.py::test_the_installer_validates_the_mapping_before_applying_it`
asserted the resolved checker path equals `$TARGET/sysop/scripts/check_skill_models.py` —
the vendored copy. That is the defect, not the contract, so **the fix arrived red because a
guard required the broken path**. Rewritten to the property it was always defending (the
gate resolves a real checker, invokes it, and precedes `--apply`) and strengthened with the
ordering `Q-330` turns on: source preferred over vendored, both candidates existence-tested.
Replaced rather than deleted — Phase 204's lesson about a guard a phase removes.

Two other suite failures were mine and both were classes this repo has named. **Pass 5b**
reddened on `upstream #513` written into `install.sh`; the next-session brief had warned
about exactly this, citing Phase 241 writing "PR #518" into skill prose. And the diff's
insertion shifted `install.sh:3212` to `:3325`, breaking a registered citation in
`cleanup_worktrees.sh` — fixed at both the citation and the registry.

### The first battery measured the fixtures, not the fix

**8 of 19 killed, 11 survivors.** The survivors were not scattered: eight of them
(`P01`–`P05`, `D02`, `A01`, `A02`) attacked the capability probe and the two rc-3 arms —
a region **no fixture could reach**, because every fixture aged the *vendored* checker and
after the structural fix nothing reachable reads it. The second half of the fix had no
coverage at all, and the battery is the only reason I know that.

The remedy was a stale **source** tree fixture: `install.sh` plus `core/` and `packs/`, about
4 MB. **The first draft of this paragraph said `install.sh` "reads only `core/` and `packs/`
from `$REPO_ROOT` — verified by grep rather than assumed", and that is false** — it also
reads `$REPO_ROOT/.git` at a dozen sites (the lock's `sysop_commit`, divergence detection's
temp worktree, `--ref`). The claim was self-refuting in its own next sentence, which is the
tell: the fixture's first cut failed on Phase 125's no-anchor `--update` fail-closed
*because a copied tree is not a git repo*. That failure IS `install.sh` reading
`$REPO_ROOT/.git`. The fixture git-initialises now. **A grep narrower than the claim it is
cited for is not verification.**

Three more defects the battery found **in guards written this phase**:

- **`D04` is `Q-340`'s class, minted fresh.** The PyYAML test asserted `"PyYAML" in stdout`
  — and *both* branches of the polarity it meant to pin say "PyYAML", so inverting the

- **`D05`** — the dry-run's rc-2 path was never exercised; the tests only ever supplied an

- **`C05` survived because the battery's own verifier population was wrong.** It omitted
  `tests/test_phase223_derivations.py`, the module carrying the structural guard this phase

  in the instrument, not in the guards.

**Second run: 18 of 19, 4 of 4 controls green, 0 false kills.** The last survivor (`P03` — a
probe matching a bare `managed` rather than the exact flag) was closable in kind rather than
merely unattempted, so it was closed: the fixture now plants the word in a *different*

collect argparse's exit 2 as a verdict. **Final: 19 of 19 killed, 4 of 4 controls green, 0
false kills.**

The number moved 8 → 19 without the fix changing at all. That gap is the phase's real
product: it is the brief's own *"an executed column is only as good as what its fixture
contains"*, reproduced on my own work.

### What the round found — three lenses, and it reversed the phase's central claim

Three fresh-context reviewers in throwaway clones pinned at `97aed4a` (*does it execute* /
*are the guards real* / *are the claims true*), three on the governor's behaviour-plus-
numeric-record condition. Config baseline captured before the first spawn; no reviewer
mutated the shared tree.

**The headline: the phase had introduced a defect worse than the one it fixed.** Lens 1
built a state I had not — a consumer whose vendored `_model_roles.py` resolves every role
to `best` — and measured, same fixture both ways: **`main` refused and left every pin at
`opus`; this phase's first cut applied `model: best` across 21 files with a green install
and no refusal.** `best` is rejected by the Agent tool's `model` enum at spawn time, which
is verbatim the failure the gate exists to prevent. The cause is that the checker is only
the **judge**; `resolve_skill_models.py` + `_model_roles.py` are the **executor**, and on the
apply path the executor is always the vendored copy — all three inside the Phase 24b
preserve scope this phase's own record leaned on. Sending both arms to the source stack
decoupled them. Fixed by giving the chooser an explicit mode: apply judges vendored,
preview judges source, an unrecognised mode returns 1 rather than defaulting. **This is what
made fix #2 load-bearing rather than defensive** — a stale preserved checker on the apply
path is now rc 3 ("applying UNVALIDATED"), not a false refusal.

**"Preview and apply agree by construction" was false, and two lenses falsified it
independently.** The gate has four inputs; the fix aligned one. `--config` and `--root` are
still pre-update in the preview and post-update in the apply, and both lenses reproduced
disagreements from that — a fabricated refusal when the source adds a model to `served:`
(Q-330's own symptom, on the flow Phase 95 created), Phase 223's original false negative
when the source sunsets one, and an empty-population refusal on a partial install. Lens 2's
`S01`/`S02` mutations — repointing `--config` and `--root` at the source — **both survived**:
nothing in the suite observes which config or skills tree the gate reads. Filed, not fixed;
the claim is corrected above and the agreement test is scoped to where agreement holds.

**Lens 2 wrote its own battery and scored the guards far below my 20/20: 41 mutations, 17
real survivors, and 3 of 11 controls falsely reddened.** The pattern this project has
measured since Phase 169 — an all-killed author battery, an independent one finding tens of
survivors — reproduced exactly. What it caught in guards written *this phase*:

- **My ordering assertion was a tautology.** `_checker="$(…)"` is a substring of
  `_dry_checker="$(…)"`, so `body.index` bound to the dry-run arm; the apply-arm gate could
  be moved *after* `--apply` with the test green. **Lens 2 and lens 3 found it separately,
  both by executing the move rather than reading the assertion.** Now anchored on the line.
- **The record's claim that the rewrite "preserved Phase 223's original property" was
  false.** The original followed the wiring (`local {var}="…"`); mine asserted path literals
  in textual order — which a reviewer defeated by inverting the real preference while
  keeping the literals ordered, and which three legal reformats falsely reddened. Both
  assertions now follow the wiring.
- **`Q-340`'s class, twice more, in code guards.** The rc-3 arm emits `UNVALIDATED` from a
  `note` *and* a `record`; asserting the bare token was satisfied by either alone, so each
  could be deleted separately. Both sites are now asserted.
- **The message payload had no guard at all.** `check_skill_models.py` writes its exit-1
  `FAIL:` block to stdout but every exit-2 diagnostic to **stderr**, so dropping `2>&1`
  leaves the headline with an empty body — and the entire module stayed green, because every
  assertion read the note and none read what the note was introducing.
- **Nothing anywhere asserted that `--dry-run` writes nothing.** Deleting the dry-run
  block's `return 0` lets the preview rewrite 30 pins in the consumer's tree, and that
  survived 297 tests across twelve install modules. A whole-tree git assertion now covers it.
- **A live defect the phase introduced:** the capability probe ran `--help` without
  `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1`, so every install wrote `__pycache__` into the Sysop *source*
  clone — Phase 212's discipline broken one directory over, new because nothing ran the
  source checker before.
- **The rc-3 wording blamed Sysop** ("this is a Sysop-side problem, not your mapping") for
  what the chooser may well have taken from the consumer's own preserved copy. Reworded to
  disclaim the mapping without asserting fault.

**Lens 3 found the record in worse shape than the code, and its sharpest finding is about a
correction this phase was explicitly asked to make.** The `Q-322` amendment was wrong in all
three of its claims — no third copy exists, the four "out-of-span" duplicates are phantoms,
and the `66`/`63` it declared non-reproducing reproduce exactly. All of it from one defect:
re-deriving with `grep -oE '^## Phase [0-9]+[a-z]?'`, which under `-o` extracts `## Phase 185`
from both the phase heading and its `'s adversarial round` sibling. **The entry already
carried an `AMENDED` and a `RE-AMENDED` note that had derived the right numbers and named
that exact mechanism** — and the paragraph was written after reading the entry through
`cut -c1-1200`, which showed the original filing and hid both. Retracted in full, with the
failure kept in the entry. The `Q-340` recurrence note was also inflated: the entry says
**four** instances and "nothing prevents the fifth"; this is the fifth, and the draft said
"ninth" by trusting a figure in `tools/NEXT_SESSION_PROMPT.md` over the entry — the exact
failure that page's own header warns about.

**Verified and left standing by the round:** the `Q-330` fix itself (reproduced broken on
`main`, fixed at HEAD), the "not latent" mechanism, `Q-344`, the `C05` instrument-defect
account, all four of the filing's line numbers, the Phase 241 backfill hash, and the battery
